candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants from Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric Utility Steam Generating Units (EGUs)

criteria.criterion: If the unit is an oil-fired electric utility steam generating unit as defined (i.e., a fossil fuel-fired unit >25 MWe that serves a generator producing electricity for sale and that burned oil above the percentage thresholds in the definition), then the unit is subject to this subpart.

If an affected coal-fired, liquid oil-fired, or solid oil-derived fuel-fired EGU is in a period that meets the definition of 'startup' in 40 CFR 63.10042(1), then the applicable emission limits do not apply during that period and the startup work practice standards in Table 3 apply.

If you elect to rely on paragraph (2) of the 'startup' definition (only allowed before January 2, 2025), and the firing is for the purpose of initiating operation to produce electricity or useful thermal energy (including on-site steam), then that operation is a 'startup' period that begins on first firing for those purposes and ends 4 hours after generating electricity sold/used or 4 hours after making useful thermal energy, and during that startup period emission limits do not apply while the Table 3 work practices apply.

If the boiler is fired after a shutdown for the sole purpose of producing useful thermal energy for on-site use (for example auxiliary steam to heat fuel tanks), then under the paragraph (1) startup definition that firing is a 'startup' event but startup ends when the steam is used for any purpose (including on-site use), so the period qualifying as 'startup' is limited accordingly.

If the unit does not meet the definition of an EGU subject to this subpart (e.g., it does not serve a generator that produces electricity for sale or it fails the oil-fired EGU fuel-share criteria), then the unit is not subject to this subpart.

checklist: Confirm the boiler is an 'electric utility steam generating unit (EGU)' that serves a generator producing electricity for sale and has >25 MWe capability.
Determine whether the unit qualifies as an 'oil-fired EGU' by calculating oil heat input share (average annual oil heat input over the last 3 years and any single year) per the definition.
Verify whether the fuels fired are residual oil (and whether the unit is liquid oil-fired vs limited-use liquid oil-fired) and whether residual oil is combusted during the events in question.
For the auxiliary-steam-only firing, document whether the firing occurs after a shutdown event (i.e., was the unit in shutdown immediately prior to the firing).
Document the purpose of the firing (is it to produce electricity, or to produce useful thermal energy/steam for on-site use such as heating fuel tanks?).

If relying on the alternative startup definition in paragraph (2), confirm the calendar/date limitation (that paragraph (2) is only allowed before January 2, 2025) and whether you are electing to use it.

Establish and retain records showing the time/date fuel firing began, when clean fuel (if used for startup) began/ended, quantity/heat input per hour during the event, and gross output per hour as required for startup reporting if relying on paragraph (2).

Check whether the unit is subject to Table 3 work practices during startup/shutdown and ensure required monitoring systems, data collection, and tune-up/work-practice procedures are in place per the subpart.
Verify whether the unit has any status (e.g., converted to natural gas or biomass, or limited-use oil-fired) that would remove or change applicability under §63.10000 or §63.9983.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The answer explicitly cites the 63.10042 startup definition and includes a criterion stating that startup ends when steam is generated for any purpose (including auxiliary steam), which matches the EPA note that producing auxiliary steam is not part of startup."}

candidates.title: Utility mercury and air toxics standards (EGU MACT) — Subpart UUUUU

criteria.criterion: If the unit meets the definition of an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) — i.e., a fossil fuel-fired combustion unit capable of producing more than 25 MWe that serves a generator producing electricity for sale (or, for cogeneration, meets the distribution tests) — then it is potentially subject to Subpart UUUUU.

If the unit is an oil-fired EGU (i.e., it burns oil for more than 10.0 percent of the average annual heat input during the 3 previous calendar years after the compliance date or for more than 15.0 percent of the annual heat input during any one of those calendar years), then it falls within the oil-fired subcategories of Subpart UUUUU.

If the unit's annual capacity factor for oil (total annual heat input from oil divided by maximum hourly heat input × 8,760, computed over the required averaging period) is less than 8 percent averaged over the specified 24-month block commencing on the first month after the compliance date, then the unit qualifies as a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU and is not subject to the numeric emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 but must comply with the tune-up work practice requirements in Table 3.

If the unit does not meet the definition of an EGU subject to this subpart (for example, it qualifies as a natural gas-fired EGU under the subpart definitions or it has the capability of combusting >25 MW of coal or oil but did not fire sufficient coal or oil to meet the oil-/coal-fired thresholds), then the unit is not subject to Subpart UUUUU.

candidates.title: Boiler MACT — Subpart DDDDD (Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters)

criteria.criterion: If the unit is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) covered by Subpart UUUUU, then it is not subject to Subpart DDDDD.

If a unit is in the limited-use boilers and process heaters subcategory, then it is not subject to the emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 (and Tables 11–15) of Subpart DDDDD and instead must complete a tune-up every 5 years as specified in § 63.7540.

checklist: Establish whether the unit is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU): confirm nameplate/net electrical capacity (MWe), whether it serves a generator that produces electricity for sale, and for cogeneration units whether it meets the >1/3 and >25 MWe distribution tests (see 40 CFR 63.10042).
Obtain the unit's maximum hourly heat input (nameplate or documented maximum hourly heat input, in MMBtu/hr).

Compile fuel use records (heat input by fuel) for the relevant periods: (a) the most recent 24-month contiguous block starting the first month after the compliance date (to compute the limited-use oil capacity factor), and (b) the three previous calendar years after the compliance date (to evaluate the oil-fired EGU >10%/15% thresholds) (see 40 CFR 63.10042 and 63.9990(b)).

Calculate the liquid-oil capacity factor per Subpart UUUUU: capacity factor = (total annual heat input from oil) ÷ (maximum hourly heat input × 8,760); compare the 24‑month averaged result to the 8% limited‑use threshold (see 40 CFR 63.10042).

Determine the percent of average annual heat input provided by oil over the previous 3 calendar years (or in any one calendar year) to test the oil-fired EGU thresholds (>10% average over 3 years or >15% in any one year) (see 40 CFR 63.10042).

Confirm fuel types actually burned (No. 2 = distillate; No. 4 = residual) and whether oil is used only for startup/shutdown or for regular operation (fuel used only for startup/ shutdown/transient flame stability may affect applicability and fuel-analysis requirements) (see 40 CFR 63.7521(c)).

Check whether the facility has a federally enforceable permit condition that limits the unit's annual capacity factor (e.g., ≤10%) or otherwise limits oil burning (relevant for limited-use designations under boiler rules and recordkeeping) and retain a copy per recordkeeping requirements (see 40 CFR 63.7555(a)(3)).

Confirm the facility's applicable compliance date (referenced for averaging periods and definitions) so you can determine the correct 24‑month block and the three previous calendar years used for applicability calculations (see 40 CFR 63.10042 and 63.9984 reference in the definitions).

If the unit produces electricity for sale, confirm the hours and amounts of electricity sold and any changes in operations over the lookback periods that could affect whether the unit is an EGU subject to Subpart UUUUU (see 40 CFR 63.10042 and 63.9983(f)).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Both key EPA reasons are reflected: the answer includes the oil‑fired EGU criterion under 40 CFR 63.10042 (oil is the primary fuel) and the limited‑use liquid oil‑fired criterion (the <8% oil capacity factor / limited‑use subcategory), with supporting checklist items to calculate oil share and capacity factor."}

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Coating Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations that (1) are located at or part of a major source of HAP, (2) manufacture coatings as defined in §63.8105, (3) process, use, or produce HAP, and (4) are not part of an affected source under another subpart, then the operations are subject to Subpart HHHHH.

If a material is produced by a process where a formulation component is synthesized by chemical reaction or separation activity and then transferred to another vessel where it is formulated (i.e., the component was synthesized or separated prior to the coating formulation), then that material is not a 'coating' for purposes of Subpart HHHHH and Subpart HHHHH would not apply to that process.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing Process Units (MCPU)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) that are located at or are part of a major source and the MCPU produces materials described in §63.2435(b) and processes, uses, or generates organic HAP or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP, and the MCPU is not an affected source under another subpart, then the operations are subject to Subpart FFFF.

If the filtering step is a 'unit operation' or other separation/purification activity (for example filtration equipment) that is part of the process used to produce the product, then that filtering is part of an MCPU (a process includes separation, recovery, purification, and unit operations) and Subpart FFFF requirements apply.

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Plastic Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you perform surface coating (application of coating to a substrate, including associated activities directly related to application) of plastic parts/products, you use 378 liters (100 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP, and the operation is at or part of a major source of HAP, then the surface coating operations are subject to Subpart PPPP.

If the filtering of the finished product is not an activity 'directly related to the application of the coating' (i.e., it is a downstream finishing or unrelated quality-control separation and not part of the coating application/associated activities), then that filtering would not be 'surface coating' under §63.4481(a)(1) and Subpart PPPP would not apply to the filtering operation.

candidates.title: Chemical Manufacturing Process (definitions for Subpart VVVVVV)

criteria.criterion: If your operation is a chemical manufacturing process (CMPU) as defined (i.e., all equipment that collectively functions to produce a product or isolated intermediate, including reaction, recovery, separation, purification, cleaning, and unit operations such as filtration), then the definitions and applicability tests in Subpart VVVVVV apply and you may be subject to that subpart.

checklist: Is the plant a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy total HAP)?

Does the operation 'manufacture coatings' as defined in 40 CFR 63.8105 (produced by blending, mixing, diluting, or otherwise formulated) or is any formulation component synthesized or separated prior to formulation (which would exclude it from the 'coating' definition)?

Is the final filtering step performed as part of the coating formulation/production (in a process vessel/unit operation) or is it a downstream quality-control finishing step not directly related to coating application?
Does the filtering step constitute a 'separation' or 'unit operation' (e.g., filtration equipment) that is integral to producing the product (per the MCPU/unit operation definitions)?

Is the surface coating activity (application to a substrate) occurring at the facility, or is the facility only producing/formulating a coating product (i.e., are you applying the coating or just manufacturing the coating material)?
If surface coating: do you use ≥378 L (100 gallons) per year of coatings that contain HAP (threshold in Subpart PPPP)?
What HAP are present in feedstocks, intermediates, and the finished product (identify concentrations and annual usage) to determine 'in organic HAP service' and group/status thresholds?
Is the filtering operation followed by transfer to another vessel for formulation/application (i.e., was a component synthesized/separated then transferred and later formulated)?
Are the operations (process vessels, storage tanks, transfer racks) assigned to or shared with an MCPU as defined in Subpart FFFF (check predominant use rules and assignment procedures)?

Is any portion of these operations already part of an affected source under another NESHAP subpart (e.g., surface coating NESHAPs for specific substrates) which would make that equipment exempt from the other subpart per the 'not part of an affected source under another subpart' tests?

Quantify uncontrolled emissions (or coating/HAP usage) from the filtering and associated vents to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 thresholds under Subpart FFFF (if treating as MCPU)—keep records needed to sum uncontrolled emissions or HAP consumption.
Document whether the filtering is performed in equipment meeting the 'process vessel' or 'process tank' definitions (≥250 gal process vessel for Subpart HHHHH; check vessel capacity and function).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Some key elements are present (the HHHHH criteria for coating manufacture and the §63.8105 formulation/synthesis exclusion are cited), but the answer fails to state the EPA's decisive points: that final filtering is not a “separation activity” under §63.8105 and therefore the operation remains coating manufacturing, and that Subpart FFFF expressly excludes coating manufacturing per §63.2435(b)(3). The candidate criteria even treat filtration as a possible MCPU separation, contradicting the EPA notes."}

candidates.title: Petroleum Refinery NESHAP (Subpart CC)

criteria.criterion: If a combustion device lacks an enclosed combustion chamber and uses an uncontrolled volume of ambient air to burn gases, then that device meets the definition of a flare and is subject to the flare requirements in this subpart.

If the combustion device is an enclosed combustion device (for example, an incinerator, boiler, or process heater with an enclosed combustion chamber), then it is not a flare (i.e., the device is an enclosed combustion device under the definitions) and the flare-specific monitoring requirements in §63.670 do not apply to that device.

If a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent uses a combustion device to comply and the control device is a flare, then the flare control and monitoring requirements in §63.670 (including pilot flame, visible emissions, flow/composition/temperature monitoring, and CPMS) apply to that control device.

If a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent uses an incinerator as the control device to meet the §63.643(a)(2) reduction criterion, then temperature monitoring with a continuous recorder (installed in the firebox or immediately downstream of the firebox) is required instead of flare pilot/composition monitoring.

If vapors from a gasoline loading rack are controlled by a combustion device, then determine whether the device meets the flare definition (per §63.641); if it does, the loading-rack control is treated as a flare and must meet the flare requirements in §63.670 on and after January 30, 2019.

If an emission stream is routed to a fuel gas system (and then to flares receiving fuel-gas system gas), then flares receiving gas from that fuel gas system are subject to §63.670 on and after January 30, 2019.

candidates.title: Gasoline Loading Racks (Subpart R) as referenced by Subpart CC

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator has a Group 1 gasoline loading rack located within a contiguous area and under common control with a petroleum refinery, then the loading rack is required to comply with subpart R and the listed CC provisions specified in §63.650(a).

If a flare is used as the control device for a gasoline loading rack, then on and after January 30, 2019 that flare must meet the requirements of §63.670 (i.e., it is treated as a flare under the refinery rules).

If vapors from the gasoline loading rack are routed to an enclosed vapor combustor that has an enclosed combustion chamber and does not burn using an uncontrolled volume of ambient air, then the device is not a flare for purposes of Subpart R/CC and the flare-specific requirements in §63.670 do not apply to that enclosed combustor.

checklist: Confirm whether the loading rack is a 'gasoline loading rack' (SIC 2911) and whether it meets the Group 1 criteria (e.g., gasoline throughput thresholds) per §63.641 and §63.650(a).
Confirm that the plant site is a petroleum refinery major source (per §63.640(a)(1)) and that the loading rack is part of the affected source (§63.640(c)).

Determine exactly where the loading-rack vapor stream is routed: (a) directly to the enclosed vapor combustor, (b) to a flare/header, or (c) to a fuel gas system that could feed a flare (see §63.640(d)(5) and §63.650(d)).

Characterize the combustion device: document whether it has an enclosed combustion chamber (enclosed chamber, stack, firebox) or instead is an open tip device that relies on uncontrolled ambient air (use the device design/spec drawings and operating descriptions).

Determine whether the device intentionally uses assist air/steam or has uncontrolled entrainment of ambient air at the tip (assist air/steam vs. uncontrolled ambient air is relevant to the flare definition) (§63.641 definitions).

If the combustor is enclosed, obtain the manufacturer's description/specification that it is an incinerator/boiler/process heater (enclosed combustion device) and note where temperature monitoring would be installed per §63.644(a)(1).

If the device may function as a flare (open tip), identify monitoring and control hardware locations: pilot(s), pilot monitoring, vent gas flow and composition measurement points, and whether CPMS/GC/composition monitoring would be required per §63.670 and §63.671.

Determine whether the vent stream meets the definition of a miscellaneous process vent and whether it is Group 1 (TOC/HAP concentration and emission thresholds) per §63.641 and §63.643—this affects whether the Group 1 control/monitoring rules apply.

Verify whether the vapors are ever routed to the fuel gas system (and from there to any flare) rather than directly to the combustor; if routed to the fuel gas system, flares receiving those fuel gas streams are subject to §63.670 after Jan 30, 2019 (§63.640(d)(5)).

Document whether the combustor is continuously manned/observed and whether its operation is routine or limited to maintenance/occasional events (maintenance vents may be treated differently per §63.643(c)).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The EPA Notes hinge on the device not meeting the 63.641 flare definition (so §§63.670/63.671 don’t apply) and that the combustor remains subject to Subpart CC testing/operating-parameter monitoring. Our Answer includes the enclosed-combustor vs. flare definition (§63.641), explicit criteria that enclosed combustors are not flares (and thus §63.670 doesn’t apply), and the alternative testing/monitoring requirements for enclosed combustors/incinerators ( §§63.643/63.644 and checklist items). These key reasons are therefore captured."}

candidates.title: Paper and Other Web Coating

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a major source of HAP and operates one or more web coating lines (a continuous substrate fed from an unwind/feed station to a rewind/cutting station where a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating is applied) then the facility is subject to Subpart JJJJ.

If an individual web coating line is covered by one of the listed exclusions (e.g., stand-alone equipment or product/packaging rotogravure or wide-web flexographic press under Subpart KK, web coating subject to Subpart EE, SSSS, or OOOO, lithography/screenprinting/letterpress/narrow-web flexographic printing, or is research/laboratory equipment as defined) then that web coating line is not part of the affected source under Subpart JJJJ.

If a web coating line coats both paper or another web substrate and another substrate type then the subpart applicability is determined by the predominant activity (predominant = 90 percent or more of the mass of substrate coated during the compliance period) and the owner/operator must demonstrate and document the predominant activity annually.

If all of the web coating lines at the affected source utilize only non-HAP coatings then the owner/operator may be exempt from the reporting requirements of this subpart provided a one-time report documenting use of only non-HAP coatings is submitted to the permitting authority.

candidates.title: Refractory Products Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a refractory products manufacturing facility (a plant site that manufactures refractory products as defined in §63.9824) and that plant site is a major source of HAP (≥9.07 megagrams (10 tons) of any single HAP per year or ≥22.68 megagrams (25 tons) combined HAP per year) then you are subject to Subpart SSSSS.

If the finished mica insulation product does not meet the definition of a 'refractory product' (nonmetallic materials containing less than 50 percent carbon by weight and used for structures or components exposed to environments above 538 °C (1000 °F)) then manufacture of that mica product would not make the facility a refractory products manufacturing facility for Subpart SSSSS.

If the refractory products manufactured either are resin-bonded, pitch-bonded, or otherwise 'refractory products that use organic HAP' (i.e., produced using a substance that is an organic HAP, releases an organic HAP during production, or contains an organic HAP) then those products fall within the Subpart SSSSS definition that addresses refractory products using organic HAP.
citations: 40 CFR 63.9824 (refractory products that use organic HAP)

checklist: Determine whether each coating operation meets the 'web coating line' definition: is the substrate continuous/flexible and fed from an unwind/feed to rewind/cutting with a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating applied? (See 40 CFR 63.3310)
For the roll-fed line, confirm whether substrate is a 'web' (paper, film, foil) and whether coating is applied continuously across some or all of the width.
For the sheet-handled line, confirm whether the process is discontinuous (sheets) and therefore does not meet the 'web' definition.

Check whether any web coating line is already covered by another NESHAP (Subpart KK, EE, SSSS, OOOO, or printing exemptions) or is research/laboratory equipment (see 40 CFR 63.3300(a)-(g) and 63.3310).

If a line coats multiple substrate types, calculate the mass fraction of substrate types coated over a representative period (≥1 year or other reasonable period) to determine the predominant activity (90% threshold) and plan annual documentation (see 40 CFR 63.3300(h)).
Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP by calculating actual and/or potential to emit for single HAP (≥10 tons/yr) and total HAP (≥25 tons/yr) (see 40 CFR 63.9782(b)).

Assess whether the finished mica insulation product meets the 'refractory product' definition: nonmetallic, <50% carbon by weight, and intended for use in environments above 538 °C (1000 °F) or similar refractory applications (see 40 CFR 63.9824).

If the mica product uses binders, resins, pitch, or other organic HAP-containing materials, document formulations and amounts to determine whether the product is a 'refractory product that uses organic HAP' (see 40 CFR 63.9824).

Gather process details for refractory-manufacturing-like activities (crushing, mixing with binders/additives, forming, drying, firing/curing) to compare to the refractory products manufacturing facility description (see 40 CFR 63.9824 and 63.9782(a)).
If claiming any exemption (e.g., non-HAP coatings for Subpart JJJJ), prepare the one-time report and retain formulation records per the cited provisions (see 40 CFR 63.3300(j) and 63.3370(s)).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key reasons are represented: the roll-fed line is evaluated against the web-coating definition/exclusions (40 CFR 63.3300/63.3310) and the sheet line is treated as non-web, and the mica product is evaluated against the refractory-product definition in 40 CFR 63.9824 (showing it does not meet Subpart SSSSS coverage)."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Glycol Dehydration Units (Natural Gas Transmission and Storage NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a natural gas transmission and storage facility that is a major source and contains a glycol dehydration unit, then Subpart HHH applies to that glycol dehydration unit.

If a glycol dehydration unit process vent is required to be controlled under this subpart and the owner/operator connects the process vent to a control device through a closed-vent system, then the control device must meet the control device requirements in § 63.1281(d).

If a boiler or process heater is used as the enclosed combustion control device for the glycol dehydration unit process vent, then the vent stream must be introduced into the flame zone of the boiler or process heater and the device must meet the performance requirements in § 63.1281(d)(1)(i).

If an enclosed device uses controlled flame combustion and its primary purpose is transferring heat to a process fluid/material rather than steam generation, then it is a 'process heater'; if its primary purpose is recovering/exporting thermal energy as steam or hot water, then it is a 'boiler' for purposes of this subpart.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters (Boiler and Process Heater MACT)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater that is located at or is part of a major source of HAP, then Subpart DDDDD applies to that boiler or process heater unless excluded by § 63.7491.

If the boiler or process heater is part of an affected source that is subject to another subpart of this part (for example, if the unit is being used as a control device to comply with another subpart), then the boiler/process heater is not subject to Subpart DDDDD under the exclusions in § 63.7491(h).

If the boiler or process heater is used as a control device to comply with another subpart and at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years is provided by regulated gas streams that are subject to another standard, then the boiler/process heater is not subject to Subpart DDDDD under § 63.7491(i).
If the boiler or process heater falls into one of the specific categories listed in § 63.7491(a) through (n), then it is exempt from Subpart DDDDD.

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is a 'natural gas transmission and storage' facility and whether it is a major source of HAP (per 40 CFR 63.1270(a)/(b)).
Identify whether the unit in question is a glycol dehydration unit (confirm large vs small per definitions and thresholds in 40 CFR 63.1271 and flow/benzene criteria in 40 CFR 63.1282(a)).

Document how the glycol dehydration unit process vent is routed (to a flare, to the reboiler/flame zone, to a fuel gas line, or uncontrolled) and whether a closed-vent system is installed and operates with no detectable emissions (40 CFR 63.1281(c)).

Determine whether the reboiler is designed and operated primarily to generate steam/hot water (boiler) or to transfer heat to a process fluid/material (process heater) — i.e., establish the unit's 'primary purpose' (40 CFR 63.1271).

If the reboiler is claimed to be acting as the control device for the glycol vent, verify whether the glycol vent stream is introduced into the reboiler's flame zone (required by 40 CFR 63.1281(d)(1)(i)(D)).

Record the reboiler's design heat input capacity (MW) to check applicability/exemption thresholds in Subpart DDDDD and HHH (e.g., 44 MW thresholds referenced in 40 CFR 63.1282(d)(1)(ii)-(iii) and 63.1283(d)(2)).

Confirm the reboiler fuel(s): does it burn only field gas (natural gas) or hazardous waste/other fuels (relevant to Subpart DDDDD exceptions in 40 CFR 63.7491 and HHH control-device provisions in 40 CFR 63.1282).

If claiming an exemption from Subpart DDDDD because the unit is used as a control device for another subpart, calculate the fraction of average annual heat input over any 3 consecutive calendar years that is provided by regulated gas streams subject to another standard to evaluate the 50% test in 40 CFR 63.7491(i).

If the reboiler is a control device model tested under manufacturers' performance test provisions, assemble the model test documentation and ensure operating parameters (e.g., max inlet gas flowrate, pilot flame monitoring, visible emissions) are met per 40 CFR 63.1282(g)/(h).
If the reboiler is used as a control device, verify continuous monitoring, pilot flame presence, visible emissions testing, and records required by Subpart HHH (40 CFR 63.1283(d) and 63.1284(b)).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Some key reasons are captured (the answer addresses whether the reboiler is a process heater vs boiler, checks fuel not regulated by another subpart, and documents whether the exhaust/venting makes it a control device—all relevant to DDDDD applicability). However the EPA note that Subpart HHH’s scope is limited to the still vent and flash tank emissions (i.e., that the reboiler combustion chamber is outside HHH) is not explicitly stated in the criteria—so a key element of the EPA reasoning is missing."}

candidates.title: Area source standards for electric arc furnace steelmaking facilities

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking facility that is an area source of HAP emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.
If your facility meets the definition of an EAF steelmaking facility but the EAF is located at a steel foundry or is used to produce nonferrous metals, then this subpart does not apply to that EAF.
If your facility is a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), then this subpart does not apply.
If you are an area source subject to this subpart, then you must have or obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 40 CFR part 71.

candidates.title: Area source standards for iron and steel foundries

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an iron and steel foundry that is an area source of HAP emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.

If your facility melts scrap, ingot, and/or other forms of iron and/or steel and pours the resulting molten metal into molds to produce final or near-final shaped products for introduction into commerce, then it meets the definition of an 'iron and steel foundry' and is potentially subject to this subpart.
If your facility is a research and development facility or only produces non-commercial castings, then this subpart does not apply to those operations.

If your facility is an existing affected source, you must determine small vs large foundry status based on calendar year 2008 metal melt production (<=20,000 tons = small; >20,000 = large); if new, determine based on annual metal melt capacity at startup (<=10,000 tons = small; >10,000 = large).
If on or after January 2, 2008 your iron and steel foundry becomes a major source as defined in § 63.2, then you must meet the requirements of 40 CFR part 63, subpart EEEEE.

candidates.title: NESHAP for iron and steel foundries (subpart EEEEE)

criteria.criterion: If you are a new or existing iron and steel foundry (i.e., a facility that melts scrap/ingot/other iron or steel and pours molten metal into molds), then this subpart covers emissions from your metal melting furnaces, scrap preheaters, pouring areas/stations, automated cooling and shakeout lines, mold/core making lines, and fugitive emissions from foundry operations.
If your affected source is existing or new is determined by whether construction or reconstruction commenced before or on/after December 23, 2002, respectively.

If your facility meets the foundry definition in this subpart and you perform metal melting in electric arc or induction furnaces (or cupolas), then those metal melting furnaces are 'metal melting furnaces' covered by this subpart's definitions and requirements.

checklist: Do you operate an electric arc furnace (EAF) that produces molten steel? (Verify equipment meets the EAF definition.)

Does the facility melt scrap/ingot/other iron or steel and then pour the resulting molten metal into molds to produce final or near-final shaped products for sale? (Confirm whether pouring into molds occurs or whether you instead atomize the melt.)
Do you produce shot, grit, or powders by water atomization of molten metal rather than pouring into molds? (If yes, document the atomization process and whether any pouring into molds also occurs.)

Is the EAF physically and operationally part of a foundry whose primary activity is making castings, or is it a standalone EAF steelmaking facility separate from foundry operations? (Determine whether the EAF is 'at a steel foundry'.)
Is the facility an area source or a major source of HAPs? (Prepare an emissions inventory to determine area vs major source status per § 63.2.)

What are the dates of construction or reconstruction for the affected equipment/facility? (Compare to cutoff dates: EAF subpart new/existing date: 9/20/2007; foundry subpart new/existing date: 9/17/2007; subpart EEEEE new/existing date: 12/23/2002.)

If the facility is a foundry, what was the annual metal melt production for calendar year 2008 (for existing foundries) or what is the annual metal melt capacity at startup (for new foundries)? (Compare to small/large thresholds: existing <=20,000 tons = small; >20,000 = large; new <=10,000 tons = small; >10,000 = large.)
Is the facility a research and development operation or does it produce only non-commercial castings? (If so, check for R&D/non-commercial exemption.)
Does the EAF instead produce nonferrous metals? (If yes, EAF steelmaking subpart may not apply.)

If claiming applicability or non-applicability under a foundry provision, assemble records showing the process steps (melting, pouring, atomization), product descriptions, sales/commercial introduction of products, and process flow diagrams to document whether the 'foundry' definition is met.

If uncertain about area vs major status or classification (foundry vs EAF steelmaking), prepare emissions estimates, product/process descriptions, and construction dates to support an applicability determination and any required notifications or permits (e.g., 40 CFR part 70/71, notifications required by § 63.10890 and subpart YYYYY).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The EPA Notes hinge on the foundry definition in 40 CFR 63.10906 (requirement to pour molten metal into molds) and thus that without pouring the facility is not an iron & steel foundry and remains subject to the EAF steelmaking area source subpart (YYYYY). OUR ANSWER explicitly cites 63.10906, states the pouring-into-molds criterion, includes checklist questions about atomization vs pouring, and includes the EAF subpart criteria (including the exclusion if the EAF is at a foundry). (EPA’s additional mention of NSPS AAa is not in the Answer but the key definitional reasoning from the Notes is captured.)"}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers at Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler that is located at, or is part of, an area source of hazardous air pollutants (HAP), then the boiler is subject to this subpart except as provided in § 63.11195.

If a boiler meets the definition of a gas-fired boiler (burns gaseous fuels and burns liquid fuel only during periods of gas curtailment, supply interruption, startups, or for periodic testing/maintenance/operator training and such liquid-fuel testing/maintenance/training does not exceed a combined total of 48 hours during any calendar year), then the boiler is not subject to this subpart under the gas-fired boiler exemption.

If a boiler is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) as defined (a fossil fuel-fired combustion unit of more than 25 megawatts that serves a generator producing electricity for sale and meeting the fuel-fired fraction criteria), then the boiler is not subject to this subpart under the EGU exemption.

If the boiler is any of the types specifically listed in § 63.11195(a) through (k) (for example, boilers subject to another part, hazardous waste boilers covered by subpart EEE, R&D boilers, hot water heaters, temporary boilers, residential boilers, electric boilers, seasonal boilers, or other listed exemptions), then the boiler is not subject to this subpart.

checklist: Is the facility an area source of HAP (i.e., total potential-to-emit HAP below major source thresholds) located at the site of these boilers?
Are the three boilers classified as industrial, commercial, or institutional boilers under § 63.11237 (i.e., enclosed devices producing steam and/or hot water by controlled flame combustion)?

Do the boilers burn only gaseous fuels for normal operation and burn liquid fuel only during bona fide periods of gas curtailment/supply interruption, startups, or for periodic testing/maintenance/operator training, and is the combined annual liquid-fuel periodic testing/maintenance/training use ≤ 48 hours per calendar year?

Are the boilers designed, permitted, and equipped to combust liquid fuel routinely (i.e., not limited to emergency/curtailment/testing use) or have they been physically modified or permitted to burn liquid or solid fuels as regular fuels?

Are any of the boilers electric utility steam generating units (EGUs) as defined (serve a generator that produces electricity for sale and have nameplate capacity >25 MW and meet the fossil-fuel-fired fraction criteria)? If so, verify nameplate MW, whether electricity is sold, and fuel-fired heat-input fractions over the relevant years.

Do any of the § 63.11195 exemptions besides the gas-fired or EGU exemptions apply (e.g., boiler covered by another NESHAP, hazardous waste boiler covered by subpart EEE, hot water heater, temporary or residential boiler)?

Are there any federally enforceable limits (e.g., permit limits) that make a boiler a limited-use boiler (annual capacity factor ≤ 10%) or otherwise change subpart applicability? If yes, obtain the permit language and actual operating hours/fuel use.

Document historical fuel use: monthly and annual hours and quantities of natural gas and any liquid fuel burned (to demonstrate whether liquid fuel use is limited to the allowed curtailment/testing hours and to evaluate fuel fractions for EGU definition).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's notes say the boilers are exempt as gas-fired under 63.11195(e) if they meet the 63.11237 conditions (oil only during curtailment/supply interruption and limited testing hours) and that those conditions should be locked in by permit limits. OUR ANSWER explicitly includes the 63.11195(e)/63.11237 gas-fired exemption language (including the ≤48 hours testing limit and curtailment/supply-interruption restriction) and the checklist asks for permit limits and documentation of fuel use. All key reasons from the EPA notes are captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Plywood and Composite Wood Products (PCWP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plywood and/or composite wood products (PCWP) manufacturing facility located at a major source of HAP, then this subpart applies to the affected source at that facility.

If the unit(s) in question are part of the affected source defined as the collection of dryers, refiners, blenders, formers, presses, board coolers, and other process units associated with PCWP manufacturing (including any combustion unit exhaust stream routinely used to direct fire process unit(s)), then those units are included within the affected source covered by this subpart.

If a combustion unit is used to directly-fire a PCWP dryer or lumber kiln, then the work practice requirements (including annual combustion unit tune-ups and bypass stack monitoring) in this subpart apply to that combustion unit.

If you have a process unit bypass stack that allows a process unit exhaust stream to temporarily vent to the atmosphere while bypassing a control device used to meet the compliance options in tables 1B/1C/1D/1E, then the process unit bypass stack monitoring and operating requirements of this subpart apply.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters (Boiler and Process Heater MACT)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater located at, or part of, a major source of HAP, then you are subject to this subpart unless an exclusion in § 63.7491 applies.
If the boiler or process heater is one of the specific types listed in § 63.7491(a) through (n), then that boiler or process heater is not subject to this subpart.

If the boiler or process heater is part of an affected source that is subject to another subpart of this part (for example boilers/process heaters used as control devices to comply with other NESHAP subparts), then the boiler/process heater is not subject to this subpart under § 63.7491(h).

If the boiler or process heater is used as a control device to comply with another subpart of this part (or part 60, 61, or 65) and at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years to the boiler/process heater is provided by regulated gas streams that are subject to another standard, then the boiler/process heater is not subject to this subpart under § 63.7491(i).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers (area/source boilers subpart JJJJJJ)

criteria.criterion: If a boiler is specifically listed as, or included in the definition of, an affected source in another standard under this part, then that boiler is not subject to this subpart.
If the boiler is gas-fired as defined in this subpart, then the boiler is not subject to this subpart.

If the boiler is used as a control device to comply with another subpart of this part (or part 60, 61, or 65) and at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years to the boiler is provided by regulated gas streams that are subject to another standard, then the boiler is not subject to this subpart.
If the boiler is required to have a permit under section 3005 of the Solid Waste Disposal Act or covered by subpart EEE (hazardous waste boilers), then the boiler is not subject to this subpart.

checklist: Is the facility a PCWP manufacturing facility as defined in 40 CFR 63.2231(a) (does the facility manufacture plywood and/or composite wood products)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥ 10 tons/year of any single HAP or ≥ 25 tons/year combined)? (see 40 CFR 63.2231(b))

Are the gasifiers and/or secondary combustion chamber physically and operationally part of the PCWP affected source (i.e., do their exhaust streams routinely direct-fire the PCWP dryers or other listed process units)? (see 40 CFR 63.2232(b))

Do the gasifiers/combustion units directly fire the PCWP dryers or lumber kilns (routine direct firing), triggering the subpart DDDD combustion unit tune-up and bypass monitoring requirements? (see 40 CFR 63.2241(d), 40 CFR 63.2271(c))

Is any portion of the gasifier/combustion exhaust routinely routed to a bypass that vents to the atmosphere (combustion unit bypass stack or process unit bypass stack), or does the bypass only transfer heat internally (e.g., to thermal oil closed-loop) without venting to atmosphere? (see 40 CFR 63.2240(e), 40 CFR 63.2269(k) and (l))

Is the gasification unit, secondary combustion chamber, or other unit an "industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater" as defined for Subpart DDDDD or JJJJJJ (verify applicable definitions and unit classification)? (see 40 CFR 63.7485)

Is the boiler/process heater claimed to be part of an affected source already regulated under another NESHAP subpart, such that § 63.7491(h) or 63.11195(a) may exempt it from the boiler/process heater subpart(s)? (see 40 CFR 63.7491(h), 40 CFR 63.11195(a))

If claiming exemption as a control device under § 63.7491(i) or § 63.11195(g), can you document that at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years to the unit is provided by regulated gas streams that are subject to another standard? (see 40 CFR 63.7491(i), 40 CFR 63.11195(g))

What fuels are burned in the gasifier/combustion chamber (wood residue, syngas, hazardous waste, natural gas, etc.), and does burning hazardous waste or other specific fuel types trigger coverage under or exclusion from other subparts (e.g., Subpart EEE)? (see 40 CFR 63.7491(m), 40 CFR 63.11195(c))

Quantify routine usage: what fraction of heat or gas from the gasifier/combustion unit is directed to PCWP dryers versus other uses (e.g., heating thermal oil), and over what time periods (to establish whether streams are 'routinely used' and to evaluate the 50% heat-input test)? (see 40 CFR 63.2232(b), 40 CFR 63.7491(i))

Does any bypass to heat thermal oil result in an atmospheric vent (bypass stack) or is it fully closed-loop with no venting to atmosphere (this affects applicability of bypass-stack monitoring/requirements)? (see 40 CFR 63.2240(e), 40 CFR 63.2269(k) and (l))

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key EPA points are reflected: the answer treats gas flowing directly through dryers as part of the PCWP (Subpart DDDD) affected source (and thus not automatically covered by the boiler MACT), requires evaluation of whether gas is diverted for indirect heat transfer to thermal oil (and whether those units meet the boiler/process heater definitions under Subpart DDDDD/JJJJJJ), and calls for consideration of §63.7491(h)/(i) and bypass/closed-loop venting — matching EPA’s reasoning that direct-fired gas is DDDD-covered while indirect thermal-oil heating makes the gasifiers/SCC subject to the boiler MACT and §63.7491(h) does not apply."}

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit any hazardous air pollutant and is subject to any standard, limitation, prohibition, or other federally enforceable requirement established pursuant to part 63, then the provisions of this part apply to the owner or operator of that stationary source.

If an area source that previously was a major source becomes a major source again, then the area source is subject to the applicable major source requirements established under this part immediately upon becoming a major source again, provided the compliance date for the major source requirements has passed.

If a major source reclassifies to area source status under this part, then the source remains subject to any applicable major source requirements established under this part until the reclassification becomes effective; after reclassification is effective the source is subject to any applicable area source requirements immediately (provided the compliance date for those area-source requirements has passed).

If a facility emits or has the potential to emit 10 tons per year or more of any single hazardous air pollutant (or 25 tpy or more of any combination of HAP), then it meets the part 63 definition of a 'major source' for purposes of applicability determinations under this part.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Plywood and Composite Wood Products (PCWP) (Subpart DDDD)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a PCWP manufacturing facility (which, as defined in this subpart, includes facilities that manufacture dry veneer and lumber kilns located at any facility) and the PCWP manufacturing facility is located at a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP), then this subpart applies to you.
citations: 40 CFR 63.2292 (Plywood and composite wood products manufacturing facility definition)

criteria.criterion: If an affected source (the collection of dryers, refiners, blenders, formers, presses, board coolers, and other process units associated with PCWP manufacturing, including lumber kilns) exists at the PCWP manufacturing facility, then this subpart applies to each new, reconstructed, or existing affected source.

If an area source increases its emissions or its potential to emit such that it becomes a major source of HAP, then the source must be in compliance with this subpart by October 1, 2007 or upon initial startup of the affected source as a major source, whichever is later.

If you operate lumber kilns at a PCWP manufacturing facility or at any other kind of facility, then those lumber kilns are included within the affected source definition in this subpart (and therefore are subject to the subpart's affected-source requirements if the facility meets the subpart applicability criteria).

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is considered a 'PCWP manufacturing facility' under §63.2231/§63.2292 (does the facility manufacture plywood or composite wood products, or do you operate lumber kilns that are included in the PCWP definition?).

Calculate current and projected potential-to-emit (PTE) and actual emissions of methanol (and other HAP) in tons per year, accounting for control devices and any federally enforceable limits in permits, to determine whether any single HAP ≥ 10 tpy or combined HAPs ≥ 25 tpy (see §63.2231(b) and §63.2).
Determine whether your facility is part of a contiguous area under common control that should be aggregated for major-source determination (see the 'major source' definition in §63.2).

Verify whether lumber kilns at your facility are considered part of the 'affected source' (per §63.2232(b)) and whether those kilns are new, reconstructed, or existing (and note construction/startup dates relevant to §63.2232(c)-(e) and §63.2233).

Check whether any title V / part 70 permit contains enforceable emissions limits that cap PTE below major-source thresholds (federally enforceable limits per §63.2) and whether those limits remain valid after permit revision.

If you are an area source increasing to a major source, determine the effective date for applicability and required compliance date per §63.2233(c) and whether the compliance deadlines in §63.2233(e) (and related tables) have passed for the affected-source requirements you would become subject to.

Confirm the effective date of any permit reclassification (when the revised title V/part 70 permit becomes effective) to determine when reclassification legally takes effect (see §63.1(c)(6)(i)(A) about remaining subject to prior status until reclassification is effective).

Determine which notifications and initial reports are required and their deadlines (see subpart DDDD notification schedule §63.2280 and the General Provisions notification requirements in §63.9 and §63.1(c)(5)/(c)(6)), and whether those have been or must be submitted upon becoming a major source.

Document whether the affected lumber kilns will need to meet specific lumber-kiln work practice, monitoring, O&M, or tune-up requirements in subpart DDDD (see §§63.2241 and 63.2253) and identify applicable compliance schedules in §63.2233(e).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The answer includes the key bases EPA cited: (1) PTE ≥10 tpy of a single HAP makes the facility a major source (cites §63.2); (2) an area source that becomes a major source is subject to major-source Part 63 requirements immediately upon becoming a major source/reclassification effective date (cites §63.1(c)(6)(i)(B) and guidance about permit effective date); and (3) lumber kilns are included as affected sources under §63.2232(b) of Subpart DDDD. The compliance-date caveat and permit‑effective timing are also addressed in the checklist."}

candidates.title: Chemical Manufacturing Area Sources (Subpart VVVVVV)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chemical manufacturing process unit (CMPU) that is located at an area source and Table 1 HAP are present in the CMPU as specified in paragraphs (a)(2)(i)–(iv), then the CMPU is subject to this subpart.

If your operations fall within any of the exclusions listed in paragraph (c) (for example, the listed area source categories or specified NAICS/operations), then this subpart does not apply to those operations.

If an affected CMPU at an area source has had a federally enforceable control device installed and that control device is necessary to maintain the source's emissions at area source levels, then the area source is required to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or part 71.

If the collection of CMPUs, heat exchange systems, and wastewater systems associated with CMPUs meets the criteria in paragraphs (a) and (b), then the facility-wide collection is the affected source for this subpart.

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit any hazardous air pollutant and is subject to any standard, limitation, prohibition, or other federally enforceable requirement established pursuant to this part, then the provisions of this part apply to the owner or operator of that source.

If an area source is subject to an area-source standard under this part, then the standard will specify whether States may exclude or defer title V permitting for those area sources, and if a standard fails to specify permitting, area sources subject to the standard will be subject to the requirement to obtain a title V permit.

If the source's potential to emit (including the effect of enforceable limitations and control devices treated as part of the design) is below the major source thresholds, then the source is an area source for purposes of these regulations; conversely, if potential to emit considering those limits is at or above the thresholds, the source is a major source.

checklist: Confirm whether the facility operates one or more CMPUs as defined for NAICS code 325 and whether those CMPUs are located at an area source.

Inventory Table 1 HAP present in each CMPU (feedstocks, byproducts, products, process/waste streams, continuous and batch vents) and verify concentrations against the thresholds in 63.11494(a)(2)(i)–(iv) using SDS, supplier formulation data, process knowledge, or engineering assessment.

Determine whether any of the exclusions in 63.11494(c) apply to your facility or specific operations (e.g., listed area source categories, specified NAICS activities, R&D, QA/QC labs, ancillary activities).

Identify any federally enforceable control devices or federally enforceable limits in place that affect HAP emissions from CMPUs, and document whether those controls/limits are relied upon to keep the facility below major source thresholds (i.e., are 'necessary to maintain the source's emissions at area source levels').

Calculate the facility's potential to emit for single HAP and combined HAP both with and without the federally enforceable limits and control devices to confirm area vs major source status (compare to 10 tpy single / 25 tpy combined thresholds).

Check whether a title V (part 70/71) permit already exists or whether a title V application has been submitted relying on a control device or limit; if not, determine whether 63.11494(e) would trigger a title V obligation (control device necessary to stay an area source).

Document dates of any relevant changes (e.g., when federally enforceable limits or control devices were installed and whether they predate the applicability/compliance dates in 63.11494) and retain records supporting decisions (SDS, engineering assessments, permit language, control device installation records).

candidates.title: Lead acid battery manufacturing plant area-source standards (Subpart PPPPPP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a lead acid battery manufacturing plant or a lead acid battery component manufacturing plant that is an area source of HAP emissions, then this subpart applies to the plant (affected source).

If the new Humidity Curing and Drying Oven Chambers are lead‑emitting operations associated with the plant (e.g., part of grid casting, paste mixing, three‑process operations, lead oxide manufacturing, lead reclamation, or any other lead‑emitting operation), then they are included in the affected source subject to this subpart.

If you are an existing affected source and a prior performance test was conducted using the same methods and either no process changes have been made since the test or you can demonstrate that the prior test results (with or without adjustments) reliably demonstrate compliance despite process changes, then you are not required to conduct an initial performance test for that affected source.

If you elect to group similar affected sources and the grouped units are the same process type and have the same type of air pollution control device, then you may conduct subsequent performance tests on one representative affected source to represent the group instead of testing each unit.

If construction or reconstruction of the affected source was commenced on or before April 4, 2007 (or the component‑plant dates in §63.11421(3)–(4) as applicable), then the source is an existing affected source; otherwise it is new and different compliance/test timing may apply.

candidates.title: Performance testing requirements (General Provisions, Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a relevant standard requires performance testing and you have not obtained a waiver, then the owner or operator must perform the required performance tests within 180 days of the compliance date.

If you submit a written application and the Administrator, in the Administrator's judgment, determines the source is meeting the relevant standard(s) on a continuous basis or the source is being operated under an extension (or an extension has been requested and is under consideration), then individual performance tests may be waived.

If you request a waiver of an initial or subsequent performance test, then the waiver application must be submitted at least 60 days before the performance test (unless submitted with an extension request or as otherwise specified) and include information justifying the waiver (e.g., technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality).

candidates.title: Extension of compliance, and performance test, monitoring, recordkeeping and reporting waivers and alternatives (Subpart YY)

criteria.criterion: If you apply in writing for a waiver of a performance test and the Administrator, after review (including consideration with any extension request), determines the source is achieving the relevant standard(s) or other conditions for waiver are met, then the Administrator may grant the waiver.

If you request an extension of compliance, then an application for a waiver of an initial performance test shall accompany the extension request; if no extension is requested the waiver application must be submitted at least 60 days before the performance test.

If you submit an application for a waiver of a performance test, then the application should include justification (such as technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality) to support the Administrator's review and decision.

checklist: Confirm the facility is a lead acid battery manufacturing plant or lead acid battery component manufacturing plant and an area source of HAPs (40 CFR 63.11421(a)).

Confirm whether the new Humidity Curing and Drying Oven Chambers are lead‑emitting operations associated with the affected source (i.e., part of grid casting, paste mixing, three‑process ops, lead oxide manufacturing, lead reclamation, or other lead‑emitting operations) (40 CFR 63.11421(b)).

Determine whether the plant (and the new ovens) are 'existing' or 'new' for Subpart PPPPPP by recording the construction/reconstruction commencement dates relevant to §63.11421 and the compliance dates in §63.11422 (40 CFR 63.11421(1)-(4); 40 CFR 63.11422).
Locate and obtain prior performance test reports: date, methods used, units tested, scope, and whether tests were conducted using the same methods specified in the subpart (40 CFR 63.11423(c)(1)).
Document whether any process changes have occurred since the prior performance test for those ovens or for the representative unit(s) (40 CFR 63.11423(c)(1)).

If you intend to rely on prior test results, verify that the prior test results (with or without adjustments) can be demonstrated to reliably show compliance for the new ovens (40 CFR 63.11423(c)(1)).

If you plan to group similar units, verify that the new ovens are the same process type and use the same type of air pollution control device as the group (and prepare the grouping/test plan listing units and representative unit) (40 CFR 63.11423(c)(5)(i)-(iii)).

If a prior waiver was previously granted, locate the Administrator's written waiver approval and confirm its scope (which units it covered) and whether it remains effective or could be rescinded (40 CFR 63.7(h)(5)).

Prepare waiver application materials and justification (continuous compliance history, monitoring/records, technical/economic infeasibility if applicable) and plan to submit at least 60 days prior to the scheduled performance test or with any extension request, per the applicable procedure (40 CFR 63.7(h)(3)(i); 40 CFR 63.1112(b)(3)(i),(iii)).

If relying on Subpart A/YY waiver authorities, confirm deadlines and that you will retain and be able to provide monitoring, operational, and test records to support the waiver request and the Administrator's review (40 CFR 63.7(h); 40 CFR 63.1112(b)(4)).

candidates.title: Stationary Combustion Turbines (Subpart YYYY)

criteria.criterion: If the stationary combustion turbine is a new or reconstructed lean premix gas-fired, lean premix oil-fired, diffusion flame gas-fired, or diffusion flame oil-fired stationary combustion turbine, then it must comply with the emission limitations and operating limitations in Table 1 and Table 2 of this subpart.

If the stationary combustion turbine is required to comply with the formaldehyde emission limitation and is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst, then you must petition the Administrator for operating limitations to monitor to demonstrate compliance with the formaldehyde emission limitation (or petition for approval of no additional operating limitations), measure the operating parameters during the initial performance test, continuously monitor thereafter, and not conduct the initial performance test until after the petition is approved or disapproved.

If you petition the Administrator for approval of additional operating limitations to demonstrate compliance with the formaldehyde emission limitation, then your petition must include identification of the specific parameters proposed, a discussion of the relationship between these parameters and HAP emissions and how limitations will limit HAP emissions, a discussion of how upper and/or lower values for the parameters will be established, a discussion of methods and instruments to measure and monitor the parameters with relative accuracy and precision, and a discussion of frequency and methods for recalibrating the instruments.

If you petition the Administrator for approval of no additional operating limitations, then your petition must include identification of parameters that could change, a discussion of the relationship (if any) between parameter changes and HAP emissions, explanations why establishing limitations is not possible for parameters that could increase HAP emissions, discussion of methods and instruments that could be used to measure and monitor such parameters and their recalibration, and a discussion of why adopting parameters as operating limitations is infeasible, unreasonable, or unnecessary.

If you are operating a stationary combustion turbine that is required to comply with the formaldehyde emission limitation and you use an oxidation catalyst, then you must continuously monitor catalyst inlet temperature to comply with the operating limitations in Table 2 as specified in this subpart.

If you are required to perform parametric monitoring under this subpart, then you must conduct parametric monitoring at all times the stationary combustion turbine is operating except during monitor malfunctions, associated repairs, and required QA/QC activities, and you must not use data recorded during those excluded periods for meeting subpart requirements.

If you are required to conduct performance tests to demonstrate compliance, then you must conduct the tests according to the requirements in this subpart (including three separate runs each at least 1 hour and tests at high load defined as 100 percent ±10 percent) and observe the initial performance test timing restrictions in this subpart.

checklist: Confirm turbine classification: is the unit a lean premix gas-fired stationary combustion turbine as defined by the subpart?
Confirm unit status: was the turbine new or reconstructed (check construction and startup dates and applicable compliance date in §63.6095)?
Confirm whether the turbine is required to comply with the formaldehyde emission limitation in Table 1 (verify applicability via Table 1/2 and §63.6100 and compliance date in §63.6095).
Confirm whether an oxidation catalyst is installed on the turbine (yes/no).

If no oxidation catalyst, confirm intention to petition the Administrator for operating limitations (or for approval of no additional operating limitations) and do not perform the initial performance test until after petition approval/disapproval per §63.6120(e).

Prepare draft petition contents if petitioning for operating limitations: identify proposed parameters (e.g., %Load and inlet air temperature T1), explain relationship between each parameter and HAP/formaldehyde emissions, explain how numeric upper/lower values will be set, specify measurement/monitoring instruments and their accuracy/precision, and specify recalibration frequency/methods (address §63.6120(f)(1)-(5)).

If petitioning for no additional operating limitations, document parameters that could change, their relationship to HAP emissions, reasons limits are infeasible/unnecessary, possible measurement/monitoring methods and recalibration, and why adoption of parameters is infeasible/unreasonable/unnecessary (address §63.6120(g)(1)-(7)).

Confirm capability to measure proposed parameters during the initial performance test and to continuously monitor them thereafter (including data recording and QA/QC procedures required by §63.6125 and §63.6135).
Ensure monitoring operation plans meet continuous monitoring and CMS quality control program requirements if required (see §63.6125(e) and §63.6135).

Plan initial performance test timing and conditions: tests must be within required timeframe per §63.6110, conducted at high load (100% ±10%), three runs each ≥1 hour, and do not perform initial test until petition resolved if turbine lacks an oxidation catalyst (§63.6120(c),(d),(e) and §63.6110).

Prepare for required notifications and reporting: Initial Notification and Notification of Compliance Status deadlines, and semiannual/annual compliance reporting requirements and contents per §§63.6145 and 63.6150.
Document procedures to exclude and track data during monitor malfunctions, repairs, and QA/QC activities and not use those data in compliance demonstrations as required by §63.6135(b).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Municipal Solid Waste Landfills

criteria.criterion: If the MSW landfill accepted waste since November 8, 1987 (or has additional capacity) and is a major source, is collocated with a major source, or (if an area source) has a design capacity ≥ 2.5 million Mg and estimated uncontrolled NMOC ≥ 50 Mg/yr, then the landfill is subject to Subpart AAAA.

If the landfill has a design capacity ≥ 2.5 million Mg and the calculated NMOC emission rate is equal to or greater than 50 Mg/yr (using Tier 1, 2, or 3 procedures), then the owner must submit a gas collection and control system design plan within 1 year and install and operate a gas collection and control system within 30 months.

If the landfill meets all three criteria in §63.1957(b)—(1) the landfill is closed, (2) the gas collection and control system has been in operation a minimum of 15 years or the owner demonstrates the system will be unable to operate for 15 years due to declining gas flow, and (3) the calculated NMOC emission rate is less than 50 Mg/yr on three successive test dates (each no less than 90 days and no more than 180 days apart) using the procedures in §63.1959(c)—then the collection and control system may be capped, removed, or decommissioned.

If the owner/operator intends to remove or cease operation of control equipment, then the owner/operator must submit an equipment removal report to the Administrator at least 30 days prior to removal that includes a closure report, documentation that the 15‑year minimum control period has expired or information demonstrating inability to operate for 15 years due to declining flows, and dated copies of three successive NMOC emission rate reports.

If a well is decommissioned, then that well may experience static positive pressure after shutdown to accommodate declining flows but any design changes associated with decommissioning must be approved by the Administrator as specified in the design plan approval process.

If a collection and control system has been installed and started up, then for purposes of determining when the system (or equipment) can be decommissioned the owner/operator must calculate the NMOC emission rate using Equation 3 and must determine landfill gas flow by measuring total landfill gas flow at the common header pipe and determine average NMOC concentration from samples collected from the common header pipe before gas moving or condensate removal equipment as specified in §63.1959(c)(1)-(2).

checklist: Confirm whether the landfill accepted waste after November 8, 1987 or has additional capacity for waste placement.
Determine whether the landfill is a major source or is collocated with a major source (permitted emissions/major source determination).

Obtain and verify the landfill design capacity (maximum design capacity mass in Mg and volume in m3) from the most recent permit or engineering calculation and confirm whether it is ≥ 2.5 million Mg (the facility stated ~5.9 million Mg).

Determine current and historical NMOC emission rate calculations (Tier used) and obtain the latest NMOC emission rate report and the two preceding reports (dates and values) to see if NMOC < 50 Mg/yr on three successive test dates spaced 90–180 days apart.
Confirm whether the landfill is 'closed' per §63.1990 (no additional solid waste will be placed without filing a notification of modification).

Document the date the gas collection and control system and each well (including EW-308A) were installed and how long the system has been in operation (to evaluate the 15‑year minimum control period).

If claiming the system will be unable to operate for 15 years due to declining gas flow, assemble evidence demonstrating declining gas flow (measured header flow trends, well productivity data, and any performance tests).

If decommissioning an individual well, verify whether that action constitutes a design change to the approved collection system and whether Administrator approval (design plan revision) is required under §63.1981(d)(2).
Confirm whether EW-308A is connected to the common header pipe and whether its removal will affect total header flow measurements used in NMOC calculations (per §63.1959(c)(1)).

Prepare to submit an equipment removal report to the Administrator at least 30 days before removal containing: closure report, documentation of 15‑year minimum control period expired or demonstration of inability to operate 15 years, and dated copies/statements of three successive NMOC emission rate reports (or statement that reports were previously submitted to CDX with dates).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Plywood and Composite Wood Products (PCWP) Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If your facility is a plywood and composite wood products (PCWP) manufacturing facility with a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source, then Subpart DDDD applies to that affected source.

If the equipment at issue is a reconstituted wood product press or a reconstituted wood product board cooler as defined in § 63.2292, then each is a process unit subject to the compliance options and operating requirements in this subpart.

If you choose a production-based compliance option, then you must apply a production-based compliance option for each process unit (and you may not use an add-on control system or wet control device to meet a production-based option).

If you attempt to apply different types of compliance options (production-based versus add-on control system) to different vents or portions of the same process unit, then that is not allowed and you must use one compliance option for the entire process unit.

If you operate a reconstituted wood product press at a new or existing affected source or a reconstituted wood product board cooler at a new affected source and you choose a concentration-based compliance option for a control system outlet, then the capture device for that unit must be a wood products enclosure as defined in § 63.2292 or must achieve a capture efficiency ≥ 95 percent.

If you operate a reconstituted wood product press or a reconstituted wood product board cooler, then you must either use a wood products enclosure or measure the capture efficiency of the capture device using Methods 204 and 204A–204F (or the subpart's alternative tracer gas method) and submit the documentation with your Notification of Compliance Status.

If you plan to demonstrate compliance using production-based mass-per-unit-production options, then you must measure and record process unit throughput during the performance test and include the unit's capture efficiency in the mass-per-unit-production calculation as specified in § 63.2262(i) and (f).

If emissions from two or more process units were co-mingled (a mixed PCWP process stream) prior to July 6, 2026, then special mixed-stream provisions may apply and the pre-July 6, 2026 compliance approach must be identified per the subpart.

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is an affected source under Subpart DDDD (new, reconstructed, or existing PCWP affected source) per 40 CFR 63.2232(a).
Verify that the equipment in question are separately-classified process units: a reconstituted wood product press and a reconstituted wood product board cooler (see definitions in 40 CFR 63.2292).

Decide which compliance option you intend to use for each process unit (production-based option OR an add-on control system option) because one option must be met for each process unit individually (40 CFR 63.2240).
If choosing a production-based option for a unit, confirm that no add-on control system or wet control device is being used to meet that production-based option (40 CFR 63.2240(a)).

If choosing a concentration-based/add-on control option for either unit, confirm the capture device either meets the wood products enclosure design criteria or can achieve ≥95% capture efficiency (40 CFR 63.2240(b), 63.2292).

If relying on capture efficiency for a press or board cooler, plan to demonstrate it using EPA Methods 204/204A–204F or the subpart's alternative tracer gas method and prepare the documentation for the Notification of Compliance Status (40 CFR 63.2267).

For production-based compliance demonstrations, ensure you will measure and record process unit throughput during performance testing and include capture efficiency in the mass-per-unit production calculation per 40 CFR 63.2262(f) and (i).

Determine whether any vents/streams from the press and board cooler are co-mingled with other process streams (mixed PCWP process stream) and, if so, whether they were co-mingled before or after July 6, 2026, to identify applicable provisions (40 CFR 63.2240(d)(5), 63.2292).

Prepare for required performance testing and sampling site locations (e.g., sampling prior to any release to atmosphere for uncontrolled units) as specified in 40 CFR 63.2262(d) and related testing provisions.
