Those elements cover the reasons underlying EPA's conditional approval."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Portland Cement Manufacturing (Subpart LLL)

criteria.criterion: If the gases are discharged from an affected source that is one of the units listed in §63.1345 at a facility which is a major source subject to this subpart, then those gases are subject to a 10 percent opacity limit.

If the emissions originate from a kiln or a clinker cooler (each of which is an affected source under this subpart), then opacity is not specified for those units in §63.1345 and instead the source must follow the pollutant-specific limits and testing requirements in Table 1 and §63.1343 (e.g., PM, HCl, THC, mercury, D/F).

If kiln and clinker cooler exhausts are commingled in a single stack and any component in that commingled stream is an affected source subject to the opacity limit in §63.1345, then the commingled exhaust is subject to the opacity requirements and must be tested by Method 9 using the maximum 6-minute average during the performance test period per the performance testing and monitoring provisions.

If kiln and clinker cooler exhausts are commingled in a single stack but none of the component sources in that combined stream are among the specific source types listed in §63.1345 for the 10% opacity limit, then Subpart LLL does not establish a 10% opacity limit for that commingled kiln/clinker-cooler stream and you must instead follow the applicable pollutant-specific limits, commingling/test-accounting provisions (e.g., PM alternative calculations), and monitoring requirements in §63.1343, §63.1349, and §63.1350.

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is a major source or an area source for Subpart LLL (per 40 CFR 63.1340(a)).

Identify each emission point routed to the common stack and classify each as kiln, clinker cooler, raw mill, finish mill, storage bin, conveying transfer point, bagging, bulk loading/unloading, or raw/finish mill dryer.

Determine whether any of the sources routed to the common stack are among the source types listed in 40 CFR 63.1345 (raw material, clinker, or finished product storage bins; conveying system transfer points; bagging; bulk loading/unloading; raw and finish mills; existing raw material dryers).

Quantify flows and fractions: measure or calculate the volumetric flow from the clinker cooler and from the kiln into the common stack (document the 20% average clinker-cooler flow that does not pass through the inline kiln/raw mill and the flows that are commingled).

If any source in the commingled stream is subject to the 10% opacity limit, plan to conduct Method 9 opacity testing (3-hour duration or the 1-hour exception conditions) and use the maximum 6-minute average from the performance test per 40 CFR 63.1349(b)(2) and 63.1348(a)(2).

If no component of the commingled stream is listed in §63.1345, determine and apply the pollutant-specific limits and commingling accounting procedures in Table 1 and §63.1343 (e.g., PM alternative limits, flow-weighted calculations for HCl/THC when diverting gases), and follow the performance testing and continuous monitoring requirements in §§63.1349 and 63.1350.

Review whether monthly Method 22 visible-emission checks and the corrective-action/monitoring frequency provisions in 40 CFR 63.1350(f) apply to any affected source that could trigger opacity testing.
Check permit conditions and local (Puerto Rico) opacity or visible-emission requirements that may be more stringent than Subpart LLL and confirm which limit governs the common stack.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's key reason—that the more stringent opacity limit applies to the commingled stack when any component is subject to the §63.1345 opacity limit—is reflected in the submitted criteria (notably criterion 3 which requires applying the opacity limit and Method 9 testing when any component in the commingled stream is subject to §63.1345)."}

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you perform surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products (application of coatings to substrates including associated surface preparation, cleaning, mixing, and storage), then the operations are in the source category to which this subpart applies.

If you use 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain hazardous air pollutants (HAP) in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and the facility is a major source (or located at / part of a major source), then you are subject to this subpart; if you do not meet both the volume and major-source criteria, then you are not subject under §63.3881(b).

If the coatings you use meet the definition of rubber-to-metal coatings (contain heat-activated polymer systems that, when applied to metal substrates, dry to a non-tacky surface and react chemically with the rubber and metal during a vulcanization process), then those coating operations are in the rubber-to-metal coatings subcategory.

If a coating operation does not meet the definition of high performance, magnet wire, rubber-to-metal, or extreme performance fluoropolymer coatings, then the operation is in the general use coating subcategory.

If your facility uses only coatings, thinners, other additives, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP as determined under §63.3941(a), then this subpart does not apply to that coating operation.

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Plastic Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you perform surface coating of plastic parts and products (application of coatings to plastic substrates including associated surface preparation, cleaning, mixing, and storage), then the operations are in the source category to which this subpart applies.

If you use 378 liters (100 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP in the surface coating of plastic parts and products and the facility is a major source (or located at / part of a major source), then you are subject to this subpart; if you do not meet both the volume and major-source criteria, then you are not subject under §63.4481(b).

If the coating operation is not an automotive lamp, TPO, or assembled on-road vehicle coating operation (i.e., it does not meet those subcategory definitions), then it is a general use coating operation under this subpart.
If the operation is specifically excluded in paragraph (c) (for example, surface coating of magnet wire), then this subpart does not apply to that operation.

checklist: Is the substrate you coat metal (miscellaneous metal parts/products) or plastic parts/products?

Does the coating formulation contain a heat-activated polymer system that dries to a non-tacky surface and chemically reacts with rubber and metal during a vulcanization process (i.e., does the bonding involve rubber vulcanization)?
If bonding uses a heating step, does that heating step constitute vulcanization of rubber (versus another heat cure or adhesive bonding that does not vulcanize rubber)?
What is the annual volume (liters or gallons) of coatings that contain HAP you use for this operation (compare to 946 L/yr for Subpart MMMM and 378 L/yr for Subpart PPPP)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥ 9.07 Mg (10 tons) of any single HAP or ≥ 22.68 Mg (25 tons) of combined HAP per year)?
Do your coatings, thinners, additives, and cleaning materials qualify as non-HAP (no more than 0.1% by mass for listed organic HAP and ≤1.0% for other HAP) per the subpart definition?

Does the operation fall into any listed exclusions in §63.3881(c) or §63.4481(c) (e.g., magnet wire coating, research/lab, hobby shop, certain web/coil/coating processes, or other exclusion criteria)?

Would the operation be better classified under another surface-coating NESHAP at your facility (and thus possibly use the predominant-activity or facility-specific emission limit options) — if so, determine predominant activity using liters (or kg) of coating solids over a representative period and document it.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's sole key reason—that the bonding is not performed during vulcanization so the rubber-to-metal subcategory does not apply—is directly covered by the answer: the criteria include the rubber-to-metal coating definition requiring chemical reaction during a vulcanization process and the checklist explicitly asks whether the bonding/heating step constitutes vulcanization."}

candidates.title: Wool Fiberglass Manufacturing NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator of a wool fiberglass manufacturing facility is a major source or is located at a facility that is a major source, then the requirements of this subpart apply to that owner or operator.

If a rotary spin manufacturing line at the facility produces a bonded wool fiberglass building insulation product (bonded wool fiberglass having a loss on ignition of less than 8 percent and a density of less than 32 kg/m3), then that rotary spin line is subject to this subpart.
If a flame attenuation manufacturing line at the facility produces a bonded wool fiberglass product, then that flame attenuation line is subject to this subpart.

If the owner or operator demonstrates to the Administrator that the wool fiberglass manufacturing facility is not a major source as defined in § 63.2, then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to that facility.

checklist: Measure the product loss on ignition (LOI %) for the specific product(s) using the method in Appendix A to Subpart NNN (cut sample, ignite at 540 °C, calculate percent weight loss).
Measure the product density (kg/m3 or lb/ft3) for the specific product(s) using the method in Appendix C to Subpart NNN (sample area weight and thickness to compute density).
Verify the product is 'bonded' (i.e., wool fiberglass with a phenol-formaldehyde binder applied) per the subpart definition.
Determine which manufacturing process produces the product (rotary spin vs. flame attenuation) for the specific line producing the metal building insulation.
Determine whether the line producing this product is a rotary spin line producing 'building insulation' (LOI <8% and density <32 kg/m3) or a flame attenuation line producing a bonded product.
Determine whether the wool fiberglass manufacturing facility is a major source (or is located at a facility that is a major source) as defined in 40 CFR 63.2.
If the facility claims non-applicability based on not being a major source, assemble documentation sufficient to demonstrate that to the Administrator (per § 63.1380(c)).

If performing LOI and density tests, record and retain results and the test methods used, since performance testing and records are required by the subpart for applicable lines (see performance test and recordkeeping provisions).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes. The EPA note’s key reason—that the metal building insulation meets the Subpart NNN definition of ‘building insulation’—is captured by the answer’s criteria and checklist (explicit LOI <8% and density <32 kg/m3 thresholds, bonded product and process-line determinations, and applicability tied to lines producing building insulation)."}

candidates.title: Polyether polyol manufacturing NESHAP (Subpart PPP)

criteria.criterion: If a process unit's primary product is a polyether polyol and the plant site is a major source, then that process unit is a PMPU and the PMPU and associated equipment are an affected source subject to this subpart.

If a PMPU does not use or manufacture any organic hazardous air pollutant (organic HAP) during production, then the PMPU is not subject to the provisions of this subpart other than the requirement to retain documentation and to demonstrate that determination when requested by the Administrator.

If a PMPU uses tetrahydrofuran (THF) to produce one or more polyether polyol products and the PMPU is part of an affected source, then each process vent in that PMPU must comply with the HON process vent requirements (40 CFR parts 63.113–63.118) as modified by § 63.1425(f).

If a source is an affected source under this subpart, then the owner/operator must comply with the emission standard and associated control, testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements in §§ 63.1425 through 63.1439 (process vents, storage vessels, wastewater, equipment leaks, heat exchangers, monitoring, and reporting) as applicable.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing NESHAP (Subpart FFFF)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) located at (or part of) a plant site that is a major source, and the MCPU produces materials described under the referenced SIC/NAICS categories and the MCPU processes, uses, or generates any CAA section 112(b) organic HAP, and the MCPU is not an affected source under another part 63 subpart, then the MCPU is subject to subpart FFFF.

If the operation falls within one of the exclusions listed in § 63.2435(c) (for example research and development facilities or the listed NAICS exceptions and affiliated operations), then the requirements of subpart FFFF do not apply to that operation.

checklist: Determine whether the plant site is a 'major source' of HAP (check your facility-wide potential to emit and permit status).
For the vessel/process unit in question, determine the primary product using § 63.1420(e) procedures (is the primary product a polyether polyol?).
Confirm whether tetrahydrofuran (THF) is used as a raw material in that process unit (not only as an impurity).

Determine whether any organic HAPs are used or produced in the polymerization step (including THF and any other reactants, solvents, by-products, or intermediates) or whether organic HAPs are present only as impurities.

If you determine no organic HAP are used or manufactured, assemble and retain documentation relied on for that determination (e.g., purchase records, process stream analyses, engineering calculations, process knowledge) per 40 CFR 63.1420(b)(1)(i).
Determine whether the process unit is a PMPU (process unit whose primary product is polyether polyol) and whether it is part of an affected source at the plant site per § 63.1420(a)(2) and (e).

Identify all process vents, reactors, condensers, distillation receivers, storage vessels, wastewater streams, and equipment leaks associated with the PMPU; classify vents as batch or continuous and note vent flow rates and organic HAP concentrations (to evaluate 'process vent' and Group 1/2 status under § 63.1423 and §§ 63.1425–63.1428).

If THF is used, determine whether each process vent in the PMPU will be subject to the HON process vent requirements as incorporated by § 63.1425(f) and whether additional monitoring/control (e.g., incinerator/flare/adsorber/condenser or ECO) will be required.

If you plan to rely on extended cookout (ECO) instead of control devices for epoxide or similar control, determine whether ECO applies and whether you must perform the ECO demonstrations and monitoring per § 63.1427 (e.g., measure or estimate reactor liquid/vapor epoxide concentrations, establish product classes, record pressure decay curves, establish monitoring levels).

If controls will be used on process vents, identify the type of control (flare, incinerator, absorber, condenser, carbon adsorber, boiler/process heater) and verify capability to meet monitoring requirements in § 63.1429 (e.g., temperature recorder, pilot flame detector, condenser exit temperature recorder, scrubbing liquid flow/pH, adsorption regeneration flow/temperature or organic monitoring device).

For any determination that the unit is not subject to Subpart PPP, be prepared to demonstrate that determination to the Administrator when requested (retain supporting data and calculations per § 63.1420(b)(1)(ii)).

Determine whether the process unit or equipment could instead meet the definition of an MCPU under Subpart FFFF (assess NAICS/SIC classification, whether the unit processes/uses/generates any section 112(b) organic HAP, and whether the unit is already regulated under another part 63 subpart) per § 63.2435(b) and (c).

If wastewater or storage vessels are present, determine whether they meet Group 1/Group 2 definitions and applicable HON-derived wastewater/storage requirements as incorporated in §§ 63.1433 and 63.1432.
Document whether any catalysts are used or removed (catalyst extraction steps), since §§ 63.1425(c)/(d) address nonepoxide organic HAP in catalyst extraction and making/modifying product.

Maintain records of decisions, monitoring levels, parameter setpoints, and initial demonstrations or precompliance reports as required by the cited subpart PPP provisions (e.g., Notification of Compliance Status and Precompliance Report requirements referenced in §§ 63.1425(f) and 63.1427(k)).

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"The submission captures EPA’s concern about lacking a §63.1420(b) no‑HAP demonstration (it lists the documentation/retention and demonstration steps), but it fails to reflect EPA’s primary legal point that the §63.1420(d)(3) exemption is limited to epoxide polymerization and does not cover THF polymerization—this limitation is not referenced in the criteria."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Paper and Other Web Coating

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a major source of HAP and operates web coating lines, then the facility is subject to Subpart JJJJ.

If a process meets the definition of a web coating line (continuous application of a liquid or semi-liquid coating material across any portion of the width of a web substrate between an unwind/feed station and a rewind or cutting station), then that operation is an affected web coating line under Subpart JJJJ.

If a web coating line is instead included in the affected source under one of the other NESHAPs listed in §63.3300(a)–(f) (for example subpart KK, EE, SSSS, or OOOO), then that web coating line is not part of the affected source under Subpart JJJJ (i.e., Subpart JJJJ does not apply to that line).

If a web coating line coats both paper (or other web) and another substrate and 90 percent or more of the mass of substrate coated during the compliance period is paper (predominant activity), then that line is subject to Subpart JJJJ rather than subpart OOOO.

If all of the subject web coating lines at the facility utilize only non-HAP coatings and you submit the one-time report required by §63.3370(s) to your permitting authority documenting use of only non-HAP coatings, then you can be exempt from the reporting requirements of this subpart.

If the equipment is research or laboratory equipment (primary purpose research and development, operated under close supervision, not engaged in commercial manufacture except de minimis), then that equipment is excluded from the affected source under this subpart.

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (confirm major-source status under the CAA definition used by 40 CFR part 63)?

Does the operation include a web coating line as defined: continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating material applied to a flexible web substrate between an unwind/feed station and a rewind or cutting station?
Is the applied material an adhesive or other liquid/semi-liquid 'coating material' (adhesives are listed as coating materials in the definition)?

Are the web(s) being coated paper (core stock) or another substrate; what fraction (by mass) of substrate coated over a representative period (≥1 year or other chosen period) is paper (to test the 90% predominant-activity rule)?
Is the web coating line already included in an affected source under one of the other NESHAPs referenced in §63.3300(a)–(f) (e.g., subpart KK, EE, SSSS, OOOO)?
Is the equipment research/laboratory equipment (R&D exempt per §63.3310 and §63.3300(g))?

Are all coatings used on the web coating lines non-HAP per §63.3370(s) (i.e., OSHA carcinogens <0.1% and other organic HAP <1.0%), and if so, has the one-time report been submitted to the permitting authority?
Is the source new or existing (determine construction/reconstruction dates relevant to compliance timelines referenced in the subpart)?
Do any work stations operate as always-controlled, intermittently-controlled, or never-controlled (determine control status because monitoring and compliance procedures differ)?

If controls are used: what type of control (solvent recovery, oxidizer, other control device), is there a capture system, and are monitoring/operational controls (CEMS, CPMS, bypass monitoring, capture-parameter monitoring) in place/required?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA’s note cites two key reasons: the activity is subject to Subpart JJJJ when it occurs at a major HAP source (major-source status) and the core-making operation meets the web-coating definition (adhesive applied between unwind and rewind). Those points are explicitly covered in the provided criteria and checklist (major source test, web coating definition, and adhesives-as-coating inclusion)."}

candidates.title: Wood Furniture Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If a facility is engaged, either in part or in whole, in the manufacture of wood furniture or wood furniture components and is located at a plant site that is a major source, then the facility is an affected source subject to this subpart.

If the owner or operator of the source uses no more than 250 gallons per month (for every month) of coating, gluing, cleaning, and washoff materials at the source (including materials used for source categories other than wood furniture) and meets the other recordkeeping conditions, then the source is an area source for purposes of this subpart and is not subject to other provisions of this subpart.

If the source meets the definition of incidental wood furniture manufacturer (i.e., is a major source primarily engaged in manufacture of products other than wood furniture and uses no more than 100 gallons per month of finishing material or adhesives in manufacture of wood furniture/components), then the owner/operator must maintain records demonstrating that definition and the source is not subject to other provisions of this subpart.

If surface coating of metal parts and products other than metal components of wood furniture meets the applicability criteria for miscellaneous metal parts and products surface coating (subpart MMMM), then those metal coating operations are not subject to subpart JJ.

If surface coating is of metal components of wood furniture performed at a wood furniture or wood furniture component manufacturing facility, then those metal components are subject to subpart JJ (not excluded).

candidates.title: Metal Furniture Surface Coating

criteria.criterion: If you perform surface coating of metal furniture (including metal furniture components) and you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source as defined in §63.4882 that is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source of HAP, then you are subject to this subpart.

If the surface coating of metal components is performed in an operation that is subject to the wood furniture manufacturing NESHAP (subpart JJ), then the metal-component coating is excluded from subpart RRRR (i.e., RRRR does not apply to those metal components).
If the surface coating operation uses only coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP, then the operation is not subject to this subpart.

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an affected source that uses 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain hazardous air pollutants in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and you are a major source, are located at a major source, or are part of a major source of HAP, then you are subject to this subpart.

If coatings used in a coating operation are in volumes of less than 189 liters (50 gallons) per year and the total volume of coatings exempt under this provision does not exceed 946 liters (250 gallons) per year at the facility, then those coating operations may be exempt from this subpart.

If the surface coating is of metal components of wood furniture that meet the applicability criteria for wood furniture manufacturing (subpart JJ), then those metal-component coating operations are excluded from subpart MMMM.

checklist: Confirm whether the plant site is a major source of HAPs (per 40 CFR part 63.2) and document the basis.
Determine and document whether the facility performs manufacture of wood furniture or wood furniture components (not just finishing) at the plant.
Identify which metal parts you coat: are they metal components of wood furniture or standalone metal parts/products (i.e., metal furniture or miscellaneous metal parts)?
Record monthly gallons used of coatings, glues, cleaning, and washoff materials plantwide (including metal coating materials) for each month (to compare to 250 gal/month and rolling 12-month limits).

Calculate rolling 12-month gallons of coatings (and HAP-containing coatings) used facilitywide and specifically for the metal coating activities (to compare to 3,000 gal/yr and 250 gal/yr thresholds).
Verify annual gallons of HAP-containing coatings used specifically for the metal refinishing/coating activities (you stated just under 250 gal/yr) and retain purchase/usage records.

Determine whether finishing materials, adhesives, cleaning and washoff solvents used for wood furniture manufacturing account for at least 90% of annual plantwide HAP emissions (if relying on the 90% area-source criterion in subpart JJ(b)).

Check whether the facility meets the 'incidental wood furniture manufacturer' test (uses no more than 100 gal/month of finishing materials or adhesives for wood furniture) and retain supporting records if claiming that status.
Determine whether coatings, thinners, or cleaning materials used in the metal coating operations contain any organic HAP (if they contain no organic HAP, some subparts may not apply).
If claiming an exemption for small-volume coatings under MMMM(c)(3), verify and document that each exempt coating is <50 gal/yr and total exempt volume does not exceed 250 gal/yr.
If metal coatings are for repair/maintenance only (not commerce), determine whether that meets any exemption criteria in RRRR (see 63.4881(c)(5)) and document the purpose of the coatings.

Identify whether the metal coating activity fits the definition of 'metal furniture' (RRRR) versus 'miscellaneous metal parts and products' (MMMM) and document product descriptions and SIC/NAICS codes if needed.
Retain all purchase and usage records for at least five years as required for demonstrations under these subparts (per 40 CFR 63.800(b) record retention language).

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "Yes. The response includes the JJ provision excluding metal parts/coatings from subpart JJ when they are not metal components of wood furniture (references 40 CFR 63.800(d)(1)) and points to applicability under MMMM/RRRR as appropriate, which captures the EPA's key reason that metal equipment refinishing is excluded from the wood furniture NESHAP."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Printing, Coating, Slashing, Dyeing, and Finishing of Fabrics and Other Textiles

criteria.criterion: If your facility performs printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing of fabric or other textiles (as defined in this subpart) and you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source that is a major source or is located at a major source of HAP, then the facility is subject to this subpart.

If the operation that applies materials to textile substrates meets the definitions of coating, printing, slashing, dyeing, or finishing in this subpart, then that operation falls within the scope of the subpart's regulated activities.

If the coating, printing, slashing, dyeing, or finishing operation uses only regulated materials that contain no organic HAP (as defined in this subpart), then that operation is not subject to this subpart.
If the operation is a research or laboratory operation or is part of janitorial, building, or facility maintenance operations, then that activity is not subject to this subpart.

If the coating/printing web operation is conducted at ambient temperatures and does not involve drying or curing equipment (such as ovens, tenter frames, steam cans, or dryers), then that web coating or printing operation is not subject to this subpart.

If the application of coating material is performed using handheld, non-refillable aerosol containers, touch-up markers, or marking pens, then that application is not considered a coating operation for the purposes of this subpart.

If the web coating/printing, slashing, dyeing, or finishing operations are performed at a facility but are not for commerce and organic HAP emissions from those operations are below major source levels, then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If your operations are part of an affected source as defined (including application equipment, storage/mixing containers, conveying equipment, waste handling, and wastewater treatment units used in the listed subcategories), then those items are included in the affected source subject to this subpart.

If a web coating line coats both textiles and other substrates, then the subpart that applies is determined by the predominant activity (90 percent mass of substrate coated during the compliance period); if textiles are the predominant activity, then this subpart applies, otherwise another subpart may apply.

If the web coating operation is covered by other listed NESHAP subparts for specific industries (e.g., subpart JJJJ, XXXX, or KK) because it is part of those affected sources, then that web coating operation is not part of this subpart's affected source.

checklist: Determine whether your facility is a major source of HAP (check annual HAP emission totals and major-source thresholds).

Confirm whether the task 'tipping' on shoelaces involves applying a material that (a) forms a continuous solid film on the thread (coating) or (b) impregnates the fiber without forming a film (finishing), or is another listed operation (printing, slashing, dyeing) per the definitions in 40 CFR 63.4371.
Document the substrate type: are the items treated considered 'fabric', 'thread', or a continuous 'web' as defined in the subpart?
Identify the exact material applied to tips (e.g., methanol solution): obtain manufacturer's formulation data and calculate the mass fraction of organic HAP in the material as purchased.
If applicable, measure or estimate mass of material applied and total organic HAP mass emitted to determine whether emissions reach major source levels or applicable emission limits.

Verify whether any drying, curing, or other thermal equipment (ovens, tenter frames, steam cans, dryers) is used after application or whether application is at ambient temperature without such equipment.
Confirm application method: is the material applied by handheld non-refillable aerosol, touch-up markers, or marking pens (which are excluded), or by another method (which may be included)?
Determine whether the operation is performed for commercial production or only for research/laboratory or janitorial/maintenance purposes.
Check whether the treated substrate mix includes non-textile substrates (e.g., paper) such that the predominant activity rule (90% mass) could make another subpart applicable.

Identify all equipment and containers associated with the operation (storage, mixing, conveyance, waste handling, wastewater treatment) to see if they fall within the affected source definition in §63.4282.

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "EPA's sole rationale — the facility is not performing coating, printing, slashing, finishing, or dyeing — is directly captured by the answer's criteria and checklist (notably the criteria requiring that the operation meet the subpart definitions of coating/printing/slashing/dyeing/finishing and the checklist item to confirm whether tipping constitutes those activities)."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Halogenated Solvent Cleaning

criteria.criterion: If an individual batch vapor, in-line vapor, in-line cold, or batch cold solvent cleaning machine uses any of the listed halogenated HAP solvents (methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, or chloroform) in a total concentration greater than 5 percent by weight as a cleaning and/or drying agent, then the provisions of Subpart T apply to that machine.

If the device does not use any of the listed halogenated HAPs above 5 percent by weight as a cleaning or drying agent (or the activity is limited to wipe/spray rag cleaning), then the device is not covered by Subpart T.

If the equipment uses halogenated HAP solvent liquid or vapor to remove soils then it meets the definition of a 'solvent cleaning machine' for this subpart (and is therefore within scope if it is one of the machine types in §63.460(a)).

If the equipment boils solvent and uses the resulting solvent vapor as part of the cleaning/drying cycle then it is a vapor cleaning machine, and if it contains and uses liquid solvent without boiling to clean parts then it is a cold cleaning machine, with differing standards for each type.

If the cleaning machine does not have a solvent/air interface (as defined in §63.461), then the owner/operator may be required to treat it as a machine without an interface and comply with the alternative emissions/logging and cleaning-capacity based limits and procedures in §63.464(a)(2) and the emissions-calculation/test procedures in §63.465(c) (including Table 6 or equation 1 based on cleaning capacity).

If the owner/operator does not elect the alternative standards, then each solvent cleaning machine that is subject to this subpart must meet the design, control, work-practice, idling emission limits, monitoring, and recordkeeping standards specified in §63.463 (or the continuous-web provisions in §63.463(g)/(h) where applicable).

If the facility constitutes an 'affected facility' as defined in §63.471(a) (i.e., all solvent cleaning machines at a major source subject to the facility-wide limits, or for area sources the set of machines specified), then the facility-wide weighted, 12-month rolling emission limits and related monthly/annual demonstration and reporting requirements of §63.471 apply.

If the machine is a continuous web cleaning machine, then the continuous-web-specific compliance paths and alternative in §63.463(g)/(h) and the alternative overall-control-efficiency demonstration in §63.464(d) apply instead of some §63.463(a)-(f) provisions.

checklist: Identify the exact solvent(s) used and confirm whether any listed halogenated HAP (methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform) is present at >5% by weight (use MSDS, Method 18, or engineering calculation).

Determine whether the unit uses liquid solvent only (cold cleaning), boils solvent and uses solvent vapor for cleaning/drying (vapor cleaning), or a combination (document process steps and temperatures).
Confirm machine type: batch vs in-line vs continuous-web (how parts are loaded and flow through the cycle).

Determine whether the machine has a solvent/air interface as defined in §63.461 (for vapor machines: midline of primary condenser coils; for cold machines: liquid surface contact with air) or is effectively 'without a solvent/air interface' (nearly airless/airtight).

If no solvent/air interface, measure or calculate cleaning capacity (volume in cubic meters) to apply Table 6 or equation 1 per §63.464(a)(2) and §63.465(c)/(e)(2) (document method used to determine capacity).

If there is a solvent/air interface, measure or calculate the solvent/air interface area (square meters) as defined in §63.461 to apply Table 5 or idling emission limits and the calculations in §63.465(c).

Document presence and characteristics of controls: primary condenser, freeboard refrigeration, covers (working/idling), reduced-room-draft measures, carbon adsorber, squeegee/air knife, superheated vapor/part systems, and freeboard ratio (freeboard height and smaller interior dimension).
Measure or confirm automated parts-handling/hoist capability and maximum speed (is it ≤3.4 m/min (11 ft/min)?), and whether parts dwell/drain times are enforced where applicable.

Decide whether to elect the alternative standards in §63.464 or to comply with §63.463 design/operational standards; if electing §63.464, prepare solvent addition/deletion logs and emissions calculations per §63.465/§63.464.
If using a carbon adsorber, verify ability to meet weekly exhaust concentration monitoring and maintenance requirements in §63.466(e) and recordkeeping in §63.467(b)(4).

Calculate potential to emit (PTE) from all solvent cleaning operations per §63.465(e) and determine facility status (major vs area source) and whether facility-wide limits in §63.471 apply; if applicable, prepare logs and monthly/12-month rolling calculations per §63.471(c).

Prepare required notifications, initial compliance statements, and reporting timelines (initial notification, initial statement of compliance, annual/solvent emission reports, and exceedance reporting) described in §63.468.

Maintain required records (owner manuals, installation dates, solvent composition, solvent addition/deletion logs, monitoring results, test reports, calculations) for the retention periods specified in §63.467.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note states the equipment applies because it is considered a 'solvent cleaning machine' subject to Subpart T. OUR ANSWER includes the criterion that equipment using halogenated HAP solvent liquid or vapor to remove soils meets the definition of a 'solvent cleaning machine' and therefore is within scope (citing §§63.460(a), 63.461), so the key EPA rationale is captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Printing, Coating, Slashing, Dyeing, and Finishing of Fabric and Other Textiles

criteria.criterion: If the facility performs printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing of fabric or other textiles (finishing includes chemical treatment such as stain repellents), then the source category of subpart OOOO applies.

If you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source as defined in §63.4282 that is a major source of HAP or is located at a major source, then Subpart OOOO applies to that affected source.

If the web coating/printing, slashing, or dyeing and finishing operations use only regulated materials that contain no organic HAP (as defined by the 'no organic HAP' thresholds in §63.4371), then those operations are not subject to this subpart.

If a web coating line is conducted at ambient temperature and does not involve drying or curing equipment (ovens, tenter frames, steam cans, or dryers), then that web coating/printing operation is not part of the affected source subject to this subpart.

If the solvent is added after receipt to dilute (i.e., is used as a thinning material for a coating/printing material), then that solvent is a regulated thinning material and must be accounted for in determining organic HAP content and compliance using the procedures in §§63.4321 and 63.4331.

If the solvent is purchased as part of a dyeing or finishing material (i.e., included in the finishing material as purchased), then its organic HAP mass fraction as purchased must be used to demonstrate compliance with the dyeing/finishing emission limits using the compliant-material or emission-rate procedures in §§63.4321(c) and 63.4331(b).

If you choose the compliant material option, then each thinning and cleaning material (for web coating/printing) or each dyeing/finishing material (for dyeing/finishing) as purchased must contain no organic HAP or must have a mass fraction of organic HAP less than or equal to the applicable limit in Table 1, demonstrated using the supplier data or test methods in §63.4321(e).

If the solvent is used only as a cleaning material for equipment associated with web coating/printing operations, then for the compliant material option that cleaning material must contain no organic HAP as defined in §63.4371.

checklist: Is the operation at the plant printing, coating, slashing, dyeing, or finishing fabric or other textiles (does 'finishing' include your stain-repellent process)?
Is the affected source new, reconstructed, or existing as defined in 40 CFR 63.4282, and is the source a major source of HAP or located at a major source (per 40 CFR 63.4281(b))?
Does the operation use any drying or curing equipment (ovens, tenter frames, steam cans, dryers) or is it only at ambient temperature?

Is the solvent purchased already blended into the finishing material (i.e., part of the material as received) or is the solvent purchased/added separately at the facility to dilute the finish (i.e., post-purchase thinning/alteration)?
For the solvent: what is the manufacturer's/supplier's formulation data or test result for organic HAP mass fraction (use Method 311, Method 24, or supplier data per §63.4321(e)(1))?
Does the solvent (or finished material as purchased) meet the 'no organic HAP' thresholds in §63.4371 (0.1% for listed organics, 1.0% for others)?
Is the solvent used as a cleaning material for equipment or as a thinning material (coating/printing) or is it part of a dyeing/finishing material?

Which compliance option does the facility plan to use (compliant-material option, emission-rate without add-on controls, emission-rate with add-on controls, overall control efficiency, or oxidizer outlet concentration)?

If using an emission-rate or add-on control option, what are the monthly/rolling 12-month material usage records and organic HAP mass fractions to calculate emissions per §§63.4331–63.4332 (or the appropriate equations in §63.4341 for add-on controls)?

If considering the wastewater allowance or equivalent emission-rate option for dyeing/finishing, does wastewater receive POTW or onsite secondary treatment and has a wastewater characterization/performance test been (or will be) performed per §63.4331(c)?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The EPA note’s key reason — that a solvent added after receipt to dilute finishing materials is a regulated thinning material and must be included in the organic HAP emission limits for textile finishing — is explicitly captured (criterion on thinning material and related citations). The answer also includes the textile-finishing source applicability and major-source criteria referenced by EPA, so the key rationale is covered."}

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Wood Building Products

criteria.criterion: If you apply coatings (including adhesives) to wood building products (products that contain more than 50 percent by weight wood or wood fiber excluding the weight of any glass components and are used in construction, e.g., doors, windows, window components) and the affected source uses 4,170 liters (1,100 gallons) per year or more of coatings in that source category and the source is a major source (or located at/part of a major source), then the source is subject to this subpart.

If the surface coating operation meets any of the exclusions listed in § 63.4681(c)(1) through (c)(5) (for example, plywood/composite wood processes covered by subpart DDDD, wood furniture covered by subpart JJ, prefabricated homes, noncommercial/hobby operations, or wood treatment by pressure impregnation), then that operation is not subject to this subpart.

If the affected source uses coatings subject to another surface-coating subpart that account for at least 95 percent of the total annual coating usage for the affected source, then you may demonstrate compliance with that other subpart for the entire affected source (i.e., QQQQ need not be applied separately to the remainder).
If the material you apply is an adhesive as defined in § 63.4781, then it is considered a 'coating' for the purposes of determining applicability and affected‑source coverage under this subpart.

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If you apply coatings (including adhesives) to miscellaneous metal parts or products and you use 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and the source is a major source (or located at/part of a major source), then the source is subject to this subpart.
If the metal components you coat are metal components of wood building products that meet the applicability criteria for Subpart QQQQ, then Subpart MMMM does not apply to those metal components.

If the facility uses only coatings, thinners, and other additives and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP (as determined under the referenced test/criteria), then the coating operation is not subject to this subpart.

If the coatings you apply meet the definition of high performance architectural coating (i.e., coatings required to meet AAMA 605.2-2000), then the operation falls within the 'high performance' subcategory included in this subpart.

If you use less than 946 liters (250 gallons) per year of coatings that contain HAP for miscellaneous metal parts and products (and do not otherwise meet other applicability criteria), then you are not subject to this subpart on the basis of the annual‑use threshold.

checklist: For wood coatings: confirm the coated item is a 'wood building product' (contains >50% wood/wood fiber by weight excluding glass and is used in construction; e.g., doors, windows, window components).
For wood coatings: total annual volume of all coatings (including adhesives, thinners, cleaning materials) used for wood building products (liters or gallons per year).

For wood coatings: determine whether the facility is a 'major source' of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tons/year of any single HAP or ≥25 tons/year of combined HAP) or is located at/part of a major source.

For wood coatings: check whether the operations fall within any §63.4681(c) exclusions (plywood/composite processes covered by subpart DDDD, wood furniture/subpart JJ, prefabricated homes, noncommercial/hobby operations, pressure impregnation wood treatments).
For metal coatings: confirm the coated item is a 'miscellaneous metal part or product' (or whether it is a metal component of a wood building product covered by QQQQ).
For metal coatings: total annual volume of coatings that contain HAP used for coating metal parts (liters or gallons per year) and whether any individual coatings are non‑HAP.
For metal coatings: determine whether the facility is a 'major source' of HAP (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP) or is located at/part of a major source.
For metal coatings: if using high performance architectural coatings, verify whether the coating meets the AAMA 605.2‑2000 specification (i.e., qualifies as 'high performance architectural coating').

For both: identify and inventory all materials applied (coatings, adhesives, thinners, cleaning materials), obtain manufacturer's formulation data or test results to determine organic HAP content and solids content as needed to evaluate applicability and compliance options.

For both: if multiple surface‑coating NESHAPs could apply at the facility, determine the percent of total annual coating usage by each activity (liters or liters of solids) to evaluate predominant‑activity, facility‑specific limit, or 95% alternative (see respective subparts).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The EPA Notes’ key reasons (wooden window components meet the QQQQ definition as wood building products and aluminum window components are covered as miscellaneous metal parts under MMMM) are reflected in the answer: it includes the >50% wood/wood-fiber definition, explicitly counts adhesives as coatings for QQQQ, and identifies miscellaneous metal parts/parts-of-wood-building-product exclusion and the MMMM high‑performance category plus the major‑source and annual‑use applicability criteria. Thus the EPA Notes’ rationale is captured."}

candidates.title: Aerospace manufacturing and rework operations NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If the facility is engaged in the manufacture or rework of commercial, civil, or military aerospace vehicles or components and is a major source, then cleaning operations at the facility are within the scope of this subpart (unless an exemption applies).
If the facility is not a major source as defined in § 63.2 or is not engaged in aerospace manufacture or rework, then the cleaning-operation provisions of this subpart do not apply.

If the cleaning is of electronic parts and assemblies (except cleaning and topcoating of completed electronic assemblies when that activity is part of aerospace rework/manufacture), then that cleaning is exempt from the cleaning requirements of this subpart.

If the cleaning is of aircraft or ground support equipment fluid systems that are exposed to the fluid (including hydraulic fluid systems and air-to-air heat exchangers), then that cleaning is exempt from the cleaning requirements of this subpart.

If the cleaning solvent(s) used meet the definition of non-HAP material, then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to those primers, topcoats, specialty coatings, chemical milling maskants, strippers, and cleaning solvents (except where such materials are included in an averaging scheme as specified).

If a cleaning operation at the facility is subject to the subpart (i.e., not exempt), then the owner or operator must implement the housekeeping measures in § 63.744(a) (closed storage/containers, transfer practices) for cleaning solvents and solvent-laden materials unless equivalent measures are demonstrated.

If a hand-wipe cleaning operation is subject to the subpart, then the owner or operator must use cleaning solvents that either meet the Table 1 composition requirements, have a composite vapor pressure ≤45 mm Hg at 20 °C, or demonstrate a ≥60% volume reduction from an approved baseline.

If a spray-gun cleaning operation is subject to the subpart, then the owner or operator must use one of the techniques in § 63.744(c)(1)–(4) (enclosed system, nonatomized cleaning, disassembled gun cleaning in a closed vat/soak, or atomizing cleaning with capture device) and inspect enclosed cleaners monthly for leaks.

If a flush cleaning operation is subject to the subpart, then the owner or operator must drain used solvent into an enclosed container or a system with equivalent emission control that is kept closed when not in use.

If a cleaning operation is subject to this subpart, then the owner or operator must maintain the specific records and semiannual reporting for cleaning operations (solvent identity, vapor pressure or composition documentation, monthly volumes, and semiannual compliance reports) as required in §§ 63.752(b) and 63.753(b).

checklist: Is the facility a major source as defined in 40 CFR 63.2 and engaged in manufacture or rework of aerospace vehicles or components (even in part)? (40 CFR 63.741(a))
Is the specific cleaning activity part of manufacture or rework of aerospace vehicles/components or a separate non‑regulated activity? (40 CFR 63.741(c))
Is the object being cleaned an electronic part or assembly, or a completed electronic assembly (note the exception for completed assemblies)? (40 CFR 63.744(e)(4); 40 CFR 63.741(f))
Is the cleaning activity on aircraft or ground support equipment fluid systems exposed to the fluid (e.g., hydraulic fluid leaks, air‑to‑air heat exchangers)? (40 CFR 63.744(e)(5))
Are the solvents used classified as non‑HAP material per § 63.742 (manufacturer data or MSDS to show ≤0.1% certain carcinogens and ≤1.0% other individual HAP)? (40 CFR 63.742; 40 CFR 63.741(f))

For hand‑wipe cleaning: for each solvent, do you have manufacturer composition data showing compliance with Table 1, or documentation of composite vapor pressure ≤45 mm Hg at 20 °C, or an approved 60% reduction baseline plan? (40 CFR 63.744(b); 40 CFR 63.750(a),(b))

For spray‑gun cleaning: which technique is used (enclosed system, nonatomized pressure‑pot flush, disassembled soak/vat, or atomizing with capture), and are enclosed cleaners inspected monthly and repaired within 15 days of leaks? (40 CFR 63.744(c); 40 CFR 63.751(a))
For flush cleaning: is used solvent emptied into an enclosed/closed collection system or equivalent emission control? (40 CFR 63.744(d))

Do you maintain records for each cleaning solvent used (name, vapor pressure, organic HAP constituents), monthly volumes as applicable, and logs of any enclosed cleaner leaks and repairs per § 63.752(b)? (40 CFR 63.752(b))

Are semiannual reports prepared that identify any noncompliant solvent use, new solvents, noncompliant spray‑gun methods, leaking enclosed cleaners unrepaired >15 days, and a certification of compliance as required by § 63.753(b)? (40 CFR 63.753(b))

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "EPA’s note cites that the rule only partially applies because some cleaning activities are exempt under §63.741(f); the submitted criteria explicitly include the major‑source/manufacture scope plus the exemptions for electronic assemblies, aircraft/ground‑support fluid systems, and non‑HAP solvents (and the related compliance requirements), so the key reasons in the EPA notes are captured."}

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator requests permission to use an alternative non-opacity emission standard and demonstrates that the alternative will achieve at least equivalent reductions of the applicable HAPs, then the Administrator may permit use of the alternative emission standard after public notice and comment.

If an owner or operator requests permission to use an alternative means of emission limitation or monitoring, then the owner or operator must submit proposed test plans or results and monitoring descriptions consistent with the requirements in §§ 63.7 and 63.8 to support the request.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants From Petroleum Refineries (Subpart CC)

criteria.criterion: If the emissions point is at a plant site that is a major source and is part of a petroleum refining process unit that contains one or more hazardous air pollutants listed in table 1 of subpart CC, then that plant site and its listed emissions points are subject to Subpart CC.

If a vent stream from a distillation unit (or other process unit in a petroleum refinery) contains greater than 20 parts per million by volume total organic HAP, then the vent is a miscellaneous process vent and is included in the affected source under this subpart.

If the vent is a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent (total organic HAP concentration ≥ 20 ppmv and TOC emissions ≥ 33 kg/day for existing sources or ≥ 6.8 kg/day for new sources), then the owner or operator must either use a flare meeting requirements or reduce emissions by 98 weight-percent or to a concentration of 20 ppmv (whichever is less stringent) using an approved control device.

If a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent uses a combustion device to comply, then the owner or operator must install and operate the monitoring equipment specified in § 63.644(a) for that device unless approval is requested and granted to monitor alternative parameters under § 63.644(b).

If the owner or operator uses a control device other than an incinerator, boiler, process heater, or flare for a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent or seeks to monitor a parameter other than those specified in § 63.644(a), then the owner or operator must request approval for alternative monitoring (procedures referenced in § 63.644(b)).

If a process vent is used only as a result of startup, shutdown, maintenance, or inspection (i.e., is a maintenance vent), then the owner or operator may designate it a maintenance vent and comply with the maintenance-vent provisions in § 63.643(c) instead of the Group 1/Group 2 requirements.

candidates.title: Process Vent Provisions (Subpart G)

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator is responsible for a Group 1 process vent as defined in subpart G, then the owner or operator may comply by reducing emissions of total organic HAP by 98 weight-percent or to a concentration of 20 ppmv (dry, corrected to 3% O2) using combustion, recovery, and/or recapture devices consistent with § 63.113(a)(2).

If a combustion device (incinerator, flare, boiler, or process heater) is used to meet the process-vent reduction requirement, then the owner or operator must install the monitoring equipment specified for that device in § 63.114(a) (e.g., continuous firebox temperature for incinerators, pilot-flame detector for flares, firebox temperature recorder for small boilers/heaters).
If the owner or operator proposes to monitor parameters other than those specified in § 63.114(a) or (b), then the owner or operator must request approval for alternative monitoring per § 63.114(c).

checklist: Confirm whether the plant site is a major source of HAPs (to determine Subpart CC applicability).
Confirm that the orthoxylene rerun column vent is part of a petroleum refining process unit at the plant site (assignment rules in § 63.640(f) and (e)).

Measure or calculate the vent's total organic HAP concentration (ppmv) at the outlet and the TOC/HAP mass emission rate (kg/day or lb/hr) to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 classification under § 63.641 and § 63.640.
Verify whether the vent stream is routed to a refinery fuel gas system or to the atmosphere (vents routed to a fuel gas system may be excluded per definitions in § 63.641 and § 63.640(d)(5)).

Determine whether the vent is routine/continuous or is used only for startup/shutdown/maintenance (if only used for maintenance events, evaluate maintenance-vent provisions in § 63.643(c) / § 63.113(k)).
Identify the existing control device (flare, incinerator, boiler/process heater, recovery/adsorber, condenser, etc.) and whether it meets the specific device requirements in § 63.643 and § 63.114.

If using a flare, collect flare design and monitoring capability data: pilot presence monitoring, smokeless capacity, tip area, assist steam/air design and metering capability, and current monitoring instrumentation (per § 63.670 requirements referenced by Subpart CC).

Document current control effectiveness (percent reduction and/or outlet concentration) and the test methods used (Method 18/25A/TOC or other methods referenced by applicable subpart) to show whether the proposed revision will meet 98% or 20 ppmv.

If proposing alternative monitoring parameters or a change to the approved monitoring plan, prepare test/monitoring data and a plan consistent with the alternative-approval requirements referenced in § 63.644(b) and the general provisions on alternative means in § 63.6(g) (including supporting test plan/results per § 63.7/§ 63.8).

Assemble the performance-test and monitoring-QA/QC documentation (sensor specifications, calibration/maintenance schedules, CPMS quality control per Table 13 in Subpart CC appendix if applicable) to support any alternative-monitoring approval request.

Confirm whether Subpart G (chemical process vent rules) or Subpart CC is the relevant subpart for this particular vent (i.e., whether the vent is a subpart G Group 1 process vent versus a Subpart CC miscellaneous process vent) and retain documentation supporting that determination.

If requesting site-specific flare operating limits under § 63.670(r) (for flares), prepare a site-specific performance-evaluation plan and data showing that the site-specific limits achieve the required combustion/destruction efficiency and include the elements listed in § 63.670(r)(1)–(4).

Verify compliance deadlines and whether any extension, prior approvals, or previously granted alternative approvals affect the timing or content of the submittal (see general timing and extension provisions in § 63.6).

Identify the permit submission route and required report types referenced by the subparts (Notification of Compliance Status, Periodic Reports) and the location/procedure to submit alternative-monitoring requests (note § 63.644(b) references submission procedures in § 63.655(h)).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA’s note cites approval under 40 CFR part 63 Subpart G; OUR ANSWER includes Subpart G criteria (process-vent reduction requirements at §63.113, required monitoring at §63.114(a), and the alternative-monitoring approval path at §63.114(c)) and also cites the general provisions for alternative monitoring (§63.6(g)). Thus the key reason given in the EPA NOTES is captured."}

candidates.title: Performance testing requirements

criteria.criterion: If you submit a written application with justification showing technical or economic infeasibility or that the source is meeting the standard on a continuous basis, then the Administrator may waive a required performance test or otherwise approve use of alternative test/monitoring approaches including waiving an operating parameter limit.

candidates.title: Hazardous waste combustors—monitoring and operating parameter requirements (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If you operate a hazardous waste combustor (e.g., an incinerator), then you must establish and comply with operating parameter limits based on your comprehensive performance test for parameters needed to ensure good operation of each hazardous waste firing system (including limits on waste feed characteristics and firing-system parameters) and operating parameter limits for hydrogen chloride and chlorine control devices including wet scrubber minimum liquid feed pressure for low-energy scrubbers.

If you wish to waive an operating parameter limit specified in this subpart (for example a limit on waste viscosity, feed delivery or atomization pressure, or scrubber liquid feed pressure), then you must submit an application to the Administrator (with required data and justification) no later than with the comprehensive performance test plan and follow the approval procedures in §63.1209(g)(1).

If you use an eligibility demonstration under the health-based compliance alternative for total chlorine, then you must still establish and comply with operating parameter limits on the same parameters that apply under §63.1209, and feedrate limits and emission-control equipment operating limits as specified in §63.1215(g).

If a monitoring waiver or alternative monitoring approach is requested, then the application must include data showing the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance, the timing and content requirements (submitted with the comprehensive performance test plan), and is subject to Administrator review and specified approval timelines.

If you do not include an operating parameter (e.g., viscosity, nozzle pressure) in the comprehensive performance test and in the test plan, then you cannot rely on omitting that parameter unless the Administrator approves an alternative monitoring request or waiver under §63.1209(g)(1).

candidates.title: Performance testing and test methods (wet scrubber operating parameters) (Subpart CCC)

criteria.criterion: If you use a wet scrubber as an emission control device, then during the performance test you must establish site-specific operating parameter values (at minimum minimum scrubber makeup water flow rate and, for recirculating scrubbers, minimum recirculation water flow rate) and monitor those parameters continuously and record values at least every 15 minutes.

candidates.title: Process vent monitoring requirements (Subpart PPP)

criteria.criterion: If a process vent is controlled by a scrubber, condenser, or carbon adsorber then you must install and operate continuous monitoring for the device-specific parameters (e.g., scrubbing liquid flow or pressure and pH for absorbers/scrubbers; condenser exit temperature; carbon adsorber regeneration flow and carbon bed temperature), unless an alternative parameter is approved.

If you seek to monitor parameters other than those specified for your recovery/recapture device, then you must request approval and follow the alternative-parameter approval procedures specified in this subpart.

checklist: Confirm the unit classification: is the unit a hazardous waste incinerator (hazardous waste combustor) and not a hazardous waste hydrochloric acid production furnace (Subpart EEE §63.1215(a)(1) excludes HCl production furnaces from some alternatives).

Document whether your firing system(s) use simple lances that feed pumpable wastes and whether the wastes are pumpable or otherwise characterized (viscosity/physical form) and whether viscosity, delivery pressure, and atomization pressure were included in the comprehensive performance test plan and test runs (§63.1207(f)(1)(i); §63.1209(j)(4)).

Verify whether your source is equipped with a wet scrubber for HCl/Cl2 control and determine the scrubber type (high-energy venturi style vs low-energy spray/packed tower), whether it recirculates, and whether manufacturer specifications for minimum liquid feed pressure or minimum pressure drop exist (§63.1209(o)(3)(i)-(iii); §63.1161(b)).

Check whether the comprehensive performance test plan to be (or already) submitted includes establishment of scrubber operating parameters (minimum makeup flow, recirculation flow, pH, pressure drop or liquid feed pressure) and specified monitoring frequency (continuous, ≥ once every 15 minutes for parameters established during testing) as required by §63.1161(b) and §63.1207(f)(1)(i).

Decide whether you will request a waiver or alternative monitoring for any specific operating parameter (waste viscosity limit, delivery pressure, atomization pressure, or scrubber liquid feed pressure) and prepare the supporting data/justification to submit with the comprehensive performance test plan per §63.1209(g)(1)(iii) (show that the parameter is not needed or an alternative provides equivalent assurance).

If requesting a waiver, assemble evidence that the proposed alternative monitoring provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance (technical data, past performance tests, engineering analysis) and note the Administrator's review timelines (notification with test plan; decisions within timelines in §63.1209(g)(1)(iii)).

Confirm whether any automatic waste feed cutoff (AWFCO) interlocks are or will be tied to the parameter spans (including scrubber parameters) and whether the AWFCO testing/operability schedule and interlock logic are documented (§63.1206(c)(3); §63.1209(b)(4)).

Record whether you intend to pursue a health-based compliance alternative for total chlorine under §63.1215 (if so, check additional feedrate and monitoring obligations and whether HCl/Cl2 apportionment, feedrate limits, and control-device operating limits are included).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes. The answer includes the key bases EPA cited: Administrator waiver authority (40 CFR 63.7(h)(3)), the EEE provisions requiring submission of waiver/alternative monitoring requests with justification and data and following §63.1209(g)(1) approval procedures, the requirement to show equivalent or better assurance for alternative monitoring, and the wet‑scrubber/parameter establishment requirements — collectively capturing that waivers can be approved but only with conditions and supporting data."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Iron and Steel Foundries

criteria.criterion: If your foundry commenced construction or reconstruction before December 23, 2002, then it is an existing affected source and the compliance date for applicable emissions limitations is April 23, 2007.

If you are required to conduct a performance test to demonstrate initial compliance, then you must conduct that performance test no later than 180 calendar days after the compliance date specified in § 63.7683 for your iron and steel foundry.

If you intend to use a performance test conducted before the compliance date as your initial compliance demonstration, then the test must have been conducted under conditions representative of normal operations (excluding startup, shutdown, and malfunctions) and must include recorded process information and an explanation supporting that the conditions represent normal operation.

If you are demonstrating compliance with the PM concentration limits for a pouring station or pouring area, then the performance test must follow the PM test methods and procedures in § 63.7732(b), including selecting sampling port locations (Method 1/1A), measuring volumetric flow (Method 2 series), dry molecular weight (Method 3 series), moisture (Method 4), and PM concentration (Method 5 variants), and must include a minimum of three valid test runs with at least 60 dscf collected per run.

If you are demonstrating compliance using PM or total metal HAP expressed as mass per ton for sources (where allowed), then the performance test must determine the total mass of metal charged during each run and use the required equations and inputs (mass charged, test duration, flow, concentration) specified in § 63.7732(b)(6) and (c)(6).

If you conducted a performance test, then you must have submitted a notification of intent to conduct the performance test at least 60 calendar days before the test and must submit the notification of compliance status including the performance test results no later than 60 calendar days after the completion of the performance test.

If you expect the performance test results to establish site-specific operating limits or demonstrate compliance with operating limits, then you must have established appropriate site-specific operating limits in your O&M plan and have a record of operating parameter data measured during the performance test as required in § 63.7734(b) and § 63.7736.

If you claim the April 2005 stack test is representative of current production capability (for purposes of lb/ton or flow-normalized results), then the test records must document the process parameters used (including metal charged, test duration, production rate) and include an explanation and supporting records demonstrating that those production rates reflect normal, current operation in accordance with § 63.7732(a).

checklist: Date your foundry commenced construction or reconstruction (determine if before or after December 23, 2002).
Whether the M-1 unit is a pouring area or a pouring station and whether it is at a new or existing foundry.
Date(s) of the April 2005 performance test and whether the test date is before or after the compliance date (April 23, 2007) and the 180-day window in § 63.7730(a).
Whether a notification of intent to test was submitted at least 60 calendar days before the April 2005 test.
Whether a notification of compliance status including the performance test results was submitted within 60 calendar days after test completion (or otherwise as allowed by § 63.7750(e)).
Which test methods were used (Method 1/1A, Method 2 family, Method 3 family, Method 4, Method 5 variants for PM; Method 29 for metals; Method 18/25/25A for VOHAP, as applicable).
Number of valid runs in the test (must be at least three) and the sample volume per run (at least 60 dscf).
Whether testing excluded startup/shutdown/malfunctions and whether records include an explanation that test conditions represent normal operations per § 63.7732(a).
Recorded process parameters during each test run (mass of metal charged, test duration, flow rates, Q, moisture, molecular weight) needed to calculate gr/dscf and lb/ton metrics.
Whether sampling ports were located at the outlet of the control device or at the outlet of the emissions source prior to any release to the atmosphere.
If relying on lb/ton results, verify metal charged (Mcharge) and test duration (ttest) were measured and recorded for each run per § 63.7732(b)(6) and (c)(6).

Whether operating parameter data measured during the performance test were recorded and whether site-specific operating limits were established in the O&M plan based on those test data per § 63.7734(b) and § 63.7736.

Whether any control device outlets were sampled (if a control device exists) and whether combined-stream procedures or flow-weighted calculations were applied correctly if multiple streams were combined (per § 63.7732(h)).
