candidates.title: Mercury Cell Chlor-Alkali and Mercury Recovery Units

criteria.criterion: If you operate one or more mercury thermal recovery unit vents and you choose the continuous monitoring option under § 63.8240(a), then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration for each operating day from 15-minute continuous Hg CEM readings using Equation 2 and the sampling frequency specified in § 63.8242(a)(1).

If you operate mercury thermal recovery unit vents and you choose the periodic monitoring option under § 63.8240(b), then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration using the procedures in § 63.8234(b) and the periodic monitoring requirements in § 63.8244(b).

If you have by-product hydrogen streams or end box ventilation system vents at a mercury cell chlor-alkali production facility, then you must determine weekly mercury emission rates and reduce them to 52-week average grams Hg per megagram Cl2 using Equation 1 for continuous compliance with the applicable emission limits.

If your final control device is not a nonregenerable carbon adsorber and you choose the periodic monitoring option under § 63.8240(b), then you must follow the additional periodic monitoring and CPMS hourly-average collection requirements in § 63.8244(b)(2)(ii)–(v) and related parameters in § 63.8232.

If you operate a mercury thermal recovery unit vent, then you must demonstrate continuous compliance by maintaining the outlet mercury daily-average concentration at or below the applicable limit specified in § 63.8190(a)(3).

candidates.title: Electric Utility Steam Generating Units (EGUs) — Hg CEMS and Sorbent Trap Monitoring

criteria.criterion: If you use a CEMS or a sorbent trap monitoring system to measure Hg emissions for an affected source under Subpart UUUUU, then you must demonstrate continuous compliance using all quality-assured hourly data to calculate the arithmetic average emissions rate on a continuous 30-boiler operating day rolling average (or 90-boiler operating day if alternate Hg averaging is used) updated at the end of each boiler operating day.

candidates.title: Copper Concentrators/Smelters — Mercury CEMS Monitoring Option

criteria.criterion: If you are an affected source subject to the mercury emissions limit in Subpart QQQ and you use a Hg CEMS, then you must maintain the average concentration of mercury discharged at or below the emission limit and determine the average on a 6-hour rolling basis while meeting the Hg CEMS performance and QA requirements in this section.

If you use a Hg CEMS to comply with Subpart QQQ, then you must install and operate the Hg CEMS in accordance with Performance Specification 12A and maintain QA/QC per Procedure 5 as specified in § 63.1453(g)(1)(i)–(ii).

checklist: Do you operate any mercury thermal recovery unit vents, by-product hydrogen streams, or end box ventilation system vents at this facility?
For mercury thermal recovery unit vents, have you selected the continuous monitoring option (§ 63.8240(a)) or the periodic monitoring option (§ 63.8240(b))?
If using continuous Hg monitoring under Subpart IIIII, can your Hg CEM sample, analyze, and record at least once every 15 minutes as required by § 63.8242(a)(1)?
If using periodic monitoring under Subpart IIIII, is your final control device a nonregenerable carbon adsorber (affects which periodic procedures apply)?
For by-product hydrogen and end box vents, do you record weekly mercury emission rates and weekly chlorine production so you can compute 52-week g Hg/Mg Cl2 averages per § 63.8243(a)?
Are you subject to Subpart UUUUU (is the affected source an EGU) and do you use a CEMS or sorbent trap system to measure Hg emissions?
If relying on Subpart UUUUU monitoring, can you collect and retain all quality-assured hourly Hg data and perform 30- or 90-boiler operating day rolling-average calculations using hourly data?
Are you subject to Subpart QQQ (copper smelting/concentrator processes) and do you plan to use a Hg CEMS to comply with the mercury limit?
If using a Hg CEMS under Subpart QQQ, can you meet Performance Specification 12A and Procedure 5 QA/QC requirements and compute 6-hour rolling averages as required?

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "EPA's note states the facility must calculate a daily-average Hg concentration and that confusion arose over references to hourly averages. Our Answer explicitly includes the Subpart IIIII daily-average calculation (from 15‑min CEMs or periodic monitoring) and also identifies where hourly averages appear (CPMS hourly‑average collection for certain periodic monitoring and hourly data/rolling averages in other subparts UUUUU and QQQ), so the key reasons in the EPA notes are captured."}

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (Subpart FFFF)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) located at or part of a major source of HAP, then your units are subject to Subpart FFFF.

If your process includes batch process vents, then you must determine the batch vents' Group status by summing uncontrolled organic HAP emissions using the procedures specified in § 63.1257(d)(2)(i) and (ii).

If you want EPA approval to set operating limits or monitoring/recordkeeping approaches different from those specified in §§ 63.2455 through 63.2485 (including requests to define operating scenarios or use standard-batch conventions for recordkeeping/reporting), then you must submit a precompliance report to request that approval and EPA will approve or disapprove within 90 days.

If you elect to comply with a percent reduction emission limit using emissions averaging, then you must follow § 63.150 as modified for this subpart and estimate uncontrolled emissions for a standard batch using the procedures specified in § 63.1257(d)(2)(i) and (ii) when calculating monthly debits and credits.

If you define and use a 'standard batch' for recordkeeping and emissions calculations, then you must keep records indicating whether each batch operated was considered a standard batch and estimate uncontrolled and controlled emissions for any nonstandard batch as specified in § 63.2525(d) and (e).

If you use operating scenarios (including definitions of standard batches or multiple standard-batch scenarios), then you must maintain a schedule or log of operating scenarios and update it each time a different operating scenario is put into effect and report new operating scenarios in compliance reports as required.

If you include alternative recordkeeping, calculation methods, or engineering assessments (e.g., to align annual emission estimates with AEI or TRI/SARA 313 practices), then you must submit the supporting data, rationale, and any test or engineering-assessment documentation in the notification of compliance status or precompliance report as required by § 63.2520(d) and § 63.2520(c).

checklist: Is the process an MCPU at a major source (verify applicability per 40 CFR 63.2435(a)–(b))?
Does the process have batch process vents (verify which vents meet the 'batch process vent' definition in 40 CFR 63.2550)?
What is the uncontrolled organic HAP emissions total for the batch vents (calculate per § 63.2460(b) using § 63.1257(d)(2)(i)/(ii) procedures) to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 status?

Do you currently define 'standard batch' operating scenarios in writing and document the range of operating conditions and the emissions-per-standard-batch basis (compare to the definition in 40 CFR 63.2550 and record requirements in 40 CFR 63.2525)?

Do you plan to use emissions averaging or alternative emission calculation methods (verify intent to elect emissions averaging per 40 CFR 63.2500(a) and the need to calculate standard-batch emissions per 40 CFR 63.2500(e))?

Will the proposed recordkeeping change affect initial compliance demonstrations, operating limits, or monitoring parameters (if yes, are you prepared to submit a precompliance report per 40 CFR 63.2520(c) with supporting data and rationale)?

Are you prepared to include the following in a precompliance report or Notification of Compliance Status: descriptions of operating scenarios, calculations/engineering analyses, data and rationale for any alternate methods, and identification of any new operating scenarios (per 40 CFR 63.2525(b) and 63.2520(d))?

How will you track and report rolling annual emissions (e.g., number of standard batches, emissions per batch, or alternative annual-factor approach) and can you produce the monthly/rolling calculations required by § 63.2525(e) and reporting requirements in § 63.2520(e)?

If you control vents with a control device or plan to use flares/adsorbers, have you confirmed the applicable monitoring/recordkeeping requirements and whether any referenced subpart requirements apply (e.g., control-device monitoring in §§ 63.2450–63.2505)?

If aligning to Annual Emissions Inventory or SARA 313 methods, can you supply the documentation tying your chosen standard-batch emissions factors and annualization method to the regulatory-required emission-estimation procedures requested in the precompliance/notification reports?

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Pharmaceuticals Production

criteria.criterion: If the facility manufactures a material that meets the definition of a "pharmaceutical product" (for example, a finished dosage form, an active ingredient or precursor, or a material described by SIC code 2833 or 2834 or NAICS 325411/325412) then the operations meet the definitional scope for Subpart GGG.

If the material produced is a nonreactive solvent, excipient, binder, or filler, or is produced in a chemical manufacturing process unit that is subject to subparts F or G of part 63, then that material is excluded from the definition of "pharmaceutical product" for purposes of Subpart GGG.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (MON Rule)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU) located at or part of a major source of HAP, then the process unit is potentially subject to Subpart FFFF.

If the MCPU produces materials classified under SIC codes in the 1987 282–289 range or NAICS 1997 code 325 (subject to the exceptions listed) and the MCPU processes, uses, or generates any of the organic HAP listed in section 112(b) or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP, then the unit meets the material/service criteria for Subpart FFFF.

If the operation is an exempt activity listed in §63.2435(c) (for example research and development facilities or other specifically enumerated exclusions), then the requirements of Subpart FFFF do not apply to that operation.

If an emission stream is part of an MCPU (batch or continuous) and is combined with other emission types, then applicability/compliance is determined either by applying the requirements for each emissions type or by the hierarchy in §63.2450(c) to select the controlling requirements for the combined stream.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) Production

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an HCl production facility that produces a liquid HCl product at a concentration of 30 weight percent or greater during normal operations and the facility is located at or part of a major source of HAP, then the HCl production facility is subject to Subpart NNNNN.

If the facility is also subject to one of the other listed NESHAPs (for example Subpart GGG for pharmaceuticals or Subpart MMM for pesticide active ingredient production), then the HCl production facility is excluded from Subpart NNNNN as specified in §63.8985(b).

If your operations only use HCl as a reagent (i.e., you do not produce liquid HCl product meeting the 30 wt% production criterion), then you would not meet the fundamental applicability criterion for Subpart NNNNN.

candidates.title: General MACT for Specific Source Categories (procedures for determining primary product and storage/recovery assignment)

criteria.criterion: If the process unit's primary product is a product that is a listed source category under Subpart YY (see §63.1103 and Table 1 to §63.1100), then the source must comply with the Subpart YY requirements applicable to that source category.

If a process unit is designed or operated as a flexible operation unit, then the primary product determination (based on operating time or 5-year production expectation) controls applicability of Subpart YY to that unit.

checklist: Is glucosamine hydrochloride produced at your site manufactured/marketed as a pharmaceutical active ingredient, precursor, finished dosage form, or otherwise primarily used as a pharmaceutical (i.e., does it meet the Subpart GGG "pharmaceutical product" definition)?
What is the facility's primary SIC code and NAICS code (verify whether primary manufacturing operations are classified as SIC 2833 or 2834 or NAICS 325411/325412)?
Is the plant a major source of HAP (potential to emit or actual emissions ≥10 tons/yr of any single HAP or ≥25 tons/yr total HAP)?
Do you produce liquid HCl product onsite at ≥30 weight percent during normal operations, or do you only use HCl as a reagent?
Does the process unit produce, use, or generate any organic HAP listed in CAA section 112(b) or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP (determine species and quantities)?
Are the operations research & development (R&D) only (i.e., pilot/bench-scale R&D that meet the R&D facility exemption)?

Are your production operations organized as a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU) as defined (materials classified under SIC 282–289 or NAICS 325 and meet the MCPU equipment/process criteria)?

For batch operations: determine batch process vent emissions (uncontrolled mass per year) and whether vents meet Group 1 thresholds (e.g., ≥10,000 lb/yr existing or ≥3,000 lb/yr new) and whether any continuous/batch vents, storage tanks, or wastewater streams are combined (so you can apply the hierarchy in §63.2450(c)).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Site Remediation

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility at which you conduct a site remediation that (1) cleans up a remediation material, (2) is co-located at your facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition under another subpart of 40 CFR part 63, and (3) your facility is a major source of HAP, then the site remediation is subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation only cleans up material that does not contain any of the HAP listed in Table 1 of this subpart, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a gasoline service station to clean up remediation material from a leaking underground storage tank, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a farm or residential site, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a research and development facility that meets the requirements under CAA section 112(c)(7), then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If the total quantity of the HAP listed in Table 1 contained in the remediation material excavated, extracted, pumped, or otherwise removed during all site remediations conducted at your facility is less than 1 megagram (Mg) annually, then the site remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart except for the recordkeeping requirement.

If all remediation activities at your facility subject to this subpart are completed and you have notified the Administrator in writing that all such remediation activities are completed, then those remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart (but you must maintain records of compliance).

If a site remediation is completed within 30 consecutive calendar days according to the initiation, completion, and shipping conditions specified in § 63.7884(b)(1)–(3), then that site remediation is not subject to the standards in § 63.7884(a).

If a remediation material management unit manages remediation material whose average total VOHAP concentration is less than 500 ppmw (demonstrated according to § 63.7943), then remediation material management units downstream from the point of determination meet the requirements of § 63.7886(b)(2) instead of the control-based options.

If the remediation material treated or managed by a process vent has an average total VOHAP concentration less than 10 ppmw (determined per § 63.7943), then the process vent may qualify under the alternative in § 63.7885(b)(2) instead of meeting the control requirements.

If a surface impoundment is an affected remediation material management unit subject to § 63.7886(b)(1)(iii), then you must control HAP emissions by installing and operating either a floating membrane cover or a cover vented through a closed vent system to a control device as specified in § 63.7905.

If equipment components contain or contact remediation material with total HAP ≥10 percent by weight and are intended to operate ≥300 hours/year in remediation material service, then those components are part of the affected equipment-leaks source per § 63.7882(a)(3).

checklist: Is the contaminated soil 'remediation material' (soil primarily composed of unconsolidated earth material and containing one or more HAP listed in Table 1 of Subpart GGGGG)? (see 40 CFR 63.7957 definition of remediation material)
Does the remediation activity occur at a gasoline service station UST site, a farm or residential site, or an R&D facility meeting CAA 112(c)(7) (exemptions in 40 CFR 63.7881(b)(4)–(6))?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 ton/yr single HAP or ≥25 ton/yr combined HAP) when aggregated appropriately (see 40 CFR 63.7881(a)(3))?

Is the site remediation co-located at the facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition under another 40 CFR part 63 subpart? (40 CFR 63.7881(a)(2))

What is the total annual mass (Mg/yr) of the HAPs in all remediation material excavated/removed at the facility this year (to compare to the 1 Mg/yr threshold in 40 CFR 63.7881(c)(1)) and do you have written documentation of the methodology and data used (40 CFR 63.7881(c)(2))?

Will the excavation, temporary on-site storage, and final placement (backfill) of the soil be completed within a single 30-consecutive-calendar-day period that meets the initiation and completion definitions in 40 CFR 63.7884(b)(1)–(3)?

Will any remediation material be managed in units that qualify as tanks, containers, surface impoundments, separators, or transfer systems as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957 (to determine applicable management-unit requirements under 40 CFR 63.7886)?

Have you measured or will you measure the average total VOHAP concentration of the soil (using the procedures required by the subpart) to determine whether it is <500 ppmw for remediation material management units or <10 ppmw for process-vent alternatives (40 CFR 63.7886(b)(2); 40 CFR 63.7885(b)(2))?

If shipping remediation material off-site within 30 days under the 30-day exemption, will your shipping documentation include the required statement and initiation/completion dates per 40 CFR 63.7884(b)(2)?

If claiming the <1 Mg/yr exemption for specific remediation material management units, have you identified and designated the exempt units, and prepared the initial determination and supporting documentation of annual HAP quantity placed in those units per 40 CFR 63.7886(d)(1)–(2)?
For any surface impoundment used, will you install and operate the required cover or closed vent/control device per 40 CFR 63.7905, if applicable?

For equipment components potentially in remediation-material service, do they contain remediation material ≥10% HAP by weight and are they intended to operate ≥300 hours/year (to determine if they are part of affected equipment-leaks source per 40 CFR 63.7882(a)(3))?

judge_text: {"score":2, "reason":"EPA’s sole key reason is that reuse of HAP-containing soil as backfill without any cleanup is not a ‘‘site remediation.’’ OUR ANSWER explicitly includes the applicability element that the activity must ‘‘clean up a remediation material’’ (40 CFR 63.7881(a)(1)) and asks whether the soil is remediation material, thereby capturing the EPA rationale."}

candidates.title: National emission limits, operating limits, and work practice standards for Organic Liquids Distribution (OLD) (non-gasoline) operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an organic liquids distribution (OLD) operation that is located at, or is part of, a major source of HAP emissions, then the OLD operation is subject to this subpart.

If containers, transport vehicles, storage tanks, transfer racks, or equipment leak components are used as non-permanent units in special-situation distribution loading or unloading operations (for example, maintenance or upset liquids management), then those non-permanent units are excluded from the affected source for this subpart.
If a container is loading or unloading organic liquids at a transfer rack that is part of the affected source, then that container is part of the affected source covered by this subpart.

If the collection of transfer racks at the facility meets the total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume criterion for control in Table 2 (items 7 through 10), then the transfer-rack requirements of § 63.2346(b) apply to those racks (including requirements specific to loading into transport vehicles and, for new sources, into containers).

If a storage tank storing organic liquids meets the tank capacity and liquid vapor pressure criteria for control in Table 2 (items referenced in § 63.2346(a)), then the storage-tank control options and requirements in § 63.2346(a) apply.

If the transfer rack at the facility only unloads organic liquids (i.e., no loading into transport vehicles or containers occurs at the rack), then that transfer rack may not be required to be controlled under this subpart and documentation verifying that condition must be kept.

If you have an affected source subject to control under this subpart, you must comply with the notification, recordkeeping, and reporting schedules and content requirements in § 63.2382 and related record requirements (including records of annual facility loading volume) to demonstrate applicability and compliance.

candidates.title: Referenced subpart SS (requirements for meeting emission limits for storage tanks and transfer racks)

criteria.criterion: If you choose to meet the emission limits for storage tanks or transfer racks by complying with the referenced provisions for meeting emission limits, then you must comply with the applicable requirements specified in subpart SS of this part as incorporated in § 63.2346(a)(1) and § 63.2346(b)(1).

candidates.title: Referenced subpart TT (equipment-leak control level 1)

criteria.criterion: If pumps, valves, or sampling connections operate in organic liquids service for at least 300 hours per year and the affected source has at least one storage tank or transfer rack that meets the applicability criteria for control in Table 2 or 2b, then equipment-leak requirements from subpart TT (control level 1) may apply as specified in § 63.2346(c).

candidates.title: Referenced subpart UU (equipment-leak control level 2)

criteria.criterion: If pumps, valves, or sampling connections operate in organic liquids service for at least 300 hours per year and the affected source has at least one storage tank or transfer rack that meets the applicability criteria for control in Table 2 or 2b, then equipment-leak requirements from subpart UU (control level 2) may apply as specified in § 63.2346(c).

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (i.e., meets the major-source definition)?
Are the described transfers (container-to-container and truck-to-container) part of the facility's organic liquids distribution (OLD) operation or are they separate process operations?
Are the hoses/valves used permanent transfer equipment (part of a transfer rack) or non-permanent/temporary connections used only for special situations (maintenance, upset liquids management)?
Are the container-to-container and truck-to-container transfers routine loading/unloading (i.e., part of normal distribution) or only occasional for maintenance/upset?

Do transfers occur at a transfer rack as defined by the rule (i.e., a single system used to load into or unload transport vehicles or containers including loading arms, pumps, meters, shutoff valves, relief valves, and other piping and equipment)?

If transfers occur at a transfer rack, what is the facility's total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume through transfer racks (calculate 3-year rolling average) to compare to Table 2 applicability thresholds?

Are the transfers 'loading into containers' (note: transfer-rack controls for containers are required for new affected sources) and is the affected source new or existing (verify construction/startup/reconstruction dates relative to April 2, 2002; Feb 3, 2004; and later compliance-date provisions)?

Are any of the involved storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, or equipment leak components already part of another 40 CFR part 63 NESHAP (which would exclude them under § 63.2338(c)(1))?
Do any transfer racks only unload organic liquids (no loading)? If yes, compile and maintain documentation verifying unload-only status per § 63.2343(a).

Do any pumps, valves, or sampling connectors operate in organic liquids service for ≥ 300 hours/year? If yes, list those components and determine which equipment-leak subpart (TT, UU, or H) is applicable.

Are transport vehicles vapor-tight or equipped with vapor collection equipment and do they have the required U.S. DOT certifications (49 CFR part 180 subparts E/F) when loaded at subject transfer racks?
Document dates of construction, reconstruction, and initial startup for the affected source to determine whether 'new', 'reconstructed', or 'existing' subpart provisions apply.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Both key EPA points are reflected: the answer includes that the activities meet the definition of a transfer rack (criteria referencing §63.2338(b)(5) and transfer-rack applicability/volume thresholds §63.2346) and also includes the special-situation/non‑permanent-unit exclusion (§63.2338(c)(2)) and checklist items addressing maintenance/upset/temporary connections."}

candidates.title: Monitoring requirements.

criteria.criterion: If you operate a kraft or soda smelt dissolving tank equipped with a wet scrubber, then you must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate a CPMS that can determine and record the pressure drop across the scrubber and the scrubbing liquid flow rate at least once every successive 15-minute period.

If you wish to establish or revise the minimum scrubber pressure drop operating limit, then operating limits must be established during the initial or periodic performance test or based on previous performance-test data obtained using the test methods and procedures required in this subpart, with minimum scrubber pressure drop set as the lowest of the 1-hour average pressure drop values associated with compliant test runs (except as otherwise allowed for certain dynamic/low-energy scrubbers).

If the smelt dissolving tank dynamic wet scrubber operates at ambient pressure or is a low-energy entrainment scrubber where fan speed does not vary, then you may use fan amperage or fan RPM (or percent full load amperage approaches) as an alternative to direct pressure-drop measurement to set minimum operating limits.

If you want to monitor alternative control device operating parameters or change to alternative monitoring methods, then you must obtain prior written approval by the Administrator and include in your request how the parameter operating limit is to be set (and, for other control devices, provide test results and proposed performance specifications).

candidates.title: What emission limitations must I meet? / What test methods and other procedures must I use to establish and demonstrate initial compliance with the operating limits? / What are my continuous monitoring requirements?

criteria.criterion: If a wet scrubber is applied to meet any PM, PM10, chlorine, HCl, or dioxin/furan emission limit under this subpart, then you must maintain the hourly average pressure drop and scrubber liquid flow rate at or above the minimum level established during the initial or subsequent performance test.

If you are establishing site-specific operating limits for a wet scrubber subject to pressure-drop and scrubber water flow-rate limits, then you must use the CPMS to measure and record pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate at least every 15 minutes during each run of the particulate matter performance test and set the operating limits as the lowest average individual pressure-drop and flow-rate values from any of the three runs that meet the applicable emission limit.

If your wet scrubber is subject to the operating limits in this subpart, then you must at all times monitor the hourly average pressure drop and liquid flow rate using a CPMS according to the continuous monitoring requirements of this subpart.

If you want to change (revise) the operating limits for a control device under this subpart, then you must submit written notification to the Administrator, conduct a new performance test demonstrating compliance with the applicable emission limitation, and establish revised operating limits according to the applicable procedures.

candidates.title: What test methods and other procedures must I use to establish and demonstrate initial compliance with the operating limits?

criteria.criterion: If a wet scrubber is subject to performance testing in § 63.9620 and operating limits for pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate in § 63.9590(b)(1), then you must use the CPMS to measure and record the pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate every 15 minutes during each run of the particulate matter performance test and establish operating limits as the lowest average pressure drop and the lowest average scrubber water flow rate corresponding to any of the three test runs.

If your dynamic wet scrubber is subject to the provisions in paragraph (b), then you must follow those procedures for measuring scrubber water flow rate and either fan amperage or pressure drop during test runs and establish site-specific limits as described in paragraph (b).

If you wish to change the operating limits for any air pollution control device under this section, then you must submit a written notification to the Administrator of your request, conduct a performance test to demonstrate compliance with the applicable emission limit, and establish revised operating limits according to the applicable procedures.

candidates.title: How may I change the compliance levels of monitored parameters?

criteria.criterion: If you want to change control device and process operating parameter levels that were established during performance tests and are used to monitor compliance under this subpart, then you must notify the Administrator of your desire to expand the range and, upon approval, conduct additional performance tests at the proposed new parameter levels with test results verifying that the new levels comply with the applicable emission limits before operating at those levels.

checklist: Confirm whether your smelt dissolving tank is an 'affected' kraft or soda smelt dissolving tank under Subpart MM or is regulated under Subpart TTTTT or Subpart RRRRR (determine which subpart(s) your source is subject to).
Locate and review the performance test report(s) that established the current pressure-drop operating limit (including the 1-hour average pressure drop values and which test run(s) were used).
Verify the averaging period used to set the current operating limit (e.g., 1-hour average during test runs, hourly averages, and CPMS 15-minute measurement intervals).

Verify whether your scrubber is a dynamic wet scrubber operating at ambient pressure or a low-energy entrainment scrubber where fan speed does not vary (this affects whether fan amperage/RPM may be used instead of pressure drop).

Confirm that your CPMS measures pressure drop and scrubbing liquid flow rate at the required frequency (measurements at least every 15 minutes) and that the pressure-drop sensor is certified to the manufacturer accuracy requirement (±500 pascals / ±2 inches of water) and flow sensor accuracy as required by the applicable subpart.

Determine whether historical certified performance-test data (three-run data or other eligible tests) exist that show compliant particulate/emission values corresponding to lower average pressure-drop values that could be used to set a lower operating limit.

If you propose a new lower pressure-drop limit, identify whether you will (a) rely on existing compliant test data, (b) request Administrator approval for alternative monitoring/parameters, or (c) notify the Administrator and perform a new performance test (and prepare to submit required notifications and test plans).
Check state or delegated authority procedures for submitting a written notification or alternative monitoring request and confirm the appropriate Administrator or state contact for approval.

Record the current limit (10 inches H2O), the proposed limit (5 inches H2O), and whether the proposed limit is within sensor accuracy bounds (consider ±2 inches accuracy) and the margin between measured compliant 1-hour averages and the proposed limit.

Prepare CPMS data summaries (15-minute and hourly averages) for the performance-test periods and recent operation to demonstrate how often current readings approach or fall below 10 in H2O and how close typical compliant operation is to the proposed 5 in H2O limit.

The response cites 40 CFR 63.864(j) and other subparts and explicitly states that operating limits must be set based on performance-test data (or during a performance test) and that revising limits requires notification and conducting a performance test; these capture the EPA note that 63.864(j) allows changed parameter ranges only with a performance test at the new limit."}

candidates.title: Steel Pickling NESHAP (Subpart CCC)

criteria.criterion: if a wet scrubber is used as the emission control device at a steel pickling facility or hydrochloric acid regeneration plant subject to this subpart, then the owner or operator must install, operate, and maintain systems to measure and record the scrubber makeup water flow rate and, if applicable, the recirculation water flow rate, monitor these flow rates continuously, and record them at least once per shift while the scrubber is operating

if performing a performance test to establish compliant operating parameter values for a wet scrubber under this subpart, then each operating parameter must be monitored continuously and recorded with sufficient frequency to establish a representative average value but no less frequently than once every 15 minutes during the emission test

if a monitoring device is used under this subpart, then each monitoring device must be certified by the manufacturer to be accurate to within 5 percent and must be calibrated in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions but not less frequently than once per year

if required monitoring parameters (e.g., scrubber makeup water flow rate and recirculation water flow rate) are not recorded as specified by this subpart, then the owner or operator is in violation of the monitoring requirements of this subpart

if scrubber flow rate monitoring and other required monitoring are performed, then the owner or operator must retain records (including scrubber makeup and recirculation flow rates) for 5 years with the most recent 2 years of records kept on site

if a scrubber emission control device is subject to the maintenance requirements of this subpart, then the operation and maintenance plan must require monitoring and recording the pressure drop across the scrubber once per shift while the scrubber is operating

candidates.title: Subpart TTTTT (CPMS requirements for wet scrubbers)

criteria.criterion: if a wet scrubber is subject to the operating limits in this subpart, then the scrubber water flow rate CPMS must use a flow sensor with a minimum measurement sensitivity of 2 percent of the flow rate and must conduct a flow sensor calibration check at least semiannually

if a wet scrubber is subject to the operating limits in this subpart, then each CPMS must complete a minimum of one cycle of operation for each successive 15-minute period, have valid data for at least 95 percent of every averaging period, and determine and record the hourly average of all recorded readings

if initial compliance is being demonstrated using a particulate matter or related performance test for a wet scrubber subject to pressure drop and water flow rate limits, then the owner or operator must measure and record the pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate at least every 15 minutes during each run and compute and record the average for each individual test run to establish site-specific operating limits

candidates.title: Subpart MM (CPMS monitoring for wet scrubbers at affected kraft/soda recovery furnaces and lime kilns)

criteria.criterion: if an affected kraft or soda recovery furnace or lime kiln is equipped with a wet scrubber, then the owner or operator must install a CPMS that can determine and record the scrubbing liquid flow rate at least once every successive 15-minute period and use a monitoring device certified to be accurate within ±5 percent of the design scrubbing liquid flow rate

if a CPMS is used under this subpart, then each CPMS must complete a minimum of one cycle of operation for each successive 15-minute period and must determine and record the hourly average of all recorded readings and the 3-hour average of all recorded readings

candidates.title: Subpart EEEEE (capture system and wet scrubber CPMS requirements)

criteria.criterion: if a wet scrubber is subject to the operating limits in § 63.7690(b)(2) under this subpart, then you must at all times monitor the 3-hour average pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate using a CPMS according to the installation/maintenance requirements in § 63.7741(c)

if you use a flow measurement device to monitor an operating-limit parameter for a capture system under this subpart, then you must monitor the hourly average flow rate at all times, use a flow sensor with a minimum measurement sensitivity of 2 percent of the flow rate, conduct a flow sensor calibration check at least semiannually, and visually inspect components at least monthly

if a CPMS is used under this subpart, then each CPMS must complete a minimum of one cycle of operation for each successive 15-minute period and must determine and record the hourly average and the 3-hour average of all recorded readings

checklist: Confirm whether the facility (mini-mill) and the two continuous pickling lines and the acid regeneration plant are regulated as affected sources under Subpart CCC (steel pickling facility or hydrochloric acid regeneration plant).
Identify whether each pickling line and the acid regeneration plant use a wet scrubber as the air pollution control device and whether any scrubber operates with recirculation.
Verify whether each scrubber has continuous monitoring (flow sensors/CPMS) installed for makeup water flow rate and, if applicable, recirculation flow rate.
Determine whether monitoring during any performance test recorded scrubber operating parameters at least once every 15 minutes and whether the run averages were used to set minimum operating limits.
Confirm the required recording frequency during normal operations (at least once per shift per Subpart CCC) for each scrubber and whether any additional CPMS hourly/3-hour averaging is configured.

Verify that each monitoring device is manufacturer-certified for accuracy (±5% for flow under CCC/MM or 2% sensitivity where applicable) and the calibration frequency meets the referenced requirement (manufacturer's instructions but not less than annually for CCC; semiannual flow-sensor calibration where specified).

Confirm CPMS operational settings: completes ≥1 cycle per 15-minute period; generates required data points to compute hourly and 3-hour averages; and meets valid-data percentage requirements (e.g., ≥95% where specified).

Confirm that scrubber pressure drop monitoring (if required by the O&M plan) is implemented and recorded at the shift frequency specified in the O&M plan (Subpart CCC) and that pressure tap and sensor inspection/calibration procedures are in place.

Verify recordkeeping practices: scrubber flow rate records are retained for 5 years with the most recent 2 years on site, and records of calibrations, manufacturer certifications, inspections, performance tests, and any corrective actions are maintained.

Check whether the site’s operation and maintenance plan for each emission control device has been prepared, includes required monitoring/recording procedures, and is incorporated into the Title V permit as applicable.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note hinges on two points — continuous monitoring of scrubber flow rates and recording frequency of once per shift — and those points are directly captured by the Subpart CCC criterion in the answer (40 CFR 63.1162(a)(2))."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Miscellaneous Coating Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations that are located at or are part of a major source of HAP emissions, manufacture coatings, and process, use, or produce HAP, and the operations are not part of an affected source under another subpart, then the operations are subject to this subpart.

If a tank or other vessel (stationary or portable) has a capacity greater than or equal to 250 gallons and is used for mixing, blending, diluting, temporary holding, or other processing steps in the manufacturing of a coating, then that vessel is a process vessel for this subpart.

If the operation is an affiliated operation located at an affected source subject to certain other subparts (for example mixing of coating ingredients at an affected source under subpart MMMM), then the miscellaneous coating manufacturing requirements in this subpart do not apply to those affiliated operations.

If the activity is limited to modifying a purchased coating in preparation for application at the purchasing facility, then the requirements for miscellaneous coating manufacturing do not apply to that activity.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products Surface Coating Operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an affected source that uses 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and the source is a major source (or located at/part of a major source), then this subpart applies.

If a vessel is a storage container or mixing vessel in which coatings, thinners, and/or other additives and cleaning materials are stored or mixed, then that vessel is part of the affected source covered by this subpart.

If coating use for an individual coating operation is less than 189 liters (50 gallons) per year and the total volume of coatings exempt under this paragraph does not exceed 946 liters (250 gallons) per year at the facility, then those coating operations are exempt from this subpart.

If the equipment is used for surface coating activities (including mixing and storage associated with surface coating), then it is included in the definition of a coating operation and may be part of the affected source under this subpart.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Large Appliance Surface Coating

criteria.criterion: If you operate a large appliance surface coating affected source, then the affected source includes all storage containers and mixing vessels in which coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials are stored or mixed.

If the facility is not an affected large appliance surface coating source (i.e., does not meet the applicability criteria for this subpart), then this subpart does not apply to its mixing vessels even if such vessels are present.

checklist: Confirm the mixer capacity in gallons (actual vessel working capacity) and whether it is >= 250 gallons (process vessel threshold in HHHHH).
Confirm whether the mixer is portable or permanently installed (HHHHH defines process vessel as stationary or portable).

Determine whether the mixer is used for mixing, blending, diluting, temporary holding, or other processing steps in the manufacture of coatings (i.e., formulation/manufacturing) versus only for surface-coating activities or minor touch-up.
Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥ 10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥ 25 tpy combined HAP) or is located at/part of a major source.

Determine annual volume of coatings that contain HAP used at the facility (gallons per year) to assess the 946 L (250 gal/yr) threshold for subpart MMMM applicability and the per-operation <189 L (50 gal/yr) exemption limit.

Determine whether the mixer is used to modify a purchased coating for application at the purchasing facility (exclusion under HHHHH) or is part of affiliated operations at a source subject to another subpart (e.g., MMMM), which may exclude HHHHH applicability.
Determine whether coatings/materials handled in the mixer contain HAP (and approximate HAP content) and whether the operation processes, uses, or produces HAP (required for HHHHH applicability).
Determine whether the mixer is classified or operated as a storage tank (excluded from HHHHH storage tank definition) or as a process vessel (included) under the definitions in 40 CFR 63.8105.

Determine whether the mixer is part of a large appliance surface coating affected source (for potential applicability of subpart NNNN) or part of miscellaneous metal parts surface coating operations (for MMMM).

If seeking to use any exemptions or alternatives (e.g., small-volume exemptions or emissions averaging), collect and document records of annual usage, batch counts, and process descriptions required by the cited subparts.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note cites two key reasons—mixer capacity <250 gallons and therefore not meeting the process-vessel definition. The provided criteria include the 250-gallon process-vessel threshold (40 CFR 63.8105/63.7985) and checklist items addressing capacity and process-vessel classification, so the key reasons are captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Site Remediation

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility at which you conduct a site remediation, then this subpart applies to you.
If your site remediation cleans up a remediation material, then that condition of applicability in §63.7881(a)(1) is met.

If your site remediation is co-located at your facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition for a source category regulated by another subpart under 40 CFR part 63, then that condition of applicability in §63.7881(a)(2) is met.
If your facility is a major source of HAP (≥10 tons per year of any single HAP or ≥25 tons per year combined HAP), then that condition of applicability in §63.7881(a)(3) is met.
If your site remediation only cleans up material that does not contain any of the HAP listed in Table 1 of this subpart, then you are not subject to this subpart.

If the total quantity of the HAP listed in Table 1 contained in remediation material removed during all site remediations at your facility is less than 1 megagram annually, then your site remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart except for the recordkeeping requirement in paragraph (c)(2).

If all remediation activities at your facility that are subject to this subpart are completed and you have notified the Administrator in writing that they are completed, then the site remediation is not subject to the requirements of this subpart (records retention still required).
If a site remediation is completed within 30 consecutive calendar days and meets the procedural conditions in §63.7884(b)(1)–(3), then that remediation is not subject to the standards in §63.7884(a).

If the remediation units on the property are owned or operated by a different entity and are not under common control with your facility, then those units are considered a different facility and applicability is determined for the owner/operator of that separate facility.

If affected process vents, remediation material management units, or equipment leaks at the site meet the definitions in §63.7882 and §63.7957 (process vents, tanks, containers, surface impoundments, transfer systems, equipment components, pressure relief devices), then those specific affected sources at the site are subject to the subpart's standards unless an exemption option applies.

checklist: Do you (the current property owner/operator) own or operate the remediation units, or does another legal entity own and operate them under the Consent Order?
Who is legally obligated to conduct and control the remediation activities (identify the party named in the Consent Order)?
Are the remediation units and activities under common control with your other facility operations (ownership, lease, or operational control)?
Are the remediation units located on contiguous or adjoining property under your common control or owned/operated by a different entity?

Do the remediation activities constitute 'site remediation' as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957 (i.e., activities that remove, destroy, degrade, transform, immobilize, or otherwise manage remediation material)?
Do the remediation materials contain any HAP listed in Table 1 of Subpart GGGGG?

What is the total annual quantity (mass) of the Table 1 HAP contained in all remediation material excavated, extracted, pumped, or otherwise removed during all site remediations at the facility (Mg/yr)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP) when aggregating facility emissions per 40 CFR 63.2 (or the specified aggregation rules for certain sectors)?
Are the remediation activities co-located with one or more other stationary HAP-emitting sources that meet an affected-source definition in another part 63 subpart?
Are the remediation activities completed, and if so, have you submitted written notification to the Administrator that all subject remediation activities are complete?
For any individual remediation event, was the event completed within 30 consecutive calendar days and documented per §63.7884(b)(1)–(3)?
Are the remediation units subject to CERCLA or RCRA corrective action and what are the construction/reconstruction commencement dates (to determine new vs. existing source status per §63.7882(d))?
For process vents: what are the vent stream flow rates and total HAP concentrations to evaluate the exemptions in §63.7885(c)?

For equipment: which components contact remediation material, what are their HAP concentrations, and do they operate ≥300 hours/yr (to determine equipment-leak affected-source status per §63.7882(a)(3))?
Does your current Title V operating permit already include the remediation units or any recordkeeping requirement from §63.7881(c)(2), and will the permit need revision?

The EPA note’s key reason — that Boeing (another legal entity) is legally responsible for and operates the remediation activities — is covered by the candidate criteria and checklist items stating that remediation units owned/operated by a different entity (not under common control) are treated as a separate facility and applicability is determined for that owner/operator, and by checklist questions about legal obligation/ownership under the Consent Order."}

candidates.title: Standards for Hazardous Waste Combustors (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If the unit is a hazardous waste incinerator (including all associated firing systems and combustion chamber equipment) that burns hazardous waste at any time, then it is subject to Subpart EEE requirements.

If the combustion system includes multiple combustion chambers (for example, a rotary kiln and a secondary combustion chamber), then you must measure the temperature of each combustion chamber and establish a minimum hourly rolling average limit for each combustion chamber based on the average of the test run averages.

If you propose to treat two or more chambers as a single combustion chamber (or otherwise avoid an operating parameter limit), then you must submit an application to the Administrator for approval of an alternative monitoring requirement or a waiver of the operating parameter limit with the comprehensive performance test plan and demonstrate that the alternative or waiver provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance.

If hazardous waste remains in the combustion chamber (i.e., the hazardous waste residence time has not transpired since waste feed cutoff), then you must comply with the operating parameter limits (including minimum combustion chamber temperature) at all times; different monitoring/limits may apply when hazardous waste is not in the combustion chamber.

If the automatic waste feed cutoff (AWFCO) would be triggered by an exceedance of the minimum combustion chamber temperature, then you may not ramp down pumpable hazardous waste during that AWFCO (i.e., ramp-down is prohibited when AWFCO is triggered by minimum combustion chamber temperature).

If you request an alternative monitoring requirement or waiver, then the Administrator will approve it only if the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance and you must submit the request not later than with the comprehensive performance test plan.

checklist: Verify whether your unit is classified as a hazardous waste incinerator under Subpart EEE (i.e., burns hazardous waste at any time and includes associated firing systems and combustion chamber equipment).

Document the physical configuration and gas flow path: are the rotary kiln and secondary combustion chamber separate enclosed combustion chambers, in series, and where is hazardous waste fed (which chamber/feed locations)?

Determine whether the facility has previously established operating parameter limits (OPLs) and performance-test-derived minimum combustion chamber temperatures for each chamber during a comprehensive performance test (and where the temperature measurement locations were documented).

Identify the location(s) where temperature sensors (thermocouples/pyrometers) can best represent the bulk gas temperature in the combustion zone for each chamber and record those locations in the performance test plan.

Calculate the hazardous waste residence time for your configuration (if multiple firing systems, use the longest residence time) and include the calculation in the performance test plan and operating record.
Confirm AWFCO design and interlocks: can the AWFCO be configured to interlock on the minimum combustion chamber temperature and will it prevent ramp-down when that limit triggers an AWFCO?

Collect performance-test and operational data showing temperature, CO/HC, and other relevant parameters for each chamber to support any alternative-monitoring or waiver request demonstrating equivalent assurance of compliance.

Prepare to submit any alternative-monitoring or waiver request to the Administrator not later than with the comprehensive performance test plan, including technical data, proposed alternative monitoring approach, averaging periods, and justification that the alternative equals or exceeds assurance of compliance.

Verify whether the permitting/authority in your state (Ohio) is the delegated 'Administrator' for approval of alternative monitoring requests or whether you must submit to EPA Region and plan timelines accordingly.
Document whether you will operate under any different modes of operation and, if so, prepare separate OPLs for each mode and document mode transitions in the operating record per § 63.1209(q).

Ensure the comprehensive performance test plan includes the temperature measurement location documentation and any demonstration needed to show that combining chambers (or treating them as one) will not reduce assurance of compliance (see performance test plan content requirements).

Confirm that, if an operating-parameter waiver is not approved, you will establish and comply with minimum combustion chamber temperature OPLs for each combustion chamber while hazardous waste is present.

The EPA note’s key point—that the rotary kiln and secondary combustion chamber are separate combustion chambers and thus require separate minimum combustion chamber temperature limits—is reflected in the answer (see criterion requiring temperature measurement and minimum limits for each chamber and the criterion describing that treating multiple chambers as one requires Administrator approval/waiver). The checklist also addresses documenting the chambers as separate enclosed combustion chambers."}

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Metal Furniture

criteria.criterion: If the facility conducts surface coating of metal furniture (as defined) and the affected source is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source, then the source is subject to this subpart.
If surface coating conducted at an affected source uses only coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP, then this subpart does not apply to that surface coating.

If the collection of equipment used for surface coating of metal furniture includes coating operations, storage containers and mixing vessels, conveying equipment and pumps and piping, and waste storage/conveying items as listed, then those items together constitute the affected source covered by this subpart.
If the affected source is new or reconstructed, then it must emit no organic HAP during each compliance period.
If the affected source is an existing affected source, then it must limit organic HAP emissions to no more than 0.10 kg organic HAP per liter of coating solids used during each compliance period.

If you choose the compliant material option to show compliance, then each thinner and cleaning material used must contain no organic HAP and each coating used must have organic HAP content less than or equal to the applicable emission limit as determined under the specified procedures.

If you continue to use the compliant material option after the initial compliance period, then use of any coating, thinner, or cleaning material that fails the compliant-material criteria is a deviation that must be reported.

If you use the emission rate with add-on controls option, then you must develop and implement a work practice plan (or an approved alternative) to minimize organic HAP emissions from storage, mixing, conveying, and waste handling for the coating operations using that option.

If you use either the compliant material option or the emission rate without add-on controls option for a coating operation, then you are not required to meet the work practice standards in this section for that operation.

checklist: Is the stainless steel cabinetry produced at the facility considered "metal furniture" or a metal furniture component under the subpart's definition (e.g., household, office, institutional furniture or components)?
Is the facility (or the contiguous area under common control that includes this facility) a major source of HAP (PTE of any single HAP ≥ 10 tpy or combined HAP ≥ 25 tpy)?
Is the affected source new, reconstructed, or existing (did construction commence after April 24, 2002 for a new source)?

Which physical equipment and operations are part of the coating affected source boundary (list all coating operations, storage containers and mixing vessels, pumps/piping and conveying equipment, and waste storage/handling used for coating operations)?

Do all coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials currently used contain zero organic HAP when received from the manufacturer/supplier (verify via manufacturer's formulation data, SDS, Method 311 or Method 24 test results, or equivalent supplier documentation)?
Do any adhesives, maskants, sealants, inks, or other materials applied or used in the process contain organic HAP (verify supplier data)?
If cleaning materials are reclaimed and reused onsite, were they demonstrated when received to meet the compliant-material criteria (if relying on that exception)?

If previously used methylene chloride adhesives or HAP-containing materials were used in the past, are there residues, wastes, or reclaimed streams that currently contain organic HAP that would be counted toward PTE or current usage?
Which compliance option will you use (compliant material option, emission rate without add-on controls, or emission rate with add-on controls)?

If using the compliant material option, do you have the calculations and records required to determine organic HAP content for each coating and documentation that all thinners and cleaning materials contain no organic HAP (per §63.4941 and recordkeeping requirements)?
If using add-on controls, have you prepared the required work practice plan and will you meet the operating limits and monitoring requirements for capture and control systems?

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Secondary Lead Smelting (Secondary Lead Smelting MACT)

criteria.criterion: If your facility recycles lead-bearing scrap material (primarily, but not limited to, lead-acid batteries) into elemental lead or lead alloys by smelting, then the facility is a 'secondary lead smelter' and is subject to this subpart.

If you own or operate any affected source at a secondary lead smelter (e.g., blast, reverberatory, rotary, or electric furnaces; refining kettles; agglomerating furnaces; dryers; process fugitive emissions sources; buildings containing lead-bearing materials; or fugitive dust sources) then you are subject to this subpart.
If your facility is a primary lead processor, lead refiner, or lead remelter, then the provisions of this subpart do not apply to you.

If the materials you process have lead content equal to or greater than 5 mg/L as measured by EPA Method 1311 (and note that Method 1311 considers only materials with at least 100 ppm lead), then those materials meet the subpart's definition of 'lead bearing material' relevant to determining whether you are a secondary lead smelter.

If you operate affected sources at a secondary lead smelter, then the subpart's applicability does not depend on whether current measured lead emissions are below the numeric emission limits because applicability is based on operating the affected sources and the emissions standards apply at all times.

checklist: Do you recycle lead-bearing scrap into elemental lead or lead alloys by smelting (i.e., do you perform 'smelting' as defined in 40 CFR 63.542)?
Measure or document the lead content of your feedstock using EPA Method 1311: are values >= 5 mg/L (or >= 100 ppm) so the material is 'lead bearing' under the rule?

List all process equipment and areas you operate: do you have any of the affected sources listed (blast, reverberatory, rotary, electric furnaces; refining kettles; agglomerating furnaces; dryers; battery breakers; process fugitive vents; buildings containing lead-bearing materials; fugitive dust sources)?
Are you a primary lead processor, lead refiner, or lead remelter (i.e., processing ore or performing primary refining rather than recycling scrap)?
Do you have process vents that emit lead compounds; if so, obtain most recent compliance-test concentrations and flow rates for each vent (to allow flow-weighted averaging per 40 CFR 63.543)?
Document construction or reconstruction dates for affected sources relative to May 19, 2011 (to determine any staggered compliance/implementation provisions in §63.546).

Document control devices and practices in use (baghouses, wet scrubbers, total enclosures, HEPA, CEMS, bag leak detection systems, etc.) because they affect monitoring and recordkeeping obligations under the subpart.

Collect records of current measured lead emissions and comparison to numeric limits (e.g., per §63.543: 1.0 mg/dscm single vent and 0.20 mg/dscm flow-weighted average for existing sources) but do not assume low measured emissions change applicability.

Prepare to verify required monitoring/recordkeeping items if subject (SOP manuals, baghouse monitoring, enclosure negative pressure monitoring, CEMS or annual performance tests as applicable) as referenced throughout §§63.543–63.550.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The EPA’s key reason—that the facility recycles lead-bearing scrap material and thus is subject to the Secondary Lead Smelting MACT—is directly captured by the candidate criteria (criterion 1). The response also includes related rationale (definition of lead‑bearing material via Method 1311 and that current low measured emissions do not affect applicability), so all key reasons from the EPA notes are present."}

candidates.title: General Provisions (recordkeeping and reporting requirements)

criteria.criterion: if an owner or operator is an affected source subject to this part then the owner/operator must maintain files of all information required by this part for at least 5 years and keep the most recent 2 years of data on site

if an owner or operator is an affected source subject to this part then records may be maintained in hard copy or computer-readable form and must be recorded in a form suitable and readily available for expeditious inspection and review

candidates.title: Recordkeeping requirements for storage vessels (Subpart WW)

criteria.criterion: if an owner or operator is subject to Subpart WW then the owner/operator must keep a record of the vessel dimensions, an analysis of vessel capacity, and an identification of the liquid stored for as long as the liquid is stored

if an owner or operator is subject to Subpart WW and conducts floating roof inspections or EFR seal gap measurements then the owner/operator must keep records of inspection results and must keep the raw data obtained for EFR seal gap measurements and any calculations performed

if an owner or operator is subject to Subpart WW then records required in paragraphs (b), (c), and (d) must be kept for at least 5 years and records must be kept in a manner that they can be readily accessed (including keeping them in hard copy or computer-readable form)

candidates.title: Recordkeeping requirements for tanks and control devices (Subpart DD)

criteria.criterion: if an owner or operator is subject to Subpart DD then the owner/operator must comply with the recordkeeping requirements in § 63.10 of subpart A as specified in this subpart

if an owner or operator uses an external floating roof under Subpart DD then the owner/operator must prepare and maintain records for each seal gap inspection that include the date of the measurement, the raw data obtained, and the calculations of total gap surface area

if an owner or operator uses a floating roof under Subpart DD then the owner/operator must record each inspection and each defect detected during required inspections including location, description, date of detection, and corrective action taken (and reasons/schedule if repair is delayed)

candidates.title: Recordkeeping requirements referencing storage-vessel records (Subpart HHHHHH)

criteria.criterion: if an owner or operator is subject to Subpart HHHHHH and has internal or external floating roof storage vessels then the owner/operator must maintain the records required in § 63.1065 of Subpart WW (including the raw data for EFR measurements where applicable)

if an owner or operator maintains records electronically or submits records electronically via CEDRI then the owner/operator may keep electronic copies but must still make records, data, and reports available upon request as part of an on-site compliance evaluation

checklist: Determine which NESHAP subpart(s) actually apply to your facility and the specific tanks (e.g., Subpart WW, DD, HHHHHH, or other storage-vessel subpart).
Confirm whether each tank is classified as an external floating roof (EFR) storage vessel under the applicable subpart.
Identify which records the applicable subpart requires for EFRs (e.g., inspection results, EFR seal gap measurements, and explicitly the 'raw data' and calculations for seal gap measurements).

Verify the retention period required by each applicable provision (e.g., vessel-dimensions kept while liquid is stored per 63.1065(a); other inspection/measurement records kept for at least 5 years; Subpart A: 5 years with most recent 2 years on site).
Confirm on-site accessibility requirements (e.g., records must be readily accessible within 24 hours per Subpart WW and most subparts reference §63.10(b)(1) for expeditious inspection).

Confirm whether electronic records contain the complete raw data and calculations that the rule requires (i.e., that the electronic entry is a full, auditable reproduction of field measurements and calculations).

Verify whether retention of the original field data sheets is specifically required by the applicable subpart or whether an accurate electronic record that includes the raw data and calculations satisfies the 'raw data' requirement.

Ensure the electronic recordkeeping system provides on-site access to required records (or remote access readily available from on site) and appropriate backups to meet the retention and availability requirements.
Check for any state-delegated requirements or permit (e.g., Title V) conditions that impose different retention formats, durations, or on-site original-document requirements.

If you plan to discard original field sheets after transfer, document the equivalence (date/time stamps, who entered data, original handwritten values or instrument outputs preserved) so you can demonstrate that the required 'raw data' and calculations are retained and available for inspection.

However, it does not capture the EPA QA guidance/letter point that original field records themselves must be preserved (the 2008 QA guidance/letter and the 63.654→63.123(d) citation referenced by EPA Notes are not asserted as a binding requirement), so only some key reasons are present."}

candidates.title: Area Source Standards for Plating and Polishing Operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plating and polishing facility that (1) is an area source of HAP emissions, (2) is engaged in one or more listed plating or polishing processes (such as non-chromium electroplating, electroless plating, chromate conversion coating, thermal spraying, dry mechanical polishing, electroforming, or electropolishing), and (3) uses or has emissions of plating and polishing metal HAP (cadmium, chromium, lead, manganese, or nickel), then the facility is subject to this subpart.
If a process unit is subject to the requirements of 40 CFR part 63, subpart N (chromium electroplating and chromium anodizing tanks), then this subpart does not apply to that process unit.

If any plating or polishing process uses process materials that contain cadmium, chromium, lead, or nickel (as the metal) in amounts less than 0.1 percent by weight and manganese in amounts less than 1.0 percent by weight (as used), then that plating or polishing process is not subject to this subpart.

If you own or operate an affected electrolytic (non-cyanide, pH < 12) electroplating, electroforming, or electropolishing tank that contains one or more plating and polishing metal HAP, then that tank is subject to the equipment/management-practice standards in this subpart.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Chromium Emissions from Hard and Decorative Chromium Electroplating and Chromium Anodizing Tanks

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chromium electroplating or chromium anodizing tank at a facility performing hard chromium electroplating, decorative chromium electroplating, or chromium anodizing, then that tank is an affected source subject to this subpart.

If a tank is associated with a chromium electroplating or chromium anodizing process but neither chromium electroplating nor chromium anodizing is taking place in that tank (examples include rinse tanks, etching tanks, and cleaning tanks), then that tank is not subject to this subpart.

If the process uses a chromic acid solution and the part to be processed acts as the anode to produce an oxide layer (i.e., meets the definition of chromium anodizing), then the process meets the definition of chromium anodizing and the tank could be an affected source under this subpart.

If research and laboratory operations are being conducted (as defined for this subpart), then affected sources engaged in those research or laboratory operations are exempt from this subpart while such operations are taking place.

candidates.title: General Provisions (40 CFR part 63, subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a new or existing affected source that is subject to this or another subpart, then you must comply with the General Provisions (subpart A) as specified for that subpart.

checklist: Determine whether the tank bath contains chromic acid or other chromium(VI) compounds (e.g., CrO3) and the concentration or presence of hexavalent chromium.

Determine whether the process is electrolytic and whether the part serves as the anode (confirm electrical configuration and whether an oxide layer is being produced versus an etching/cleaning reaction).

Determine whether the tank operation is performing chromium anodizing or chromium electroplating versus an etching/cleaning/other ancillary operation (note: etching tanks are explicitly given as examples not subject to subpart N).

Determine whether the facility uses or emits any plating and polishing metal HAP (cadmium, chromium, lead, manganese, nickel) in amounts above the material thresholds (>=0.1% for Cd, Cr, Pb, Ni; >=1.0% for Mn) for an operation to be considered a plating/polishing metal HAP source.
Determine whether the facility is an area source or a major source by calculating potential to emit (PTE) for single HAP (>=10 tpy) and combined HAP (>=25 tpy).
Identify whether the tank is batch, continuous, or used for short-term/flash operations and document operating durations (affects applicable management practices and cover requirements).
If the bath uses cyanide and operates at pH >= 12, document that (cyanide/cyanide-plating definitions may affect applicable provisions under subpart WWWWWW).
Verify whether the operation is research/laboratory or strictly educational, or otherwise exempt per the subpart definitions.

If subject to a subpart, determine which notification, recordkeeping, and compliance demonstration requirements will apply (e.g., Initial Notification, Notification of Compliance Status, annual compliance certification) and the applicable compliance date.
Document manufacturer specifications and operating instructions for any capture/control devices, and record whether wetting agents/fume suppressants are used and in what amounts/times if applicable.
