candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Area Sources: Carbon Black Production

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a carbon black production facility that is an area source of hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.

If you own or operate a new or existing affected source, then the affected source is each carbon black production process unit including all associated waste management units, maintenance wastewater, and equipment components that contain or contact HAP associated with the carbon black production process unit.
If you are a research and development facility as defined in section 112(c)(7) of the Clean Air Act, then this subpart does not apply to you.
If you own or operate an area source subject to this subpart, then you must obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 40 CFR part 71.
If you are subject to this subpart, then you must meet all the requirements in § 63.1103(f) of subpart YY (the carbon black production provisions in § 63.1103).

If you own or operate an existing affected source, then you must achieve compliance by July 16, 2007; if you started up a new affected source after July 16, 2007, then you must achieve compliance upon startup.

candidates.title: Source category-specific applicability, definitions, and requirements (includes carbon black production)

criteria.criterion: If a carbon black production process unit is located at a major source as defined in section 112(a) of the Act, then the affected source under § 63.1103(f) comprises each carbon black production process unit and associated waste management units, maintenance wastewater, and equipment contacting HAP.
If your process produces carbon black by the furnace, thermal, acetylene decomposition, or lampblack processes, then your process meets the definition of 'carbon black production' in § 63.1103(f)(2).

If a carbon black production main unit filter process vent or other carbon black production process vent has a HAP concentration equal to or greater than 260 parts per million by volume (as determined per the process vent applicability procedures), then beginning by the compliance dates specified you must control that vent per Table 8 (for example by routing to a flare or achieving 98 weight-percent reduction or to 20 ppmv as specified).

If you choose not to perform applicability tests or TRE calculations, then you may opt to comply with the most stringent requirements applicable to an emission point under this subpart in lieu of performing applicability assessments.
If you perform an applicability assessment for main unit filter or dryer vents, then you must follow the HAP concentration determination and reporting procedures specified in § 63.1103(f)(3)(iv)–(v).

candidates.title: NESHAP for Off-site Waste and Recovery Operations (affected plant sites receiving off-site materials)

criteria.criterion: If the plant site is a major source of HAP emissions and at the plant site one or more operations receive off-site materials and those operations are one of the listed waste management or recovery operations, then this subpart applies to the owner and operator of the plant site.
If either the plant site is not a major source of HAP or the operation does not receive off-site material of the listed types, then this subpart does not apply to the plant site.

If the material received meets all of: (i) is a waste, used oil, or used solvent as defined in § 63.681, (ii) is delivered to the plant site from outside the plant boundaries, and (iii) contains one or more Table 1 HAP at the point of delivery, then the material is an 'off-site material' for purposes of this subpart.

candidates.title: General Provisions (selected sections §§63.1–63.5 and §§63.11–63.16)

criteria.criterion: If you are subject to Subpart MMMMMM, then the General Provisions in 40 CFR part 63 Subpart A (§§ 63.1–63.5 and §§ 63.11–63.16) apply to that subpart.

checklist: Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAPs (potential to emit ≥10 megagrams/yr [10 tpy] of any single HAP or ≥22.68 megagrams/yr [25 tpy] of combined HAP).
Determine whether the facility is an area source (not a major source) — compare results from the major-source check.
Confirm whether your process is a carbon black production process as defined (furnace, thermal, acetylene decomposition, or lampblack processes).

Identify each carbon black production process unit and whether it includes reactors, main unit filter, dryer, associated recovery devices, feed/intermediate/product storage vessels, and connected ducts and piping.

Measure or determine HAP concentration (ppmv) for the main unit filter process vent and other carbon black process vents (and follow the § 63.1103(f)(3)(iv) applicability procedures) to see if any are ≥260 ppmv.
If vents are manifolded with a dryer, document whether the dryer is routed to the same control device or must be evaluated separately per applicability procedures.

Verify whether the facility receives shredded tires or other materials from off-site and whether those materials meet the 'off-site material' definition (waste/used oil/used solvent delivered from outside and containing Table 1 HAP at point-of-delivery).
If you receive off-site materials, determine whether the plant site qualifies as a major source and whether the operations match the listed off-site waste/recovery operation types in Subpart DD.
Determine whether your facility is a research and development facility per CAA § 112(c)(7) (if so, Subpart MMMMMM may not apply).

Document construction/startup dates for the affected process units (compare to April 4, 2007 and July 16, 2007 compliance/startup dates cited for MMMMMM) to classify as new or existing affected sources.
If subject to Subpart MMMMMM, prepare to comply with § 63.1103(f) (see Table 8 requirements) and confirm any required permits under 40 CFR part 70 or 71.
Keep records of any prior applicability tests (e.g., tests after November 18, 2016 or after November 19, 2021) and whether process changes have occurred since those tests that could affect emissions.

OUR ANSWER includes the defining criterion (§63.1103(f)(2)) and a checklist item to confirm whether the process is furnace/thermal/acetylene/lampblack (i.e., whether it meets the Subpart MMMMMM definition), so the EPA rationale is captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Surface Coating of Plastic Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: If the facility performs surface coating of plastic parts and products as described in §63.4481(a) (general use, automotive lamp, TPO, or assembled on‑road vehicle subcategories), then the operations are within the source category addressed by this subpart (subject to further applicability tests).

If the facility uses 378 liters (100 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain hazardous air pollutants (HAP) and is a major source or is located at a major source of HAP, then the affected source is subject to Subpart PPPP.
If the coating operation meets any of the exclusion criteria listed in §63.4481(c) (paragraphs (c)(1) through (c)(17)), then that surface coating or coating operation is not subject to this subpart.

If you elect to demonstrate compliance using the emission rate with add-on controls option, then you must demonstrate that the organic HAP emission rate (after accounting for capture and add-on control reductions) is less than or equal to the applicable emission limit and that the emission capture systems and add-on control devices meet the operating limits and work practice standards required in this subpart.

If you use an add-on control device for a controlled coating operation that is not a solvent recovery system using a liquid‑liquid material balance, then you must establish operating limits for the capture and add-on control system during the performance tests required in §63.4560 and meet those operating limits at all times.

If you plan to use an add-on control device other than those listed in Table 1 to this subpart or to monitor an alternative parameter or comply with a different operating limit, then you must apply to the Administrator for approval of alternative monitoring under §63.8(f).

If you use an add-on control device (other than a solvent recovery system with liquid‑liquid material balance) to claim emission reductions, then you must calculate monthly organic HAP emission reductions by applying the measured capture efficiency and the measured organic HAP destruction or removal efficiency (DRE) of the add‑on control device to the mass of organic HAP in materials used, using the procedures and Equation 1 in §63.4561(h).

If an operating parameter for an add-on control system is out of the allowed range specified in Table 1 to this subpart, then that is a deviation and you must treat the emission capture system and add-on control device as achieving zero efficiency for the period of the deviation unless approved alternate data are used.

If you use a solvent recovery system and elect to conduct liquid‑liquid material balances, then you must follow the liquid‑liquid material balance procedures and monthly solvent recovery efficiency calculations in §63.4561(j) instead of the operating limits in Table 1.

checklist: Confirm the operations are surface coating of plastic parts/products and determine which PPPP subcategory applies (general use, automotive lamp, TPO, assembled on‑road vehicle).
Determine annual volume of coatings that contain any HAP (liters or gallons per year) and whether that usage meets or exceeds 378 L (100 gal/yr).
Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP (≥10 tons/yr of any single HAP or ≥25 tons/yr combined HAP) or is located at a major source.
Identify whether any §63.4481(c) exclusion applies to your coating operations (review paragraphs (c)(1)–(17)).
Decide whether you will use the emission rate with add‑on controls compliance option for each coating line or group of lines.

Document whether you plan to route captured emissions to an existing boiler (describe how emissions will be captured and routed) and whether the boiler functions to destroy or remove organic HAP (i.e., will act as an add‑on control).
Check whether the boiler or control configuration is listed in Table 1 of Subpart PPPP (or otherwise characterized in the rule) or would be considered a different/novel control device.
If the boiler is not listed in Table 1 or you intend to monitor/comply using alternative parameters, prepare to apply for alternative monitoring approval under 40 CFR 63.8(f).

Estimate expected capture efficiency and estimated organic HAP destruction/removal efficiency (DRE) for the capture system + boiler; determine whether you can demonstrate these efficiencies via required performance testing and methods (performance test per §63.4560 and measurement methods referenced in §63.4561).

Plan for initial performance testing to establish operating limits and continuous monitoring as required, and prepare the required work practice plan per §63.4493 for controlled coating operations using add‑on controls.
Verify whether the control approach will require treating deviations as zero efficiency (and plan monitoring/recordkeeping to detect/report deviations per §63.4563).

If considering solvent recovery instead of combustion, determine whether a liquid‑liquid material balance approach is applicable and feasible and whether monthly solvent recovery metering can meet §63.4561(j) requirements.

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If replacement of components of an affected source results in the fixed capital cost of the new components exceeding 50 percent of the fixed capital cost that would be required to construct a comparable new source, then the activity meets the definition of reconstruction (subject to new-source standards).

If an owner or operator has undertaken a continuous program of construction or reconstruction or entered into a contractual obligation to undertake and complete, within a reasonable time, a continuous program of construction or reconstruction, then construction or reconstruction is considered to have 'commenced' for applicability/timing purposes.

candidates.title: Subpart KK

criteria.criterion: If costs associated with the purchase and installation of air pollution control equipment are incurred, then those costs are not considered in determining whether an affected source has been reconstructed.
If equipment was retrofitted or replaced specifically to comply with the requirements of this subpart, then the costs of that retrofitting or replacement are not considered reconstruction costs.

candidates.title: Engine Test Cells and Stands NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an engine test cell/stand that is located at a major source of HAP emissions, then your test cell/stand is subject to this subpart.

If the collection of equipment and activities associated with engine test cells/stands used for testing uninstalled engines is located at a major source, then that collection is the affected source for this subpart.
If reconstruction is commenced after May 14, 2002 and the activity meets the definition of reconstruction in §63.2, then the affected source is a reconstructed affected source.

If changes to an existing affected source were made primarily for the purpose of complying with revisions to engine testing requirements under 40 CFR parts 80, 86, 89, 90, 91, or 92, then those changes are not considered a modification or reconstruction for this subpart.
If the changes consist of passive measurement and control instrumentation and electronics, then those items are not included in any affected source reconstruction evaluation.

If any portion of a new or reconstructed affected source is used exclusively for testing internal combustion engines with rated power of less than 25 hp (19 kW), then that portion does not have to meet the requirements of this subpart except for the initial notification requirements.

If any portion of a new or reconstructed affected source is used exclusively for testing combustion turbine engines, rocket engines, research and teaching activities not engaged in commercial engine development or testing services, or for testing/evaluating fuels, transmissions, or electronics, then that portion does not have to meet the requirements of this subpart.

If you have a new or reconstructed affected source that is used in whole or in part for testing internal combustion engines with rated power of 25 hp (19 kW) or more and located at a major source, then the source is subject to the emission limitations in Table 1 to this subpart.
If you have a new or reconstructed affected source, then the compliance dates and timing rules in §63.9295 for new or reconstructed sources apply to your source.

checklist: Determine whether your plant site is a 'major source' (potential to emit ≥ 10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥ 25 tpy of combined HAP).
Identify and list each engine test cell/stand and confirm they test uninstalled engines (definition of uninstalled engine).

For each change, replacement, or addition since 2002, document the scope, dates, and whether work was part of a continuous program or under a contractual obligation (to establish when 'commenced' occurred).

Prepare an itemized cost estimate: (a) fixed capital cost of the new/changed components, and (b) estimated fixed capital cost to construct a comparable new affected source, to determine whether new-component cost > 50% (reconstruction test).

Identify which replaced/added items (if any) are passive measurement and control instrumentation and electronics and separately total their costs to exclude them from the reconstruction cost calculation.

Identify any purchase and installation costs for add-on air pollution control equipment or costs of retrofits/replacements made specifically to comply with a subpart and separately total those costs (to exclude per §63.826(c)).

Determine whether any changes were made primarily to comply with revisions to engine testing requirements under 40 CFR parts 80, 86, 89, 90, 91, or 92 (such changes are not considered reconstruction).

Determine whether any portion of the affected source is used exclusively for testing engines <25 hp, combustion turbine engines, rocket engines, noncommercial research/teaching, or testing fuels/transmissions/electronics (those portions may be excluded from this subpart).
If you may be a new or reconstructed affected source, compile dates of startup or reconstruction commencement to compare with the compliance date rules in §63.9295.

If planning to rely on exclusions (passive instrumentation or control-equipment cost exclusions), retain design/engineering descriptions and invoices demonstrating the nature and cost of those items for the reconstruction evaluation.

candidates.title: Asphalt Processing and Asphalt Roofing Manufacturing NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an asphalt processing facility or an asphalt roofing manufacturing facility that is a major source (or is located at/part of a major source), then the source is subject to Subpart LLLLL.

If you use a control device and monitor parameters with a continuous parameter monitoring system (CPMS), then the CPMS must complete at least one cycle every 15 minutes, meet the 3‑hour averaging/data‑validity rules, and record inspection/calibration/validation results.

If you use pressure drop (across a mist eliminator or other control device) as a monitored parameter, then the pressure measurement device must meet the sensitivity, location, daily pressure‑tap check, quarterly accuracy checks, monthly leak checks, and periodic visible inspection requirements in §63.8688(c).

If a control device is used to comply with the particulate matter standards in Table 1 to this subpart, then you may establish pressure drop operating limits (minimum and maximum) using manufacturers' specifications instead of establishing site‑specific operating limits under §63.8689(b).

If a monitoring system is required, then you must develop and make available a site‑specific monitoring plan that addresses measurement location (e.g., on or downstream of the last control device), equipment/performance specifications, performance evaluation procedures, and ongoing O&M, QA/QC, and recordkeeping.

If a control device is used to comply with the PM, THC, opacity, or visible emission standards of this subpart, then you must conduct periodic performance tests and demonstrate continuous compliance according to §63.8691 and the applicable Tables to this subpart.

If the affected source is operating, then you must monitor and collect data continuously (or at required intervals) at all times the affected source is operating, except as specified for nonoperation periods after the 2020 rule revisions.

candidates.title: Monitoring Requirements in Subpart AAAAAAA

criteria.criterion: If you are using a control device to comply with the emission limits in Subpart AAAAAAA, then you must develop and make available a site‑specific monitoring plan that addresses probe/interface installation location, equipment/performance specifications, and performance evaluation procedures.

If you are using a control device to comply with Subpart AAAAAAA emission limits, then you must install, operate, and maintain a CPMS that completes at least one cycle every 15 minutes and meets the 3‑hour averaging and data validity rules.

If you monitor pressure drop under Subpart AAAAAAA, then the pressure sensor must be located to provide a representative measurement, meet the minimum sensitivity (0.12 kPa for gauges or 5% of range for transducers), require daily pressure‑tap blockage checks, and have quarterly accuracy checks and periodic leak/visual inspections per §63.11563(e).

If you are not using a control device to comply with Subpart AAAAAAA emission limits, then you must develop and make available a site‑specific monitoring plan specifying the process parameters established during the initial compliance assessment and how they will be monitored and maintained.

If you wish to use parameters or means other than those specified in the subpart to demonstrate continuous compliance (for example, a pressure‑drop + visible emissions routine instead of an approved CPMS/COMS), then you must apply to the Administrator for approval of an alternative monitoring plan under §63.8(f) as required by §63.11563(h).

candidates.title: General Provisions (Monitoring, Opacity, O&M)

criteria.criterion: If a CMS/COMS/CPMS is required by a relevant standard, then the CMS is subject to the provisions of §63.8 (installation, operation, maintenance, QA/QC, data reduction and reporting) including minimum cycle/recording frequencies.

If you propose to use an alternative monitoring method (e.g., minimum pressure drop plus daily visible emission checks in lieu of a COMS or specified CPMS), then you must apply to and obtain approval from the Administrator under §63.8(f) before relying on that alternative for compliance; until approved you must follow the monitoring specified in the relevant subpart.

If an opacity or visible emission standard applies and a COMS is required, then compliance with the numerical opacity standard must be determined using COMS results (including COMS performance evaluation and data reduction to 6‑minute averages); if a COMS is not required the Administrator will use Method 9 (opacity) or Method 22 (visible emissions) as specified.

If your affected source is subject to a relevant standard, then you must operate and maintain the source and associated air pollution control and monitoring equipment in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices (general duty to minimize emissions) and maintain applicable SSMP/O&M records.

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is an 'asphalt processing facility' or an 'asphalt roofing manufacturing facility' as defined in 40 CFR 63.8698.
Confirm whether the facility (or the portion including the Group 2 asphalt storage tank) is a major source as defined in 40 CFR 63.2 (major source status determines Subpart LLLLL applicability).
Record the Group 2 storage tank's maximum storage temperature, maximum true vapor pressure, and capacity to verify Group 1 vs Group 2 classification (use definitions in §63.8698).
Confirm whether the mist eliminator is being used as a control device to comply with particulate matter, opacity, THC, or visible emission standards of the applicable NESHAP.

Determine whether the applicable subpart's Tables (e.g., Table 1 or Table 2 to Subpart LLLLL) establish operating limits for your tank or control device and whether a pressure‑drop operating limit is required.

If you intend to use manufacturer's pressure‑drop specifications as the operating limit, verify the control device is used to comply with PM standards in Table 1 so §63.8689(d) applies and obtain the manufacturer's documented pressure‑drop range to establish minimum/maximum limits.
Identify which monitoring system you plan to use (CPMS, COMS, CEMS, or manual visible observations) and whether the relevant subpart requires a CPMS/COMS for your control device or emission point.

If using pressure‑drop monitoring, verify the pressure sensor type and sensitivity (gauge ≥0.12 kPa or transducer ≥5% of range), sensor location (representative), and that procedures are in place for daily pressure‑tap checks, quarterly accuracy checks, monthly leak checks, and required visible inspections.

Verify CPMS/COMS cycle and data reduction capabilities (CPMS/CEMS: 15‑minute cycles and 1‑hour/3‑hour averaging rules where applicable; COMS: 10‑second cycles and 6‑minute averages) and that data recording and retention meet the subpart/§63.8 requirements.

Prepare or confirm a site‑specific monitoring plan describing measurement locations (on or downstream of last control device), equipment/performance specs, performance evaluation procedures, QA/QC, O&M, and recordkeeping per the applicable subpart.

If you intend to demonstrate compliance using minimum pressure drop plus daily visible emissions checks (instead of a COMS or required CPMS), prepare an alternative monitoring application and performance evaluation plan and apply to the Administrator under §63.8(f) (and the applicable subpart provision) before relying on that approach for compliance.

Confirm whether periodic performance tests are required for your control device and check the schedule (first periodic/performance test deadlines and 60‑month intervals) in §63.8691(e) and the applicable subpart tables.
Ensure startup/shutdown/malfunction procedures and records (SSMP where required) and operation and maintenance practices are in place consistent with §63.6(e) and the relevant subpart.
Gather existing performance test, COMS/CPMS calibration, and visible observation records (to support initial compliance demonstration or alternative monitoring approval).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator is required to do performance testing by a relevant standard, then the owner or operator must perform such tests within the timeframes in this section unless a waiver of performance testing is obtained.

If the affected source is meeting the relevant standard(s) on a continuous basis or is under an approved extension of compliance, then individual performance tests may be waived by the Administrator upon written application.

If an application is made for a waiver of a subsequent performance test and the site-specific test plan is not being submitted, then the waiver application must be submitted at least 60 days before the performance test.
If requesting a waiver of a performance test, then the application must include information justifying the request such as technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If your boiler has a heat input capacity of 10 million Btu per hour or greater, then you must conduct all applicable performance (stack) tests on a triennial basis (tests completed no more than 37 months after the previous test).

If your boiler uses a continuous emission monitoring system (CEMS) for carbon monoxide, then the boiler is exempt from the initial CO performance testing in Table 4 to this subpart and the oxygen concentration operating limit in Table 3 to this subpart.

If performance stack tests are required under this subpart, then those tests must be conducted according to §63.7 (including site-specific test plan, QA, and waiver provisions) and the procedures in §63.11212.

If you switch fuels or take a permit limit that results in the boiler switching out of this subpart, then you must provide notice of the date of the fuel switch or permit limit within 30 days of the change.

If an existing affected boiler has not operated on solid fossil fuel, biomass, or liquid fuel since the previous compliance demonstration and more than 3 years have passed since that demonstration, then you must complete the subsequent compliance demonstration no later than 180 days after re-start on those fuels.

checklist: For each boiler, confirm heat input capacity in MMBtu/hr to determine applicability of the triennial testing requirement (40 CFR 63.11220(a)).
Determine whether each boiler is located at an area source and otherwise meets the definition of an affected boiler under Subpart JJJJJJ (40 CFR 63.11194; see Subpart JJJJJJ applicability).
For each boiler, confirm whether a CO CEMS is installed and operating (if so, note the exemption from initial CO stack testing per 40 CFR 63.11212(b)).

Gather the date and full results of the last CO performance test(s) for each boiler (retain test reports and supporting QA) to document continuous compliance as the basis for any waiver request (40 CFR 63.7(g); 40 CFR 63.7(h)).
Calculate the next performance test due date for each boiler subject to triennial testing (no more than 37 months after the previous performance test) (40 CFR 63.11220(a)).

If you intend to request a waiver of a subsequent performance test, prepare a written waiver application that includes justification (technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality) and submit it at least 60 days before the scheduled test if the site-specific test plan is not being submitted (40 CFR 63.7(h)(3)(ii)-(iii)).

If a CO CEMS is used, assemble CEMS performance evaluation records and the site-specific monitoring plan (if applicable) to demonstrate continuous compliance (40 CFR 63.11205(c); 40 CFR 63.11222(a)(1)).

If planning to permanently cease coal by April 30, 2020, determine the exact date each boiler will stop burning coal and whether that fuel change will cause the boiler to switch out of Subpart JJJJJJ; if so, plan to provide the 30-day notice of fuel switch per 40 CFR 63.11225(g) and retain documentation of the change.

Verify whether any boiler has not operated on solid fossil fuel, biomass, or liquid fuel since its last compliance demonstration and whether more than 3 years have elapsed, because a restart after >3 years triggers a compliance demonstration within 180 days (40 CFR 63.11220(e)).

Keep records of notifications, waiver application, prior test reports, and all supporting documentation for at least 5 years after a performance test or as required by the subpart (40 CFR 63.7(g)(3); 40 CFR 63.11225(c) and (d)).

Our answer cites 40 CFR 63.7(h) (waiver criteria and submission timing), includes Subpart JJJJJJ fuel-switch/switch-out provisions (40 CFR 63.11225(g), 63.11220(e)), and the checklist specifically addresses permanent coal cessation and preparing a waiver application — so the EPA notes' key points are captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Halogenated Solvent Cleaning

criteria.criterion: If an individual batch vapor, in-line vapor, in-line cold, or batch cold solvent cleaning machine uses any solvent containing methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, or chloroform in a total concentration greater than 5 percent by weight as a cleaning or drying agent, then the machine is subject to Subpart T.

If the cleaning activity is limited to wipe cleaning activities (for example, a rag containing halogenated solvent or a spray cleaner containing halogenated solvent), then that activity is not covered by Subpart T.

If you are an owner or operator of an existing solvent cleaning machine subject to this subpart, then you must submit an initial notification report to the Administrator as required by § 63.468(a) by the specified deadlines.
If you are an owner or operator of a batch cold solvent cleaning machine subject to this subpart, then you must submit a compliance report as required by § 63.468(c) by the specified deadlines.

If you are an owner or operator of a batch vapor or in-line solvent cleaning machine complying with § 63.463, then you must submit an annual report by February 1 of the year following the reporting year that includes the training statement and solvent consumption estimate specified in § 63.468(f).
If you are an owner or operator of a batch vapor or in-line solvent cleaning machine complying with § 63.464, then you must submit a solvent emission report every year as required by § 63.468(g).

If you are an owner or operator of an affected facility as defined in § 63.471(a), then you must maintain a log of solvent additions and deletions for each solvent cleaning machine and ensure the facility's total PCE, TCE and MC emissions meet the applicable facility-wide 12-month rolling total emission limit in § 63.471(b)(1) and (b)(2).

If you are an owner or operator of an affected facility, then you must submit a solvent emission report every year containing the average monthly solvent consumption and the 12-month rolling total solvent emission estimates as required by § 63.471(h).

If you are an owner or operator of a batch vapor or in-line solvent cleaning machine subject to § 63.463, then you must retain the machine-specific records specified for lifetime of the machine and the monitoring/annual records for the 5-year periods required by § 63.467(a), (b), and (c).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If you are an owner or operator of any solvent cleaning machine meeting the applicability criteria of § 63.460(a), then the provisions of Subpart A (General Provisions) apply to you except as specifically noted for Subpart T.

checklist: Do you currently have any solvent cleaning machines (batch vapor, in-line vapor, in-line cold, or batch cold) physically present and available for use at the facility?

For each former or existing cleaning machine, verify the current solvent(s) in use and whether any contain methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, or chloroform at a total concentration >5% by weight (use MSDS, Test Method 18, or engineering calculations).

If machines were removed or converted, document the date and method of removal or conversion and retain records showing that no regulated halogenated HAP solvent remains in the machine inventory or in recurring use.
Is any part of your solvent cleaning operations limited to wipe cleaning (rags or spray cleaners) rather than solvent cleaning machines?
Was the machine previously subject to Subpart T (check past initial notifications, compliance reports, and annual reports)?
Are you an area source or a major source (determine facility-wide HAP potential to emit and applicable source classification)?

If you qualify as an 'affected facility' under § 63.471(a), compile 12 months of solvent addition/deletion logs to calculate 12-month rolling emissions (and verify whether facility-wide limits in Table 1 apply).
Do you maintain solvent addition/deletion logs, waste solvent composition records, and calculation sheets sufficient to demonstrate monthly and rolling-period emissions per §§ 63.465 and 63.471(c)?
Have you submitted the initial notification, compliance report, and initial statement of compliance required in § 63.468 (if previously or currently subject)?
Do you have training records showing operators received the training required to support the statement in § 63.468(f)(1) (if applicable)?

If you intend to remain solvent-free, retain an on-site applicability determination record (documenting that machines do not use regulated halogenated HAPs) and keep it for the period specified by the rule (see Subpart T recordkeeping requirements and Subpart A applicability guidance).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's sole rationale—that Subpart T no longer applies because all solvent cleaning machines were removed or converted to use non‑regulated solvents—is reflected in the answer. The applicability criterion ties coverage to use of listed halogenated solvents (>5% by weight, 40 CFR 63.460(a)), and the checklist explicitly requires verifying current solvents and documenting removal/conversion and records showing no regulated halogenated HAPs remain. Thus the key reason in the EPA notes is captured."}

candidates.title: Organic Liquids Distribution (Non-Gasoline) NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an organic liquids distribution (OLD) operation that is located at or is part of a major source of HAP, then this subpart applies to that OLD operation.

If the affected OLD operation includes storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, or equipment leak components used to distribute organic liquids into, out of, or within a facility, then those items are part of the affected source covered by this subpart.

If the storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, and equipment leak components are part of an affected source already covered under another 40 CFR part 63 NESHAP, then those items are excluded from the affected source for this subpart (i.e., not subject here).

If the collection of transfer racks at the facility meets the total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume criteria for control in Table 2 (items 7–10), then the transfer racks must meet the emission limits or compliance options required in § 63.2346(b) (e.g., meeting Table 2 limits, routing to fuel gas or process, or using a vapor balancing system).
citations: 40 CFR 63.2406 (definition of transfer rack and total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume)

candidates.title: Solvent Extraction for Vegetable Oil Production NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a vegetable oil production process that is a major source of HAP (or is collocated at a plant site that is a major source) and the process processes any combination of the listed oilseeds, then the facility is subject to this subpart.
citations: 40 CFR 63.2872 (definition of vegetable oil production process)

criteria.criterion: If your vegetable oil production process uses only mechanical extraction (no organic solvent), or uses only batch solvent extraction and batch desolventizing equipment, or processes only agricultural products not listed oilseeds, or functions only as an R&D facility and is not a major source, then the process is not subject to this subpart.

If your vegetable oil production process is a continuous direct-contact solvent-extraction system (i.e., extractors, desolventizer-toasters, solvent recovery equipment) using an extraction solvent such as hexane, then the process falls within the definition of 'vegetable oil production process' covered by this subpart.
citations: 40 CFR 63.2872 (definition of extraction solvent and vegetable oil production process)

criteria.criterion: If you elect and meet the requirements to exclusively use a low-HAP solvent where each HAP is 1 percent or less by volume in each delivery and comply with the documentation/notification/certification requirements in § 63.2840(e), then the source may follow the low-HAP solvent option in lieu of other subpart requirements referenced in §§ 63.2850–63.2870 as specified in § 63.2840(e).

checklist: Determine whether the plant (plant site) is a major source of HAPs (≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy total HAP) for applicability to both subparts.

Confirm whether hexane (or solvent delivered) meets the 'organic liquid' definition for subpart EEEE (i.e., contains ≥5% by weight of organic HAP) and whether hexane is used as an extraction solvent in the vegetable oil process.

Identify whether the transfer racks and unloading equipment are part of the vegetable oil production process equipment (extractors, solvent storage, solvent recovery, desolventizers) or instead function as general site-wide organic liquids distribution separate from the process.

If transfer racks/tanks/equipment serve the vegetable oil process, verify whether those same items are already assigned to the GGGG affected source (i.e., subject to GGGG) to determine possible exclusion under 63.2338(c)(1).

Establish whether the vegetable oil process uses continuous direct-contact solvent extraction versus only mechanical extraction or batch solvent extraction/desolventizing (GGGG exclusions in §63.2832(b)).

Calculate the total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume through transfer racks (3-year rolling average as defined in 63.2406) to determine whether the EEEE transfer-rack control thresholds in Table 2 (items 7–10) are met.

For transfer racks, document whether transfers are into/out of storage tanks or directly into process units and whether transport vehicles are loaded/unloaded at the racks (see 63.2338(b) and 63.2406 transfer rack definition).

Verify whether transfer racks, storage tanks, or other equipment are part of any other 40 CFR part 63 subpart affected source (i.e., subject to another NESHAP) which would exclude them from EEEE per §63.2338(c)(1).
Check whether solvent deliveries meet the GGGG low-HAP solvent option (each HAP ≤1% by volume) and whether documentation/notifications/certifications required by §63.2840(e) are maintained.

Document whether transport vehicles (cargo tanks/tank cars) that deliver hexane are vapor-tight or have current U.S. DOT certification (49 CFR part 180 subparts E/F) as required for EEEE-controlled transfer racks and for applicable recordkeeping per §63.2390(c).
Confirm whether any storage tanks, transfer racks, or transport vehicles are non-permanent or used only for maintenance/upset situations (excluded under §63.2338(c)(2)–(3)).

Gather/retain records of total facility-level loading volumes, solvent composition (HAP fraction), and oilseed types/throughput (tons processed) for the prior 12 and 36 operating months as needed to evaluate applicability under GGGG and EEEE (see §§63.2840, 63.2872, and 63.2406).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes. EPA's key rationale—that the racks/equipment are used solely to support the vegetable oil production process and therefore fall within Subpart GGGG—is reflected in the GGGG criteria (definition of vegetable oil production process and continuous solvent-extraction coverage) and the checklist items that direct determination of whether transfer/unloading equipment are part of the vegetable oil process. The EEEE criteria also include the exclusion (63.2338(c)(1)) for equipment that is part of an affected source under another NESHAP, which captures the same allocation logic used by EPA."}

candidates.title: Monitoring requirements (Subpart S)

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator is subject to the standards in Subpart S and uses enclosures or closed-vent systems to comply with §63.450(a), then visual inspections of each enclosure opening and each closed-vent system must be performed at least once every 30 days.

If the owner or operator uses pulping process condensate closed collection systems to comply with §63.446(d), then each such condensate closed collection system shall be visually inspected every 30 days.

If a required inspection identifies visible defects or detects ≥500 ppm above background or enclosure openings are not maintained at negative pressure, then specified corrective actions (first effort within 5 calendar days, repair by 15 calendar days) must be taken unless delay is allowed under the listed exceptions.

If an owner or operator proposes monitoring frequency, operating parameter values, or alternative parameters different from those specified in paragraphs (b)–(l) of §63.453, then the owner or operator must provide the Administrator with the rationale and receive approval for the selected monitoring frequency and parameters.

candidates.title: General provisions—Monitoring requirements (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator wishes to use minor changes, intermediate or major changes, or an alternative to any monitoring requirements or procedures in this part (including changes in monitoring frequency), then the Administrator must specify or approve that change under §63.8(b)(1) or must approve the alternative under §63.8(f).

If an owner or operator requests permission to use an alternative monitoring procedure, then they must submit a written application containing the monitoring description and a performance evaluation test plan as required by §63.8(f)(4), and must not use the alternative until approved by the Administrator.

If the Administrator approves an alternative monitoring method for an affected source, then the owner/operator shall continue to use the approved alternative until the Administrator approves another monitoring method.

candidates.title: How do I monitor and collect data to demonstrate continuous compliance? (Subpart UUUU)

criteria.criterion: If a provision in a relevant subpart uses standard calendar periods (e.g., monthly) then those terms refer to standard calendar periods, and the owner/operator may change time periods specified in the subpart by mutual agreement with the Administrator as specified in Subpart A.

If the provision requires completing a task during each of multiple successive standard calendar periods, then the owner/operator may perform the required task at any time during the specified period provided it is conducted at a reasonable interval after the previous period's completion (subject to Administrator agreement).

candidates.title: How do I apply for alternative monitoring requirements for a continuous emissions monitoring system? (Subpart EEEEE)

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator requests an alternative monitoring method for demonstrating compliance with a standard in a relevant subpart (for example modifying monitoring frequency or parameters), then the owner/operator must submit a monitoring plan containing the control technique description, the CMS or method and operating parameters to be monitored, test results demonstrating compliance, and the proposed measuring/recording frequency, and must obtain Administrator approval before using the alternative.

checklist: Determine whether your facility (the pulp and paper mill) is an affected source subject to Subpart S compliance requirements cited in §63.443–63.450 (i.e., confirm Subpart S applicability to your operations).

Identify which equipment at your mill is treated as an 'enclosure', 'closed-vent system', or 'pulping process condensate closed collection system' under Subpart S and which specific systems currently require the 30‑day inspections per §63.453(k) and (l).

Document the current inspection practice: whether inspections are performed on a fixed 30‑day rolling interval or a calendar‑month basis, who performs visual inspections, and what inspection records exist.

Confirm whether inspections you seek to change are manual visual inspections (subject to the 30‑day rule) versus continuous monitoring systems (CMS) or COMS/CEMS (which follow different monitoring rules).

Assemble evidence to support an alternative schedule (e.g., staffing patterns, historic inspection records, rationale why 'once each calendar month' provides equivalent environmental protection, safety/operational constraints on weekend/holiday inspections).

Prepare any initial performance test data, monitoring parameter data, or engineering/manufacturer recommendations that justify the proposed inspection frequency and show continuous compliance, as required by §63.453(n) and §63.8(f).

Decide which approval route to pursue: (a) an alternative monitoring procedure under Subpart A (§63.8(f)), (b) a mutual agreement to change standard calendar periods if a relevant subpart follows the UUUU calendar-period approach (§63.5560(d)(1)), or (c) submit a monitoring plan per subpart‑specific procedures (e.g., §63.7747 for CEMS alternatives).

Prepare the written application/monitoring plan addressing the four elements of 'monitoring' (per §63.8(f)(4)(ii)), including frequency of measuring/recording, and include data/calculations and rationale for why the alternate frequency demonstrates continuous compliance (per §63.453(n)(4) and §63.7747(c)).

Identify the Administrator contact (EPA regional office or delegated state agency) and plan timing for submittal; note §63.8(f)(5) timelines for Administrator response and §63.7747(d) requirements that use not begin until approval is granted.

Determine whether any exemptions apply (e.g., safety/unsafe-to-inspect provisions in other subparts) and whether corrective action timing (first repair effort within 5 days, repair by 15 or 45 days depending on subpart) would be affected by changing inspection intervals (see §63.453(k)(6) and related repair timing provisions).

Verify recordkeeping and reporting implications: what documentation you must keep at the site to support any approved alternative (inspection plans, performance evaluations, approval letters) and any changes needed in periodic reports.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA's note indicates a conditional/partial approval — i.e., the inspection frequency can be changed only with Administrator approval and subject to conditions. OUR ANSWER includes the governing 30‑day requirements, the regulatory provisions allowing alternative monitoring (§63.453(n), §63.8(f)), the need to submit a written monitoring/justification plan and performance evaluation, and checklist items covering evidence, safety exceptions, repair timing, and recordkeeping. Those elements capture the key reasons for a conditional approval reflected in the EPA note."}

candidates.title: Polymers and Resins (Thermoplastic Product Process Units) NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If the plant is a major-source site that contains one or more thermoplastic product process units (TPPUs) as defined in this subpart, then the affected source and its equipment (including pressure relief devices in organic HAP service) are subject to Subpart JJJ.

If a pressure relief device is in organic HAP gas or vapor service at an affected source subject to this subpart, then the owner/operator must comply with the Subpart JJJ equipment-leak pressure relief device operating, pressure-release, and pressure-release-management requirements (unless the PRD is routed to a control/process/drain or otherwise exempted).

If a pressure relief device in organic HAP service is designed and operated to route all releases through a closed vent system to a control device, process, or drain system, then the device is not required to comply with the operating, post-release monitoring, or pressure-release-management paragraphs referenced in this subpart.

candidates.title: Equipment Leaks / Pressure Relief Devices Standards (Subpart H)

criteria.criterion: If equipment (including pressure relief devices) is intended to operate in organic HAP service 300 hours or more during the calendar year within a source that is subject to a specific subpart referencing Subpart H, then Subpart H's equipment-leak provisions apply.

If a pressure relief device is in organic HAP gas or vapor service and is subject to Subpart H, then except during a pressure release it must be operated with an instrument reading of less than 500 ppm above background and must meet the post-release monitoring or rupture-disk replacement requirements.

If a pressure relief device in organic HAP service is routed to a process, fuel-gas system, closed-vent plus control device, or an approved drain system, then the requirements in paragraphs (a) and (b) of §63.165 (operating and post-release monitoring) do not apply to that pressure relief device.

candidates.title: Equipment Leak and Transfer Rack Provisions (Subpart PPP)

criteria.criterion: If the source is an affected source described in §63.1420(a) (i.e., the Subpart PPP affected-source description), then owners/operators must comply with the adapted HON equipment-leak requirements for equipment in organic HAP service, with certain substitutions and exceptions.

If a pressure relief device at an affected source subject to Subpart PPP is in organic HAP gas or vapor service, then it must be operated except during releases with an instrument reading of less than 500 ppm above background, and after a pressure release must meet the post-release monitoring or rupture-disk replacement requirements unless routed to an approved control/process/drain.

If a pressure relief device at a Subpart PPP affected source is designed and operated to route all pressure releases through a closed vent system to a control device, process, or drain system that meets the referenced requirements, then the Subpart PPP PRD operating, post-release monitoring, and pressure-release-management paragraphs do not apply to that device.

candidates.title: Equipment Leaks (Subpart YY) — presumptions and PRD requirements for affected sources covered by Subpart YY

criteria.criterion: If a piece of equipment can reasonably be expected to contain organic HAP, it is presumed to be in organic HAP service unless the owner/operator demonstrates (e.g., via Method 18 or other allowed procedures) that organic HAP content is below the applicability criteria, and that determination governs whether equipment-leak/PRD rules apply under Subpart YY.

If an owner/operator determines that a pressure relief device is in organic HAP gas or vapor service under Subpart YY, then except during pressure releases it must be operated with instrument readings of less than 500 ppm above background and must meet the post-release monitoring or rupture-disk replacement requirements and the pressure-release-management requirements unless routed to an approved control/process/drain.

checklist: Is the plant located at a 'major source' as defined in 40 CFR part 63 (i.e., PTE ≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP)?
Does the plant operate one or more thermoplastic product process units (TPPUs) or otherwise produce a thermoplastic product listed in Subpart JJJ definitions (to determine Subpart JJJ applicability)?

For each portable container with a pressure relief device (PRD): is the container/equipment reasonably expected to be in organic HAP service (what is the organic HAP percent by weight of the contained fluid)?
For each PRD: is it in gas/vapor service or light-liquid service, or in heavy-liquid service (heavy-liquid PRDs may be exempt)?
How many hours per calendar year is each PRD/equipment in organic HAP service (is it ≥300 hours/year for Subpart H applicability)?

Are the PRDs designed and operated to route all releases through a closed-vent system to a control device, process, fuel-gas system, or drain that meets the referenced requirements (i.e., would that route make the PRD exempt from monitoring/management paragraphs)?
Do any PRDs include rupture disks (and would post-release replacement within 5 days be feasible)?

Are the containers pressure vessels designed to operate above 204.9 kPa (potential exclusion per storage-vessel definitions) or are they considered 'containers' or 'mobile equipment' that could be excluded under some subparts?
Is the owner/operator considering compliance via an alternative regulatory mechanism (e.g., 40 CFR part 65) or routing releases to control devices such that alternate monitoring would be allowed?
Are the PRDs used for waste/wastewater (process wastewater) streams that might change applicability or classification under any of the referenced subparts?

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Some key points from the EPA notes are reflected (the answer discusses routing PRDs to controls/drains as exemptions and contemplates alternative compliance mechanisms), but the EPA’s actual rationale—that an alternative monitoring plan was approved—is not explicitly captured (no citation of the regulatory authority or provision allowing EPA approval of site‑specific alternative monitoring, nor an explicit criterion stating that EPA may approve alternate monitoring plans), so only some key reasons are present."}

candidates.title: Subpart S

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator is subject to the standards specified in §§ 63.443(c) and (d), 63.444(b) and (c), 63.445(b) and (c), 63.446(c), (d), and (e), 63.447(b) or § 63.450(d), then the owner or operator shall install, calibrate, certify, operate, and maintain a continuous monitoring system (CMS) as specified in § 63.453.

If an owner or operator uses a control device, technique, or an alternative parameter other than those specified in paragraphs (b) through (l) of § 63.453, then the owner or operator shall install a CMS and establish appropriate operating parameters to be monitored that demonstrate, to the Administrator's satisfaction, continuous compliance with the applicable control requirements.

If the owner or operator seeks to establish or reestablish monitoring parameter values or site-specific monitoring parameters (including parameters to support alternative monitoring), then the owner or operator must follow the procedures in paragraph (n) to record parameter data during performance tests and provide the Administrator the rationale, data, calculations, monitoring frequency, and averaging time for approval.

If proposing alternative analytical or monitoring methods to measure total HAP or methanol concentrations for compliance demonstrations, then the owner or operator may use any other method that measures total HAP or methanol that has been demonstrated to the Administrator's satisfaction.

candidates.title: Subpart MM

criteria.criterion: If an affected kraft or soda recovery furnace, lime kiln, or other listed unit subject to this subpart wants to monitor alternative control device operating parameters (in lieu of the default CPMS parameters), then the owner or operator must obtain prior written approval by the Administrator and include in the request how the parameter operating limit is to be set.

If an owner or operator uses an air pollution control system other than an ESP, wet scrubber, RTO, or fabric filter and seeks alternate monitoring, then the owner or operator must submit an alternative monitoring request that describes the control device, test results verifying performance, the appropriate operating parameters to be monitored, how the operating limit is set, proposed performance specifications, and quality assurance procedures for the monitors for Administrator approval.

If establishing operating limits for CPMS parameters, then the owner or operator must determine those limits during the initial or periodic performance test using procedures in § 63.864(j) or base limits on prior performance-test data as specified in § 63.864(j)(1)–(2).

candidates.title: Subpart UUU

criteria.criterion: If you wish to request approval to monitor parameters other than those required in this subpart, then you must submit to the Administrator a request that includes a description of each affected source and the parameter(s) to be monitored, the methods and procedures to demonstrate the parameter determines continuous compliance (including schedule), certification that you will establish an operating limit representing proper operation, the frequency and content of monitoring/recording/reporting, supporting calculations, and the averaging time for the alternative parameter.

If you use a control device other than a thermal incinerator, boiler, process heater, flare, ESP, or wet scrubber (or want to monitor a different parameter for those devices), then you must request approval to monitor other process or control device operating parameters as required by § 63.1573(e) and provide the information in § 63.1573(f).

candidates.title: Subpart LLL

criteria.criterion: If you seek approval for alternate monitoring requirements to demonstrate compliance with the emission standards of this subpart, then you must submit an application to the Administrator no later than the notification of performance test containing data or information justifying the request, a description of the proposed alternative monitoring requirement, and documentation that the alternative would provide equivalent or better assurance of compliance, and the Administrator will notify you of approval or denial within the timeframes specified.

If an alternative monitoring application is approved or if you demonstrate compliance via performance testing or monitoring, then you must develop and (upon request) submit a site-specific monitoring plan that addresses CMS sampling probe placement, equipment specifications, performance evaluation procedures, O&M, QA, and recordkeeping per § 63.1350(p)(1)–(4).

checklist: Confirm the facility operates a kraft pulping system and identify which specific units/equipment systems are present (e.g., continuous digester, brownstock washer vents, oxygen delignification, bleach plant vents, black liquor tanks, steam strippers, condensate collection points, wastewater treatment basins).
Identify which Subpart S standards (§§ 63.443–63.447 and § 63.450) potentially apply to each equipment system and emission point (list applicable paragraph citations for each unit).

Document the control devices currently used on each affected vent or liquid stream (e.g., thermal oxidizer, ESP, wet scrubber, RTO, closed-vent and control routing to recovery) and whether any control/technique differs from those parameterized in § 63.453(b)–(l).

Assemble recent performance-test reports for each control device and treatment system (dates, methods used, three runs data, measured HAP or methanol concentrations, flow rates, oxygen corrections if applicable).

For condensate and wastewater treatment units: identify whether methanol is measured as the compliance surrogate and which test method is used (e.g., NCASI DI/MEOH-94.03 or Method 305) and provide recent concentration and flow data for inlet/outlet streams.

If proposing alternative monitoring parameters, prepare site-specific data recorded during a performance test (continuous parameter recordings) and engineering rationale, calculations, and manufacturer recommendations used to select the parameter and operating limits per § 63.453(n).

Prepare a monitoring plan (CMS design, probe location, instruments, operating parameters to be monitored, averaging time, monitoring frequency, data recording, QA/QC procedures, calibration procedures, and O&M) consistent with the subpart-specific monitoring-plan requirements (see § 63.453(n), § 63.1350(p), or comparable subpart sections).

Provide test results or other data demonstrating the proposed alternative monitoring method correlates with HAP control performance (e.g., correlation between proposed parameter and outlet HAP concentration or percent removal).

For biological treatment systems: document system type (thoroughly mixed vs nonthoroughly mixed), BOD5 performance data, archived inlet/outlet HAP samples, and site-specific bio-rate constants or plans to determine fbio(MeOH) per § 63.457(l) and § 63.453(j).

If the affected recovery furnace or associated control is present, document whether the unit uses an ESP, wet scrubber, RTO, or other APCD and gather CPMS/COMS data and any prior operating limits established during performance tests per Subpart MM.

List proposed alternative monitor technical specifications, proposed operating limits and how limits will be derived (e.g., lowest 1-hour average during compliance runs), averaging times, and proposed corrective actions for exceedances.

Assemble quality assurance and data handling procedures (calibration gas specs, calibration frequency, data averaging and recordkeeping, procedures for out-of-control data) to include in the Administrator approval request.

Confirm timing requirements: prepare to submit the alternate monitoring application by the notification of performance test (or as allowed by the subpart) and be prepared to retain prior monitoring until approval is granted.
Identify the exact CFR citations and paragraph references you will rely on in the request (e.g., 40 CFR 63.453(m),(n); 40 CFR 63.864(e)(13)–(14); 40 CFR 63.1573(f); 40 CFR 63.1350(o),(p)).

judge_text: {"score": 2, "reason": "EPA Notes state the alternative monitoring is approved only under specific conditions (partial approval). Our Answer includes the key regulatory criteria reflecting conditional approval: requirement to obtain prior Administrator approval, required submittal content and data (performance-test data, rationale, operating limits, QA/QC, site‑specific monitoring plan), and timing requirements for the request across the cited subparts (63.453, 63.864, 63.1573, 63.1350). These capture the EPA’s stated reasons for conditional approval."}

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator of an existing affected source is unable to comply with a relevant section 112(d) standard and needs additional time for installation of controls, then the owner or operator may request up to a 1-year extension of the compliance date by submitting a written request to the Administrator (or an authorized State)

If a request for an extension arises after the 120-day prior-to-compliance-date deadline due to circumstances beyond the owner's or operator's reasonable control and is submitted before the applicable compliance date, then the request may still be submitted and will stay applicability until granted or denied

If the Administrator (or State) grants an extension, then the extension will be in writing and must identify affected sources, specify the termination date, specify dates for steps toward compliance, and specify other applicable requirements or conditions to assure installation and protection of health

If a relevant subpart requires a continuous opacity monitoring system (COMS) to determine compliance with an opacity emission standard, then compliance shall be determined using COMS data and the COMS must meet Performance Specification 1, be properly maintained and performance-evaluated, and the owner/operator must furnish COMS monitoring data in required reports

candidates.title: Lime Manufacturing (Subpart AAAAA)

criteria.criterion: If you operate an existing affected lime manufacturing source, then your compliance date for the applicable PM emission limitations and performance tests is as specified in §63.7083 (e.g., existing sources by January 5, 2007, unless modified by later paragraphs or amendments)

If you are required to monitor an add-on air pollution control device with a COMS, then you must install the COMS at the outlet of the control device and install, maintain, calibrate, and operate it as required by PS-1 and the General Provisions

If you operate an existing lime kiln and any of the conditions in paragraphs (f)(1) or (f)(3) of §63.7121 exist (positive-pressure fabric filter with multiple stacks; control device exhausts through a monovent; or installation of a PS-1 COMS is infeasible), then you may perform EPA Method 9 visual opacity (VE) measurements in lieu of installing a COMS or PM detector

If you install, operate, and maintain CPMS/COMS or other monitoring systems, then you must follow the OM&M plan and CPMS/COMS operation/maintenance/performance-evaluation requirements in §63.7113 and the OM&M plan requirements in §63.7100(d)

candidates.title: Subpart MM (Monitoring requirements for kraft/soda recovery furnaces and lime kilns)

criteria.criterion: If your lime kiln is equipped with an electrostatic precipitator (ESP), then you must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate a COMS in accordance with PS-1, §§63.6(h) and 63.8, and the sampling/averaging cycles specified in §63.864(d) and paragraphs (d)(3) and (d)(4)

If, after the compliance date, the COMS shows an average of ten consecutive 6-minute averages greater than 20 percent opacity for a new or existing lime kiln equipped with an ESP, then corrective action is required under the monitoring/ongoing compliance provisions

checklist: Is the affected kiln a new source or an existing source (record startup/commencement dates) so you can identify the correct compliance date per 40 CFR 63.7083?
What is the specific compliance date that applies to your facility under 40 CFR 63.7083 (identify which paragraph (a)-(h) applies)?
Are the kilns equipped with an ESP, fabric filter, wet scrubber, or other add-on control device (identify control device type per kiln)?
Do you currently have a COMS installed on each kiln exhaust, and if so, what is the COMS installation date and does it meet PS-1?

If you do not have a COMS, is installation technically feasible at the COMS outlet location, or do any feasibility exceptions in 40 CFR 63.7121(f)(1)–(3) apply (positive-pressure FF with multiple stacks, monovent, or infeasibility)?
Is the COMS requirement triggered by an add-on control device per Subpart AAAAA §63.7113(g) or by Subpart MM §63.864(d) (confirm which subpart controls your unit)?
Has your source prepared or submitted the required OM&M plan and SSMP called for in 40 CFR 63.7100(d) and 63.6(e)(3)?
Is the need for additional time specifically for installation of controls/COMS (document why the extension is needed and whether it is necessary for installation)?
Who will grant the extension (EPA Administrator or State with approved Part 70 program)? Verify whether your State has delegated authority to grant extensions.

Did you submit (or will you submit) the extension request within the applicable deadline: for Subpart A usually no later than 120 days before the compliance date (or later if the need arose after that date under §63.6(i)(4)(i)(C)); for Subpart YY, no later than 12 months (or 18 months if including emission points in an emissions average) before the compliance date?

Does your planned extension request include the required contents: description of controls to be installed, a compliance schedule with milestone dates (initiation of on-site construction, completion, final compliance), interim control steps/milestones, and whether you request extension of other requirements (per 40 CFR 63.6(i)(6) and 63.1112(a)(6))?

If you plan to rely on a VE (Method 9) alternative under §63.7121(f), can you document compliance with its specific conditions and observer training (Method 22 training requirement referenced in §63.7121(e))?

candidates.title: Phosphate Fertilizer Production Plants

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a phosphate fertilizer production plant that is a major source, then the facility is subject to Subpart BB requirements for affected sources at the plant.

If emissions or operations at the plant include phosphate fertilizer process lines, granular triple superphosphate process lines, or granular triple superphosphate storage buildings (or an evaporative cooling tower), then those affected sources are covered by this subpart.

If you use a continuous monitoring system (CMS) to demonstrate compliance, then you must install, calibrate, maintain and operate it according to a site-specific monitoring plan and the CMS must determine and permanently record mass flow of phosphorus-bearing material fed to the process.

If you use a CMS to demonstrate compliance, then you must develop and keep on-site a site-specific monitoring plan that includes a schedule for conducting initial and subsequent performance evaluations and submit it to the Administrator upon request at least 60 days before the initial performance evaluation.

If a performance test is required, then you must conduct the initial performance test within 180 days of the applicable compliance date and thereafter conduct a performance test once per calendar year.

If you use a CMS, then you must conduct a CMS performance evaluation as specified in § 63.8(e) in accordance with your site-specific monitoring plan and record the bag leak detection system sensitivity, range, averaging period, and alarm set points during the performance test (for fabric filters).

If you rely on control-device operating-parameter limits established from the most recent performance test, then except as provided for absorbers you must determine the operating parameter values as the arithmetic average of measurements recorded during the three test runs of the most recent performance test.

candidates.title: General Provisions (applicable portions as identified in Appendix A to Subpart BB)

criteria.criterion: If you propose an alternative monitoring method or modification to monitoring procedures (including timing of performance evaluations), then you must follow the general provisions for alternative monitoring in § 63.8(f) and the CMS performance evaluation procedures in § 63.8(e).

If you elect to change site-specific monitoring plan elements, then the general recordkeeping and reporting requirements in § 63.10 and notifications in § 63.9 (as made applicable to Subpart BB by Appendix A) apply.

candidates.title: Extension of compliance, waivers, and alternatives (use of alternative monitoring methods)

criteria.criterion: If you wish to use an alternative monitoring method (including alternatives to monitoring timing or performance-evaluation timing) to demonstrate compliance, then you must submit a written application to the Administrator and include a description of the alternative and, if required, a performance evaluation test plan.

If the alternative monitoring method is to be used to demonstrate compliance with a relevant standard, then the application must be submitted not later than with the site-specific test plan or at least 60 days before the performance evaluation is scheduled to begin.

If you submit a request to use an alternative monitoring method, then the Administrator will notify you of approval or intention to deny within 30 days after receipt of the original request and within 30 days after receipt of any supplementary information.

checklist: Determine whether the plant is a major source as defined in 40 CFR 63.2 (if not a major source, Subpart BB does not apply per 40 CFR 63.620(c)).

Identify which units are 'phosphate fertilizer process lines' or 'granular triple superphosphate process lines' or 'storage buildings' per 40 CFR 63.621 to confirm which affected sources would be covered.
Confirm whether you currently use a CMS or other CPMS to demonstrate compliance for the scrubbers/absorbers and whether that CMS is specified in your site-specific monitoring plan.

Locate and review the existing site-specific monitoring plan required by 40 CFR 63.628(c) to see whether it (a) includes the schedule for initial and subsequent performance evaluations and (b) limits timing of performance evaluations to coincide with performance tests.

Verify the dates of the last performance tests and CMS performance evaluations and the planned dates for the next performance test (performance tests are required once per calendar year per 40 CFR 63.626(b)).

Prepare the alternative monitoring application package (description of alternative timing, justification, and performance-evaluation test plan) and confirm it will be submitted at least 60 days before the performance evaluation if it will be used to demonstrate compliance (40 CFR 63.1112(c)(4)(i)).

Confirm you can keep required records and submit required notifications/reports under 40 CFR 63.9 and 63.10 if the alternative is implemented (see Appendix A applicability and Subpart BB recordkeeping/reporting requirements).

If the scrubber is an absorber and you monitor absorber parameters (e.g., pressure drop, liquid-to-gas ratio), confirm how allowable ranges were established (three-run average or alternative per 40 CFR 63.625(d)(1)(i) and (ii)).
Ensure site-specific monitoring plan revisions (if any) will be kept on-site and prior versions retained for 5 years as required by 40 CFR 63.628(c)(3).
Be prepared for the Administrator's 30-day review window for alternative-monitoring requests and for possible additional information requests per 40 CFR 63.1112(c)(5)(i).

candidates.title: Phosphate fertilizer production (Subpart BB)

criteria.criterion: If the facility operates a phosphate fertilizer process line (e.g., diammonium and/or monoammonium phosphate process line) or a granular triple superphosphate process line or storage building, then the facility is subject to the monitoring and operating requirements of Subpart BB.

If an affected phosphate fertilizer process line is subject to this subpart, then you must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate a continuous monitoring system (CMS) that has an accuracy of ±5 percent over its operating range and that determines and permanently records the mass flow of phosphorus-bearing material fed to the process and maintain a daily record of equivalent P2O5 feed.

If you use a control device to comply with the emission limits in Tables 1 or 2 of this subpart, then you must install a continuous parameter monitoring system (CPMS) and monitor the applicable control parameters and meet the CPMS requirements specified in § 63.625(d).

candidates.title: Wet-process phosphoric acid and related sources (Subpart AA)

criteria.criterion: If the facility operates a wet-process phosphoric acid process line or a superphosphoric acid process line, then Subpart AA requires installation, calibration, maintenance, and operation of a CMS with ±5 percent accuracy to determine and permanently record the mass flow of phosphorus-bearing feed and daily recording of equivalent P2O5 feed.

If you must compute equivalent P2O5 feed for performance testing under this subpart, then you must determine the mass flow of phosphorus-bearing feed using the measurement system described in § 63.605(a) and determine P2O5 content using the specified analytical methods listed in § 63.606(f)(3).

candidates.title: General provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If an affected source is subject to Subpart BB (or AA as applicable), then the general provisions in Subpart A apply to that source as specified in § 63.628(a) and in Appendix A to Subpart BB.

If you wish to use an alternative monitoring procedure (minor, intermediate, or major change) instead of the CMS or monitoring method specified in the relevant standard, then you must apply to the Administrator for approval following the procedures in § 63.8(f) (including the application contents and timing in § 63.8(f)(4)).

checklist: Determine whether you operate any phosphate fertilizer process lines (diammonium and/or monoammonium phosphate) or granular triple superphosphate process lines or storage buildings (definitions in 40 CFR 63.621).
Determine whether you operate any wet-process phosphoric acid or superphosphoric acid process lines covered by Subpart AA (see 40 CFR 63.605).

Confirm whether your existing magnetic flow meters are the CMS (i.e., used to determine and permanently record mass flow of phosphorus-bearing feed) and whether they meet the CMS accuracy requirement of ±5% over the operating range (40 CFR 63.625(a)(1) / 63.605(a)(1)).

Document current daily recordkeeping practice for equivalent P2O5 feed and the method used to calculate it (mass flow measurement system and P2O5 assay method) as described in 40 CFR 63.625(a)(2) / 63.605(a)(2) and 63.626(f)(3) / 63.606(f)(3).

If magnetic flow meters experience scaling or signal interference, collect evidence (error rates, calibration records, drift, QA records) showing inaccuracy or impracticality to use the required CMS so you can justify an alternative monitoring request under 40 CFR 63.8(f).

Prepare a draft site-specific monitoring plan per § 63.628(c) that locates the CMS measurement point, specifies performance and equipment specs, QA/QC procedures, calibration and acceptance criteria, and performance-evaluation schedule to support either the existing CMS or an alternative method.

If you plan to request an alternative monitoring procedure, assemble the application materials required by § 63.8(f)(4)(ii) (description addressing the four elements of monitoring and a performance evaluation test plan) and schedule submittal timing (≥60 days before a performance evaluation if the alternative would serve as the performance test method).

If you use control devices to meet emission limits, identify which control devices are used, the operating parameters to be monitored, and whether CPMS installation is required per § 63.625(d) (or § 63.605(d) for Subpart AA).

Verify which analytical methods you use or will use to determine P2O5 content (Association of Florida Phosphate Chemists methods or AOAC methods listed in §§ 63.626(f)(3)(ii) / 63.606(f)(3)(ii)/(g)(7)), and ensure sample frequency and documentation meet the referenced methods.

Check whether enforcement/approval authority for alternative monitoring is retained by EPA (Administrator) per § 63.632(b)(3) and identify the correct agency to which to submit any alternative-monitoring request.
